Independent check: Series combination: air part C1 = ε0A/(d/2) = 2C0, dielectric part C2 = Kε0A/(d/2) = 8C0. Equivalent C = 8C0/5, so Q = 8C0V/5. Voltage across slab V2 = Q/C2 = V/5. Energy in slab = ½C2V2² = ½·8C0·(V/5)² = (4/25)C0V². Cross-checked via energy density ½Kε0E² with E_slab = 2V/(5d): same result.
distractor_notes:
Option A encodes the mistake of neglecting the thickness factor of 2, taking $C_1 = K C_0 = 4C_0$ and $C_2 = C_0$, which gives $U_1 = \frac{1}{2}(4C_0)(V/5)^2 = \frac{2}{25}C_0 V^2$.
Option C encodes forgetting the factor of $1/2$ in the formula for stored energy, calculating $U = C_1 V_1^2 = 8C_0(V/5)^2 = \frac{8}{25}C_0 V^2$.
Option D encodes calculating the energy stored in the air gap ($U_2 = \frac{1}{2} C_2 V_2^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2C_0)(4V/5)^2 = \frac{16}{25}C_0 V^2$) instead of the dielectric slab.

brief: A wire stretched by known amount with a hanging mass; use Y = stress/strain to find elongation or the maximum load for a given breaking stress.
stem: A wire of length $2\ \text{m}$ stretches by $1\ \text{mm}$ when a mass of $5\ \text{kg}$ is suspended from it. The Young's modulus and breaking stress of the wire are $2 \times 10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2}$ and $4 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}$, respectively. The maximum mass that can be suspended from the wire without breaking it is (take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$)
working:
Step 1: Calculate the longitudinal strain under the initial load:
$$\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}}{2\ \text{m}} = 5 \times 10^{-4}$$

Step 2: Calculate the tensile stress $\sigma_1$ produced by the mass $m_1 = 5\ \text{kg}$:
$$\sigma_1 = Y \varepsilon = (2 \times 10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2}) \times (5 \times 10^{-4}) = 1.0 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}$$

Step 3: Relate stress to the suspended mass. Since stress is directly proportional to the applied load ($\sigma = \dfrac{m g}{A}$):
$$\dfrac{M_{\max}}{m_1} = \dfrac{\sigma_{\text{break}}}{\sigma_1}$$
$$M_{\max} = 5\ \text{kg} \times \dfrac{4 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}}{1.0 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}} = 5 \times 4 = 20\ \text{kg}$$

Independent check: Area from stretch data: A = FL/(YΔL) = (50×2)/(2×10¹¹×10⁻³) = 5×10⁻⁷ m². Breaking force = σA = 4×10⁸×5×10⁻⁷ = 200 N ⇒ M = 200/10 = 20 kg.
distractor_notes: Option A encodes forgetting the original length $L = 2\ \text{m}$ when computing strain (taking strain as $\Delta L = 10^{-3}$), which doubles $\sigma_1$ to $2 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}$ and yields $M = 10\ \text{kg}$. Option B encodes computing the additional mass that can be added ($20 - 5 = 15\ \text{kg}$) instead of the total maximum mass. Option D encodes misinterpreting the calculated $20\ \text{kg}$ as the additional mass and adding it to the initial $5\ \text{kg}$ to get $25\ \text{kg}$.

brief: Two long parallel wires carrying given currents; find magnetic field (magnitude and direction) at a point on a line between or outside them.
stem: Two long, straight parallel wires separated by a distance of $20\ \text{cm}$ carry currents of $4\ \text{A}$ and $6\ \text{A}$ in opposite directions. The magnitude of the net magnetic field at the midpoint between the two wires is:
working:
The magnetic field at a distance $r$ from a long straight wire carrying current $I$ is given by:
$$B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$

The midpoint lies at a distance:
$$r = \dfrac{d}{2} = \dfrac{20\ \text{cm}}{2} = 10\ \text{cm} = 0.1\ \text{m}$$

Calculating the magnitude of the field from each wire:
$$B_1 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_1}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{(2\times 10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m A}^{-1})(4\ \text{A})}{0.1\ \text{m}} = 8\times 10^{-6}\ \text{T} = 8\ \mu\text{T}$$
$$B_2 = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_2}{2\pi r} = \dfrac{(2\times 10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m A}^{-1})(6\ \text{A})}{0.1\ \text{m}} = 12\times 10^{-6}\ \text{T} = 12\ \mu\text{T}$$

By the right-hand grip rule, because the currents flow in opposite directions, their magnetic field vectors at any point between the wires point in the same direction (perpendicular to the plane of the wires).

Therefore, the net field magnitude is the sum of the two fields:
$$B_{\text{net}} = B_1 + B_2 = 8\ \mu\text{T} + 12\ \mu\text{T} = 20\ \mu\text{T}$$

Independent check: At midpoint r = 0.1 m from each wire. Opposite currents make the two fields add at the midpoint: B = (μ0/2π)(I1+I2)/r = 2×10⁻⁷ × 10 / 0.1 = 2×10⁻⁵ T = 20 μT.
distractor_notes:
Option A ($4\ \mu\text{T}$): Subtraction mistake ($12 - 8$), assuming opposite currents produce canceling fields at the center.
Option B ($10\ \mu\text{T}$): Used the total separation $d = 20\ \text{cm}$ instead of the midpoint distance $r = 10\ \text{cm}$.
Option D ($40\ \mu\text{T}$): Missed the factor of 2 in the denominator of the straight-wire field formula ($B = \mu_0 I / (\pi r)$).

brief: A nucleus undergoes alpha decay; compute energy released using given binding energies of parent, daughter and alpha, then find kinetic energy of the alpha particle.
stem: A stationary nucleus $^{220}\text{X}$ undergoes $\alpha$-decay into $^{216}\text{Y}$. The total binding energies of $^{220}\text{X}$, $^{216}\text{Y}$, and the $\alpha$-particle are $1700.0\text{ MeV}$, $1677.2\text{ MeV}$, and $28.3\text{ MeV}$, respectively. The kinetic energy of the emitted $\alpha$-particle is
working:
The nuclear disintegration reaction is:
$${}^{220}\text{X} \to {}^{216}\text{Y} + {}^4_2\text{He}$$

The total energy released ($Q$-value) in terms of binding energy (BE) is:
$$Q = \text{BE}({}^{216}\text{Y}) + \text{BE}(\alpha) - \text{BE}({}^{220}\text{X})$$
$$Q = 1677.2\text{ MeV} + 28.3\text{ MeV} - 1700.0\text{ MeV} = 5.5\text{ MeV}$$

Since the parent nucleus is initially at rest, by conservation of linear momentum:
$$p_\alpha = p_Y = p$$

The kinetic energy of each fragment is $K = \dfrac{p^2}{2m}$. Therefore:
$$Q = K_\alpha + K_Y = K_\alpha \left(1 + \dfrac{m_\alpha}{m_Y}\right) = K_\alpha \left(\dfrac{m_Y + m_\alpha}{m_Y}\right)$$

Using masses proportional to mass numbers ($m_Y \approx 216\text{ u}$, $m_\alpha \approx 4\text{ u}$):
$$K_\alpha = \left(\dfrac{A - 4}{A}\right) Q = \left(\dfrac{216}{220}\right) \times 5.5\text{ MeV} = \dfrac{54}{55} \times 5.5\text{ MeV} = 5.4\text{ MeV}$$

Independent check: Q = BE(Y) + BE(α) − BE(X) = 1677.2 + 28.3 − 1700.0 = 5.5 MeV. Momentum conservation splits Q inversely with masses: KE_α = Q·(216/220) = 5.4 MeV (recoil takes 0.1 MeV).
distractor_notes:
A: Uses $K_\alpha = \dfrac{m_\alpha}{m_Y + m_\alpha} Q = \dfrac{4}{220} \times 5.5 = 0.1\text{ MeV}$, which is the kinetic energy of the recoiling daughter nucleus.
B: Uses the elastic collision factor $\dfrac{m_Y - m_\alpha}{m_Y + m_\alpha} Q = \dfrac{212}{220} \times 5.5 = 5.3\text{ MeV}$.
D: Ignores the recoil of the daughter nucleus and assumes the $\alpha$-particle carries all the decay energy ($K_\alpha = Q = 5.5\text{ MeV}$).

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
brief: Electron accelerated through a potential difference; find how its de Broglie wavelength changes when the accelerating voltage is changed by a factor.
stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through a potential difference $V$, having a de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$. If the accelerating potential is increased to $4V$, its new de Broglie wavelength is
working:
The de Broglie wavelength $\lambda$ of a charged particle accelerated from rest through a potential difference $V$ is given by:
$$\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p} = \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2m q V}}$$
For an electron, $h$, $m$, and $q$ are constant, which gives the proportionality:
$$\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{V}}$$
When the potential difference is increased from $V$ to $4V$, the new wavelength $\lambda'$ is:
$$\lambda' = \lambda \sqrt{\dfrac{V}{4V}} = \dfrac{\lambda}{2}$$

Independent check: λ = h/√(2meV), so λ ∝ 1/√V. Increasing V to 4V gives λ' = λ/√4 = λ/2 (numeric check: ratio = 0.5). Non-relativistic assumption is standard for such problems.
distractor_notes:
$\dfrac{\lambda}{4}$: Forgot the square root in the kinetic energy-momentum relation, assuming $\lambda \propto \dfrac{1}{V}$.
$2\lambda$: Inverted the proportionality, assuming $\lambda \propto \sqrt{V}$.
$4\lambda$: Inverted the proportionality and missed the square root, assuming $\lambda \propto V$.

brief: Unpolarized light reflected off a glass surface; use Brewster's law to identify the angle at which reflected light becomes polarized, given refractive index.
stem: An unpolarized light beam in air is incident on the surface of a glass plate of refractive index $\mu = \sqrt{3}$. The angle of incidence at which the reflected light is completely plane-polarized is:
working:
According to Brewster's law, when light is incident at Brewster's angle ($i_p$), the reflected beam is completely polarized:
$$\tan i_p = \mu$$
Given $\mu = \sqrt{3}$:
$$\tan i_p = \sqrt{3} \implies i_p = 60^\circ$$

Independent check: Reflected light is fully plane-polarized at Brewster's angle: tan θ_B = μ = √3, so θ_B = 60°.
distractor_notes:
$30^\circ$ corresponds to the angle of refraction ($r = 90^\circ - i_p$) or confusing $\tan 30^\circ$ with $\tan 60^\circ$.
$45^\circ$ comes from assuming $\mu = 1$ in Brewster's condition.
$90^\circ$ is the angle between the reflected ray and the refracted ray at polarization, not the angle of incidence.

brief: A thermometer reads a temperature on one scale; convert it to another scale and pick the correct numerical value.
stem: A thermometer immersed in a water bath records a temperature of $45^\circ\text{C}$. What is the corresponding reading on the Fahrenheit scale?
working:
The relationship between the Celsius scale ($T_C$) and the Fahrenheit scale ($T_F$) is given by:
$$T_F = \dfrac{9}{5}T_C + 32$$

Substitute $T_C = 45^\circ\text{C}$:
$$T_F = \left(\dfrac{9}{5} \times 45\right) + 32 = 81 + 32 = 113^\circ\text{F}$$

Independent check: F = (9/5)C + 32 = (9/5)(45) + 32 = 81 + 32 = 113°F.
distractor_notes:
$49^\circ\text{F}$: sign error on the constant offset, calculating $\frac{9}{5}T_C - 32 = 81 - 32$.
$57^\circ\text{F}$: inverted conversion ratio, using $\frac{5}{9}T_C + 32 = 25 + 32$.
$81^\circ\text{F}$: omitted the additive offset $+32$, calculating only $\frac{9}{5}T_C = 81$.

brief: Circuit diagram of two-input gates (NAND/NOR/...) combined; determine the Boolean output for given inputs and name the equivalent gate.
stem: In the logic circuit shown in the figure, two inputs $A$ and $B$ are connected to a combination of gates to yield an output $Y$. This circuit is equivalent to a single:
working:
Let the two inputs be $A$ and $B$.

1. The upper gate is a two-input NOR gate. Its output $P$ is given by:
$$P = \overline{A + B}$$

2. The lower gate is a two-input NAND gate. Its output $Q$ is given by:
$$Q = \overline{A \cdot B}$$

3. The final gate is a two-input NOR gate with inputs $P$ and $Q$. The final output $Y$ is:
$$Y = \overline{P + Q} = \overline{\overline{A + B} + \overline{A \cdot B}}$$

Applying De Morgan's theorem ($\overline{X + Z} = \bar{X} \cdot \bar{Z}$):
$$Y = \overline{\overline{A + B}} \cdot \overline{\overline{A \cdot B}} = (A + B) \cdot (A \cdot B)$$

Expanding the Boolean product:
$$Y = A \cdot (A \cdot B) + B \cdot (A \cdot B) = A \cdot B + A \cdot B = A \cdot B$$

Alternatively, testing the input combinations via a truth table:
- For $A = 0, B = 0$: $P = 1, Q = 1 \implies Y = \overline{1 + 1} = 0$
- For $A = 0, B = 1$: $P = 0, Q = 1 \implies Y = \overline{0 + 1} = 0$
- For $A = 1, B = 0$: $P = 0, Q = 1 \implies Y = \overline{0 + 1} = 0$
- For $A = 1, B = 1$: $P = 0, Q = 0 \implies Y = \overline{0 + 0} = 1$

The output $Y = 1$ only when both $A = 1$ and $B = 1$. Therefore, the circuit functions as an AND gate.

Independent check: Intended circuit: NOR(A,B) and NAND(A,B) feed a final NOR. Y = [(A+B)' + (AB)']' = (A+B)·(AB) = AB. Truth-table check confirms Y = A AND B for all inputs.
distractor_notes:
Option A (OR gate): Results from erroneously simplifying $(A + B)(AB)$ as $A + B$ instead of $AB$.
Option C (NAND gate): Results from omitting the output inversion bubble of the final NOR gate, evaluating $P + Q = \overline{A+B} + \overline{AB} = \overline{AB}$.
Option D (NOR gate): Results from incorrectly applying De Morgan's theorem as $\overline{P + Q} = P \cdot Q = \overline{A+B} \cdot \overline{AB} = \overline{A+B}$.
notes: figure check: Input labels A and B are missing; the left-side terminal dots are unlabeled.; Output label Y is missing.; The second (lower) input of the upper NOR gate and the second (lower) input of the NAND gate are drawn as short floating stubs with no wire or connection.; The inputs of the third NOR gate are drawn as short floating stubs; they are not wired to the outputs of the upper NOR gate and the NAND gate, so the circuit is not a closed connection and the outputs of the first two gates go nowhere.

brief: Circuit of a cell with a resistor across which a voltmeter of given resistance is connected; find the voltmeter reading and the error caused by its finite resistance.
stem: In the circuit shown in the figure, a voltmeter of resistance $60\ \Omega$ is connected across a $15\ \Omega$ resistor. The cell has an emf of $30\ \text{V}$ and an internal resistance of $3\ \Omega$. The reading of the voltmeter and the absolute error caused by its finite resistance are, respectively:
working:
1. True potential difference across $R = 15\ \Omega$ without the voltmeter:
The current in the unloaded circuit is:
$$I_0 = \dfrac{E}{R + r} = \dfrac{30}{15 + 3} = \dfrac{5}{3}\ \text{A}$$
The true potential difference is:
$$V_0 = I_0 R = \left(\dfrac{5}{3}\right) \times 15 = 25\ \text{V}$$

2. Potential difference with the voltmeter connected:
The parallel equivalent resistance of the resistor and the voltmeter is:
$$R_p = \dfrac{R \cdot R_V}{R + R_V} = \dfrac{15 \times 60}{15 + 60} = \dfrac{900}{75} = 12\ \Omega$$
The total equivalent resistance of the circuit becomes:
$$R_{\text{eq}} = R_p + r = 12 + 3 = 15\ \Omega$$
The current drawn from the cell is:
$$I = \dfrac{E}{R_{\text{eq}}} = \dfrac{30}{15} = 2\ \text{A}$$
The voltmeter reading is the potential difference across $R_p$:
$$V = I R_p = 2 \times 12 = 24\ \text{V}$$

3. Absolute error in measurement:
$$\Delta V = |V_0 - V| = |25 - 24| = 1\ \text{V}$$

Thus, the reading is $24\ \text{V}$ and the error is $1\ \text{V}$.

Independent check: With voltmeter: 15||60 = 12 Ω; total = 12+3 = 15 Ω; reading = 30×12/15 = 24 V. Ideal (no voltmeter): V = 30×15/18 = 25 V. Absolute error = 25−24 = 1 V.
distractor_notes:
Option A assumes that the total circuit current remains unchanged at $5/3\ \text{A}$ after connecting the voltmeter, yielding $V = (5/3) \times 12 = 20\ \text{V}$ and an error of $25 - 20 = 5\ \text{V}$.
Option C correctly finds the voltmeter reading of $24\ \text{V}$ but computes the error relative to the cell's EMF ($30 - 24 = 6\ \text{V}$) rather than the true resistor potential difference.
Option D assumes an ideal voltmeter ($R_V \to \infty$), resulting in the unloaded reading of $25\ \text{V}$ and zero error.

brief: For an EM wave in vacuum, compare electric and magnetic energy densities and relate peak field values using E = cB; pick the correct statement.
stem: For a plane electromagnetic wave propagating in vacuum, let $\langle u_E \rangle$ and $\langle u_B \rangle$ denote the time-averaged energy densities of the electric and magnetic fields, respectively. If $E_0$ and $B_0$ are the peak amplitudes of the electric and magnetic fields, which of the following is correct?
options: $\dfrac{\langle u_E \rangle}{\langle u_B \rangle} = c^2$ and $E_0 = c B_0$
working:
1. In an electromagnetic wave propagating in vacuum, the relation between the amplitudes of the electric and magnetic fields is given by:
$$E_0 = c B_0$$
where $c = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}$ is the speed of light in vacuum.

2. The time-averaged electric energy density is:
$$\langle u_E \rangle = \dfrac{1}{4}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2$$
and the time-averaged magnetic energy density is:
$$\langle u_B \rangle = \dfrac{B_0^2}{4\mu_0}$$

3. Taking their ratio:
$$\dfrac{\langle u_E \rangle}{\langle u_B \rangle} = \dfrac{\frac{1}{4}\varepsilon_0 E_0^2}{\frac{1}{4\mu_0}B_0^2} = \varepsilon_0 \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{E_0}{B_0}\right)^2$$
Substituting $E_0 / B_0 = c$ and $c^2 = \dfrac{1}{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}$:
$$\dfrac{\langle u_E \rangle}{\langle u_B \rangle} = \varepsilon_0 \mu_0 c^2 = \varepsilon_0 \mu_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}\right) = 1$$

Thus, $\dfrac{\langle u_E \rangle}{\langle u_B \rangle} = 1$ and $E_0 = c B_0$.

Independent check: ⟨u_E⟩ = ¼ε₀E₀², ⟨u_B⟩ = B₀²/(4μ₀). For a vacuum plane wave E₀ = cB₀ with c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀), so ⟨u_E⟩/⟨u_B⟩ = ε₀μ₀c² = 1. Numeric check confirms ratio ≈ 1 and E₀ = cB₀.
distractor_notes:
Option A confuses the ratio of electric-to-magnetic energy density with the ratio of electric-to-total energy density, which is 1/2.
Option C correctly identifies equal energy densities but inverts the relation between peak fields ($B_0 = cE_0$ instead of $E_0 = cB_0$).
Option D incorrectly assumes the energy density ratio depends solely on $(E_0/B_0)^2 = c^2$, ignoring the dimensional constants $\varepsilon_0$ and $\mu_0$.

brief: Average speed question: a body covers two equal distances at speeds v1 and v2; compare its average speed with the arithmetic mean of the speeds.
stem: A particle travels the first half of a total distance with a constant speed $v_1$ and the second half with a constant speed $v_2$, where $v_1 \neq v_2$. If $v$ is its average speed for the whole journey, which of the following relations is correct?
working:
Let the total distance be $2d$. The time taken to cover the first half is $t_1 = \dfrac{d}{v_1}$, and for the second half is $t_2 = \dfrac{d}{v_2}$.

The average speed is given by:
$$v = \dfrac{\text{Total distance}}{\text{Total time}} = \dfrac{2d}{\dfrac{d}{v_1} + \dfrac{d}{v_2}} = \dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$$

Comparing $v$ with the arithmetic mean $v_{\text{am}} = \dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{2}$:
$$v_{\text{am}} - v = \dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{2} - \dfrac{2v_1v_2}{v_1 + v_2} = \dfrac{(v_1 + v_2)^2 - 4v_1v_2}{2(v_1 + v_2)} = \dfrac{(v_1 - v_2)^2}{2(v_1 + v_2)}$$

Since $v_1 \neq v_2$, $(v_1 - v_2)^2 > 0$ and $2(v_1 + v_2) > 0$. Thus,
$$v_{\text{am}} - v > 0 \implies v < \dfrac{v_1 + v_2}{2}$$

(Physically, the body spends more time travelling at the lower speed, so the time-averaged speed is weighted closer to the smaller value, making it strictly less than the arithmetic mean.)

Independent check: For equal half-distances d each: total time = d/v1 + d/v2, so v = 2d/(d/v1+d/v2) = 2v1v2/(v1+v2), the harmonic mean. For v1≠v2, HM < GM < AM, so v < (v1+v2)/2 (option A) and v ≠ √(v1v2). Numeric check v1=1, v2=3: v=1.5 < AM=2, GM≈1.732.
distractor_notes:
Option B comes from the naive misconception that average speed is always the simple arithmetic mean of the two speeds, ignoring that the time intervals are unequal.
Option C comes from reversing the inequality or confusing the direction of the AM-HM inequality.
Option D comes from assuming the average speed over equal distances is given by the geometric mean.

brief: Circuit with ideal diodes in series/parallel with resistors; determine which diodes conduct and compute the current through a specified branch.
stem: In the circuit shown in the figure, assuming the diodes $D_1$ and $D_2$ to be ideal, the current flowing through diode $D_1$ is
working:
1. Determine the biasing of each diode:
The positive terminal of the $18\ \text{V}$ battery is connected to the left junction $J_1$, and the negative terminal connects via the $2\ \Omega$ resistor to the right junction $J_2$. Thus, $V_{J_1} > V_{J_2}$.
- Diode $D_1$ has its anode connected toward $J_1$ and cathode toward $J_2$, so it is forward-biased and acts as a closed switch.
- Diode $D_2$ has its cathode connected toward $J_1$ and anode toward $J_2$, so it is reverse-biased and acts as an open circuit ($I_{D_2} = 0$).

2. Find the equivalent resistance of the parallel combination:
Only the top branch ($6\ \Omega$) and the bottom branch ($12\ \Omega$) conduct.
$$R_p = \dfrac{6 \times 12}{6 + 12} = 4\ \Omega$$

3. Calculate the total circuit resistance and total current:
$$R_{\text{total}} = R_p + 2\ \Omega = 4 + 2 = 6\ \Omega$$
$$I_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{18\ \text{V}}{6\ \Omega} = 3\ \text{A}$$

4. Calculate the current through diode $D_1$:
The voltage drop across the parallel section is:
$$V_p = I_{\text{total}} \times R_p = 3\ \text{A} \times 4\ \Omega = 12\ \text{V}$$
Therefore, the current through $D_1$ is:
$$I_{D_1} = \dfrac{V_p}{6\ \Omega} = \dfrac{12\ \text{V}}{6\ \Omega} = 2.0\ \text{A}$$

Independent check: Battery drives current from J1 to J2. D1 (pointing J1→J2) is forward biased; D2 (pointing J2→J1) is reverse biased and blocks its 12 Ω branch. Active parallel combination: 6 Ω || 12 Ω = 4 Ω, in series with 2 Ω gives 6 Ω. Total current = 18/6 = 3 A; voltage across J1–J2 = 3×4 = 12 V; current through D1 = 12/6 = 2.0 A.
distractor_notes:
Option A ($1.0\ \text{A}$) results from calculating the current through the parallel $12\ \Omega$ resistor instead of the $D_1$ branch.
Option B ($1.8\ \text{A}$) results from assuming both diodes conduct, giving $R_p = 3\ \Omega$, $I_{\text{total}} = 3.6\ \text{A}$, and $I_{D_1} = 1.8\ \text{A}$.
Option D ($3.0\ \text{A}$) is the total current supplied by the battery, forgetting the parallel branch division.

brief: Identify which carbonyl compound gives a positive Tollens' test but negative iodoform/Fehling distinction among simple options.
stem: Which of the following carbonyl compounds gives a positive Tollens' test but does not reduce Fehling's solution?
working:
1. Tollens' test: Tollens' reagent ($[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+$) is reduced to metallic silver by both aliphatic and aromatic aldehydes:
$$\text{R-CHO} + 2[\text{Ag}(\text{NH}_3)_2]^+ + 3\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{R-COO}^- + 2\text{Ag}\downarrow + 4\text{NH}_3 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$
Benzaldehyde (an aromatic aldehyde) gives a positive Tollens' test (silver mirror).

2. Fehling's test: Fehling's solution (alkaline $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ tartrate complex) is a milder oxidising agent than Tollens' reagent. It oxidises aliphatic aldehydes to carboxylate ions with the formation of a red precipitate of $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$, but it cannot oxidise aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde due to resonance stabilisation of the carbonyl group with the benzene ring.

3. Evaluating the options:
- Acetaldehyde (aliphatic aldehyde): reduces both Tollens' and Fehling's reagents.
- Acetone (ketone): does not reduce either Tollens' or Fehling's reagent.
- Benzaldehyde (aromatic aldehyde): reduces Tollens' reagent, but does not reduce Fehling's solution.
- Propanal (aliphatic aldehyde): reduces both Tollens' and Fehling's reagents.

Therefore, benzaldehyde is the correct compound.

Independent check: Tollens' reagent oxidizes all aldehydes (aliphatic and aromatic) to give a silver mirror. Fehling's solution is reduced only by aliphatic aldehydes; aromatic aldehydes like benzaldehyde do not reduce it. Acetaldehyde and propanal reduce both; acetone (ketone) reduces neither. Hence benzaldehyde: Tollens' positive, Fehling's negative.
distractor_notes:
Acetaldehyde: Mistakenly thought to be the only common aldehyde tested, but as an aliphatic aldehyde it readily reduces Fehling's solution.
Acetone: Confused because it does not reduce Fehling's solution, but being a ketone, it also gives a negative Tollens' test.
Propanal: An aliphatic aldehyde that reduces both Tollens' reagent and Fehling's solution.

brief: Among given species, identify the one with a different hybridisation/geometry than the rest (odd-one-out by shape).
stem: Among the following molecules, which one has a central atom hybridisation and molecular shape different from the other three?
working:
To determine the hybridisation and molecular shape, we find the steric number ($\text{SN}$) for the central atom of each molecule:

$$\text{SN} = (\text{number of } \sigma\text{-bonds}) + (\text{number of lone pairs})$$

1. For $\text{NF}_3$:
- Valence electrons on $\text{N} = 5$
- Forms $3$ single bonds with $\text{F}$ ($3\ \sigma$-bonds)
- Lone pairs $= \dfrac{5 - 3}{2} = 1$
- $\text{SN} = 3 + 1 = 4 \implies sp^3$ hybridisation
- Molecular shape: Trigonal pyramidal

2. For $\text{ClF}_3$:
- Valence electrons on $\text{Cl} = 7$
- Forms $3$ single bonds with $\text{F}$ ($3\ \sigma$-bonds)
- Lone pairs $= \dfrac{7 - 3}{2} = 2$
- $\text{SN} = 3 + 2 = 5 \implies sp^3d$ hybridisation
- Molecular shape: T-shaped

3. For $\text{PCl}_3$:
- Valence electrons on $\text{P} = 5$
- Forms $3$ single bonds with $\text{Cl}$ ($3\ \sigma$-bonds)
- Lone pairs $= \dfrac{5 - 3}{2} = 1$
- $\text{SN} = 3 + 1 = 4 \implies sp^3$ hybridisation
- Molecular shape: Trigonal pyramidal

4. For $\text{XeO}_3$:
- Valence electrons on $\text{Xe} = 8$
- Forms $3$ double bonds with $\text{O}$ ($3\ \sigma$-bonds, $3\ \pi$-bonds, consuming $6$ electrons)
- Lone pairs $= \dfrac{8 - 6}{2} = 1$
- $\text{SN} = 3 + 1 = 4 \implies sp^3$ hybridisation
- Molecular shape: Trigonal pyramidal

Therefore, $\text{ClF}_3$ is the odd one out with $sp^3d$ hybridisation and a T-shaped geometry, whereas the others are all $sp^3$ hybridised and trigonal pyramidal.

Independent check: NF3, PCl3, XeO3 each have 3 bond pairs + 1 lone pair → sp3, trigonal pyramidal. ClF3 has 3 bond pairs + 2 lone pairs → sp3d, T-shaped. ClF3 differs in both hybridisation and shape.
distractor_notes:
Option A (NF3): Chosen if the student incorrectly confuses NF3 with BF3, assuming zero lone pairs and sp2 trigonal planar geometry.
Option C (PCl3): Chosen if the student mistakenly assumes d-orbital involvement (expanded octet) in PCl3 by analogy with PCl5.
Option D (XeO3): Chosen if the student assumes XeO3 is trigonal planar by false analogy with SO3, neglecting the lone pair on Xe.

brief: For a gas-phase reaction with given Δn, state whether ΔH is greater than, less than or equal to ΔU and why.
stem: For a gas-phase reaction with $\Delta n_{\text{g}} = -1$ at temperature $T$, which of the following statements correctly compares $\Delta H$ and $\Delta U$?
options: $\Delta H = \Delta U$, because the reaction occurs at constant temperature
working:
The relationship between enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) and internal energy change ($\Delta U$) for a gaseous reaction is given by:
$$\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_{\text{g}}RT$$
Given that $\Delta n_{\text{g}} = -1$ and temperature $T > 0\ \text{K}$, we have:
$$\Delta n_{\text{g}}RT = -RT < 0$$
Substituting this into the equation:
$$\Delta H = \Delta U - RT$$
Since $R > 0$ and $T > 0\ \text{K}$, $RT$ is positive, which means:
$$\Delta H < \Delta U$$
Therefore, $\Delta H < \Delta U$ because $\Delta n_{\text{g}}RT < 0$.

Independent check: ΔH = ΔU + Δn_g RT. With Δn_g = −1, ΔH = ΔU − RT, and since RT > 0, ΔH < ΔU. This matches option B and its stated reason Δn_g RT < 0.
distractor_notes:
A: Encodes ignoring the negative sign of $\Delta n_{\text{g}}$, assuming $\Delta n_{\text{g}}RT > 0$ and concluding $\Delta H > \Delta U$.
C: Encodes an algebraic sign slip where the student correctly identifies $\Delta n_{\text{g}}RT < 0$ but incorrectly concludes $\Delta H > \Delta U$.
D: Encodes the misconception that for any process at constant temperature, $\Delta T = 0$ implies $\Delta H = \Delta U = 0$, confusing an isothermal physical expansion of an ideal gas with a chemical reaction.

brief: Match commonly used antiseptic chemicals (dettol, bithionol, iodine tincture) with their use.
stem:
Match the antiseptic preparations in List-I with their descriptions in List-II:

**List-I**
(P) Bithionol
(Q) Tincture of iodine
(R) Dettol

**List-II**
(1) $2\text{--}3\%$ solution of $\text{I}_2$ in an alcohol–water mixture
(2) Mixture of chloroxylenol and terpineol
(3) Substance added to soaps to impart antiseptic properties

Choose the correct match from the options given below:
working:
According to NCERT Class 12 Chemistry (Chemistry in Everyday Life):
1. Bithionol is added to soaps to impart antiseptic properties and decrease bacterial growth that causes odour (P $\rightarrow$ 3).
2. Tincture of iodine is a $2\text{--}3\%$ solution of iodine ($\text{I}_2$) in an alcohol–water mixture, used as an antiseptic on wounds (Q $\rightarrow$ 1).
3. Dettol is a widely used antiseptic consisting of a mixture of chloroxylenol and terpineol (R $\rightarrow$ 2).

Hence, the correct matching is P-3, Q-1, R-2.

Independent check: Bithionol is added to soaps for antiseptic action (P-3); tincture of iodine is a 2–3% I2 solution in alcohol–water (Q-1); Dettol is a mixture of chloroxylenol and terpineol (R-2).
distractor_notes:
Option B (P-1, Q-3, R-2): Swaps the applications of bithionol and tincture of iodine.
Option C (P-2, Q-1, R-3): Confuses bithionol with the chemical composition of Dettol and assumes Dettol is the soap additive.
Option D (P-3, Q-2, R-1): Swaps the descriptions of tincture of iodine and Dettol.

brief: Given initial and remaining concentration of a first-order reaction, count half-lives to find total time.
stem: For a first-order reaction with a half-life of $25\ \text{min}$, the time required for the reactant concentration to decrease from $0.64\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ to $0.08\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ is
working:
For a first-order reaction, the remaining concentration $[A]_t$ after $n$ half-lives is given by:
$$[A]_t = [A]_0 \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^n$$

Substitute the given values:
$$\dfrac{[A]_t}{[A]_0} = \dfrac{0.08\ \text{mol L}^{-1}}{0.64\ \text{mol L}^{-1}} = \dfrac{1}{8} = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3$$

Therefore, the number of half-lives elapsed is $n = 3$.

The total time required is:
$$t = n \times t_{1/2} = 3 \times 25\ \text{min} = 75\ \text{min}$$

Independent check: 0.64 → 0.08 is a factor of 8 = 2^3, i.e., 3 half-lives. t = 3 × 25 = 75 min (verified via t = (t½/ln2)·ln(8) = 75).
distractor_notes:
A: Corresponds to under-counting the number of half-lives as $n = 2$ ($2 \times 25 = 50\ \text{min}$).
C: Corresponds to over-counting the number of half-lives as $n = 4$ ($4 \times 25 = 100\ \text{min}$).
D: Corresponds to taking the ratio of initial to final concentration ($0.64/0.08 = 8$) directly as the number of half-lives ($8 \times 25 = 200\ \text{min}$).

brief: Ask which noble-gas fluoride does not exist / correct compositions of XeF2, XeF4, XeF6.
stem: Xenon forms several stable binary fluorides by direct reaction with elemental fluorine. Which of the following fluorides of xenon does not exist?
working:
The valence shell electronic configuration of ground-state xenon is $5s^2 5p^6$. All eight valence electrons are fully paired.

To form covalent bonds with fluorine atoms, electrons must be promoted from filled $5p$ (or $5s$) orbitals into vacant $5d$ orbitals. Each promoted electron generates two unpaired electrons. Consequently, xenon can only have an even number of unpaired electrons:
- Unpairing of 1 electron gives 2 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ oxidation state $+2$, yielding $\text{XeF}_2$.
- Unpairing of 2 electrons gives 4 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ oxidation state $+4$, yielding $\text{XeF}_4$.
- Unpairing of 3 electrons gives 6 unpaired electrons $\rightarrow$ oxidation state $+6$, yielding $\text{XeF}_6$.

Therefore, xenon forms only the three stable binary fluorides $\text{XeF}_2$, $\text{XeF}_4$, and $\text{XeF}_6$. The neutral compound $\text{XeF}_5$ would require an odd oxidation state of $+5$ with an unpaired electron, and does not exist as a stable binary fluoride.

Independent check: Known stable xenon binary fluorides are XeF2, XeF4, XeF6 (even-electron species). XeF5 would have 43 valence electrons (odd, radical) and does not exist as a stable neutral binary fluoride; only ions like XeF5+ / XeF5- are known.
distractor_notes:
Option A: $\text{XeF}_2$ is an existing, stable linear molecule prepared by heating Xe and $\text{F}_2$ in a $2:1$ ratio at $673\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ bar}$.
Option B: $\text{XeF}_4$ is an existing, stable square planar molecule prepared by heating Xe and $\text{F}_2$ in a $1:5$ ratio at $873\text{ K}$ and $7\text{ bar}$.
Option D: $\text{XeF}_6$ is an existing, stable distorted octahedral molecule prepared by heating Xe and $\text{F}_2$ in a $1:20$ ratio at $573\text{ K}$ and $60\text{--}70\text{ bar}$; students often incorrectly assume it is sterically hindered and cannot exist.

brief: Given rate constant of a zero-order reaction, find concentration remaining after a stated time (or time to reach zero).
stem: For a zero-order reaction $\text{A} \rightarrow \text{products}$, the rate constant is $4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$. If the initial concentration of $\text{A}$ is $0.60\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$, the concentration of $\text{A}$ remaining after $50\ \text{s}$ is
working:
For a zero-order reaction:
$$[\text{A}]_t = [\text{A}]_0 - kt$$
Given:
$$[\text{A}]_0 = 0.60\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
$$k = 4.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1}$$
$$t = 50\ \text{s}$$

Substitute the given values:
$$[\text{A}]_t = 0.60 - (4.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 50) = 0.60 - 0.20 = 0.40\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

Independent check: Zero-order integrated law: [A] = [A]0 − kt = 0.60 − (4.0×10⁻³)(50) = 0.60 − 0.20 = 0.40 mol L⁻¹.
distractor_notes:
Option A calculates the amount consumed ($kt = 0.20\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$) instead of the concentration remaining.
Option B assumes $50\ \text{s}$ corresponds to one half-life and halves the initial concentration ($[\text{A}]_0 / 2 = 0.30\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$).
Option D makes a sign error by adding the reacted amount to the initial concentration ($[\text{A}]_0 + kt = 0.80\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$).

brief: Use bond enthalpies of reactants and products to compute ΔH of a combustion/formation reaction via Hess-type addition.
stem:
Given the following thermochemical data:
$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\text{sub}}H^\circ[\text{C}(s)] &= 715\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} \\
\text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{H}) &= 436\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} \\
\text{B.E.}(\text{C}-\text{H}) &= 414\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} \\
\text{B.E.}(\text{C}\equiv\text{C}) &= 828\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}
\end{aligned}$$
The standard enthalpy of formation ($\Delta_f H^\circ$) of ethyne, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2(g)$, is:
working:
The standard reaction for the formation of ethyne from its elements in their standard states is:
$$2\text{C}(s) + \text{H}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_2(g)$$

Using a Hess's Law cycle, $\Delta_f H^\circ$ is given by the enthalpy required to atomize the reactants minus the bond enthalpies of the bonds formed in the product:
$$\Delta_f H^\circ = \sum \Delta H_{\text{atom}}(\text{reactants}) - \sum \text{B.E.}(\text{products})$$

1. Enthalpy required to atomize reactants:
- Sublimation of $2\text{C}(s)$: $2 \times \Delta_{\text{sub}}H^\circ[\text{C}(s)] = 2 \times 715 = 1430\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
- Dissociation of $1\text{H}_2(g)$: $1 \times \text{B.E.}(\text{H}-\text{H}) = 436\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
$$\text{Total for reactants} = 1430 + 436 = 1866\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

2. Enthalpy released upon forming bonds in $\text{C}_2\text{H}_2(g)$ (structure is $\text{H}-\text{C}\equiv\text{C}-\text{H}$):
- $1 \times (\text{C}\equiv\text{C})$ bond: $828\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
- $2 \times (\text{C}-\text{H})$ bonds: $2 \times 414 = 828\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$
$$\text{Total for products} = 828 + 828 = 1656\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

3. Enthalpy of formation:
$$\Delta_f H^\circ = 1866 - 1656 = +210\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Independent check: Formation: 2C(s) + H2(g) → C2H2(g). ΔfH = 2·ΔsubH(C) + BE(H–H) − [BE(C≡C) + 2·BE(C–H)] = 1430 + 436 − (828 + 828) = +210 kJ/mol.
distractor_notes:
Option A encodes failing to multiply the sublimation enthalpy of carbon by 2: $(715 + 436) - 1656 = -505\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
Option B encodes a sign error from applying $\Delta H = \sum \text{B.E.}(\text{products}) - \sum \text{B.E.}(\text{reactants})$.
Option D encodes counting only one $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond in ethyne: $1866 - (828 + 414) = +624\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

brief: Write the correct Ksp expression (with powers) for a sparingly soluble salt; test also solubility in common-ion solution.
stem: The solubility product of $\text{CaF}_2$ is $3.2 \times 10^{-11}$. The molar solubility of $\text{CaF}_2$ in a $0.1\ \text{M}\ \text{NaF}$ aqueous solution is:
working:
The dissolution equilibrium for $\text{CaF}_2$ is:
$$\text{CaF}_2(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{Ca}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{F}^-(aq)$$

In a $0.1\ \text{M}\ \text{NaF}$ solution, $\text{NaF}$ completely dissociates:
$$\text{NaF}(aq) \to \text{Na}^+(aq) + \text{F}^-(aq)$$

Let the molar solubility of $\text{CaF}_2$ in this solution be $s$. At equilibrium:
$$[\text{Ca}^{2+}] = s$$
$$[\text{F}^-] = 0.1 + 2s \approx 0.1\ \text{M}\quad (\text{since } s \ll 0.1)$$

The solubility product expression is:
$$K_{sp} = [\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{F}^-]^2$$
$$3.2 \times 10^{-11} = s \times (0.1)^2 = s \times 10^{-2}$$
$$s = \dfrac{3.2 \times 10^{-11}}{10^{-2}} = 3.2 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{M}$$

Independent check: CaF2 ⇌ Ca²⁺ + 2F⁻; Ksp = s[F⁻]². Common ion: [F⁻] ≈ 0.1 M (2s negligible). s = Ksp/(0.1)² = 3.2×10⁻¹¹/10⁻² = 3.2×10⁻⁹ M.
distractor_notes:
$3.2 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{M}$: Forgot the power of 2 on $[\text{F}^-]$ in the $K_{sp}$ expression, writing $K_{sp} = [\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{F}^-]$.
$8.0 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{M}$: Incorrectly multiplied the common-ion concentration by the stoichiometric factor 2, taking $[\text{F}^-] = 2 \times 0.1 = 0.2\ \text{M}$.
$2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{M}$: Ignored the common-ion effect and solved for solubility in pure water ($K_{sp} = 4s^3$).

brief: From percentage composition of C, H and O, determine empirical formula and then molecular formula from molar mass.
stem: An organic compound contains $53.3\%$ carbon, $11.1\%$ hydrogen, and $35.6\%$ oxygen by mass. If its molar mass is $90\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, its molecular formula is:
working:
1. Find relative moles of each element in a $100\ \text{g}$ sample: $n_{\text{C}} = \dfrac{53.3}{12} = 4.44$, $n_{\text{H}} = \dfrac{11.1}{1} = 11.1$, $n_{\text{O}} = \dfrac{35.6}{16} = 2.225$. 2. Divide each by the smallest number of moles ($2.225$): $\text{C} = \dfrac{4.44}{2.225} = 2$, $\text{H} = \dfrac{11.1}{2.225} = 5$, $\text{O} = \dfrac{2.225}{2.225} = 1$. The empirical formula is $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}$. 3. Empirical formula mass $= 2(12) + 5(1) + 16 = 45\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. 4. Multiplying factor $n = \dfrac{\text{Molar mass}}{\text{Empirical mass}} = \dfrac{90}{45} = 2$. 5. Molecular formula $= (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O})_2 = \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}_2$.

Independent check: Mole ratio C:H:O = 53.3/12 : 11.1/1 : 35.6/16 = 4.44 : 11.1 : 2.225 ≈ 2:5:1, so empirical formula C2H5O (mass 45). n = 90/45 = 2 → molecular formula C4H10O2. Check: C 48/90=53.3%, H 10/90=11.1%, O 32/90=35.6% — matches.
distractor_notes: Option A: Mistakenly reports the empirical formula instead of the molecular formula ($n=1$ error). Option C: Has the correct molar mass of $90\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ but assumes a 1:2:1 ratio (lactic acid) instead of calculating from percentages. Option D: Has the correct molar mass of $90\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ (oxalic acid) but completely neglects the elemental composition.

brief: Provide an aromatic ring with substituent(s) in a figure; ask major product of EAS directing the incoming group to correct position.
stem: In the electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction shown in the figure, identify the major monobromo derivative $\text{P}$ formed.
working:
1. In 1,3-dimethylbenzene ($m$-xylene), both methyl groups ($-\text{CH}_3$) are activating and $o,p$-directing via $+I$ and hyperconjugative electron donation.

2. Directive influence at the different ring carbons:
- Carbon-4 (and the equivalent C-6) is *ortho* to one methyl group and *para* to the other. The directive effects of both substituents reinforce each other here, and the position is sterically accessible.
- Carbon-2 is *ortho* to both methyl groups. Although electronically activated, it is flanked by two adjacent methyl groups, creating severe steric hindrance to the incoming electrophile ($\text{Br}^+$).
- Carbon-5 is *meta* to both methyl groups and is not activated.

3. The reaction conditions ($\text{Br}_2 / \text{FeBr}_3$) generate the electrophile $\text{Br}^+$ for ring substitution rather than side-chain free-radical bromination.

4. Therefore, substitution occurs preferentially at C-4, yielding 1-bromo-2,4-dimethylbenzene (4-bromo-1,3-dimethylbenzene) as the major product $\text{P}$.

Independent check: Substrate is m-xylene (1,3-dimethylbenzene). Both CH3 groups are o/p-directors. Position 4 (≡6) is ortho to one CH3 and para to the other, strongly activated and unhindered; position 2 is also doubly activated but lies between the two methyls (steric hindrance), and position 5 is meta to both. Major product: 4-bromo-1,3-dimethylbenzene = 1-bromo-2,4-dimethylbenzene, matching figure (A). (B) is the sterically disfavored 2-isomer; (C) would need meta substitution; (D) is benzylic (radical) bromination, not EAS.
distractor_notes:
B: Overlooks steric hindrance between the two methyl groups at the C-2 position.
C: Incorrectly treats methyl groups as meta-directing substituents.
D: Confuses electrophilic ring bromination with free-radical benzylic bromination (which requires light or high heat).

brief: Match haloalkane substrates with correct elimination/substitution product or reagent behaviour (e.g. Saytzeff vs Hofmann product).
stem:
Match the reactions in Column-I with their corresponding major elimination products in Column-II.

| | Column-I | | Column-II |
|---|---|---|---|
| (A) | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3 + \text{alc. KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta}$ | (p) | 2-Methylbut-2-ene |
| (B) | $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{ONa} \xrightarrow{\Delta}$ | (q) | 2-Methylbut-1-ene |
| (C) | $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + t\text{-BuO}^-\text{K}^+ \xrightarrow{\Delta}$ | (r) | But-2-ene |
| (D) | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{alc. KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta}$ | (s) | But-1-ene |
working:
1. Reaction (A): 2-Bromobutane undergoes dehydrohalogenation with alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ via an $\text{E}2$ mechanism. Following Saytzeff's rule, the more stable, more substituted alkene, but-2-ene, is formed as the major product. Hence, (A) $\rightarrow$ (r).

2. Reaction (B): 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane reacts with a small, unhindered base ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{ONa}$). The base preferentially abstracts a proton from the more substituted $\beta$-carbon (C3), giving the more substituted Saytzeff alkene, 2-methylbut-2-ene, as the major product. Hence, (B) $\rightarrow$ (p).

3. Reaction (C): 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane reacts with a bulky base, potassium *tert*-butoxide ($t\text{-BuO}^-\text{K}^+$). Due to steric hindrance, the base abstracts the more accessible $\beta$-proton from the less hindered terminal methyl group (C1), yielding the less substituted Hofmann alkene, 2-methylbut-1-ene, as the major product. Hence, (C) $\rightarrow$ (q).

4. Reaction (D): 1-Bromobutane has only one type of $\beta$-hydrogen (at C2), so elimination can only yield but-1-ene. Hence, (D) $\rightarrow$ (s).

Combining these results gives A-(r), B-(p), C-(q), D-(s).

Independent check: A: 2-bromobutane + alc. KOH (small base) gives Zaitsev product but-2-ene (r). B: 2-bromo-2-methylbutane + EtONa (small base) gives Zaitsev trisubstituted 2-methylbut-2-ene (p). C: same substrate with bulky t-BuOK gives Hofmann product 2-methylbut-1-ene (q). D: 1-bromobutane has only one β-carbon, giving but-1-ene (s). Matching A-r, B-p, C-q, D-s = option (A).
distractor_notes:
Option B: Reverses the selectivity between the unhindered base (ethoxide) and the bulky base (tert-butoxide) for 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.
Option C: Confuses the regiochemical outcomes of 2-bromobutane and 1-bromobutane, predicting terminal elimination for the secondary halide.
Option D: Combines both errors, inverting both Saytzeff/Hofmann selectivity for the tertiary halide and the products of 1-bromobutane and 2-bromobutane.

brief: Phenol + CHCl3/NaOH followed by hydrolysis: identify the product and the reaction name (Reimer–Tiemann).
stem: Phenol on treatment with $\text{CHCl}_3$ and aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ followed by acidification yields a compound $X$. Identify $X$ and the name of the reaction.
working:
When phenol is treated with chloroform ($\text{CHCl}_3$) in the presence of aqueous sodium hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$), the electrophilic intermediate dichlorocarbene ($:\!\text{CCl}_2$) attacks the phenoxide ring preferentially at the *ortho*-position:
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{CHCl}_3\,/\,\text{NaOH}} o\text{-}\text{NaO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHCl}_2$$
Alkaline hydrolysis of the dichloromethyl intermediate converts it to the aldehyde group:
$$o\text{-}\text{NaO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHCl}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{NaOH}} o\text{-}\text{NaO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO}$$
Subsequent acidification yields salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde):
$$o\text{-}\text{NaO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} o\text{-}\text{HO}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHO} \text{ (salicylaldehyde)}$$
This transformation is called the Reimer–Tiemann reaction.

Independent check: CHCl3 + aq NaOH generates dichlorocarbene (:CCl2), which attacks phenoxide at the ortho position; hydrolysis of the -CHCl2 intermediate and acidification gives o-hydroxybenzaldehyde (salicylaldehyde). This is the Reimer–Tiemann reaction. Kolbe's reaction (CO2/NaOH) would give salicylic acid instead.
distractor_notes:
Option A confuses the reagents ($\text{CHCl}_3/\text{NaOH}$) with Kolbe's reaction ($\text{CO}_2/\text{NaOH}$), which produces salicylic acid.
Option C correctly identifies the reaction name as Reimer–Tiemann, but names salicylic acid (which is obtained if $\text{CCl}_4$ is used instead of $\text{CHCl}_3$).
Option D correctly identifies the product as salicylaldehyde, but misnames the reaction as Kolbe's reaction.

brief: For a given complex ion (octahedral), use CF splitting to decide high/low spin and count unpaired electrons.
stem: According to crystal field theory, the number of unpaired electrons in the complex ion $[\text{Mn(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ is
working:
1. Determine the oxidation state of manganese in $[\text{Mn(CN)}_6]^{3-}$:
$$x + 6(-1) = -3 \implies x = +3$$

2. Determine the electronic configuration of $\text{Mn}^{3+}$:
Atomic number of $\text{Mn} = 25$.
Ground state configuration: $[\text{Ar}]\, 3d^5 4s^2$.
$\text{Mn}^{3+}$ configuration: $[\text{Ar}]\, 3d^4$.

3. Apply crystal field theory:
In an octahedral field, the $d$-orbitals split into $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ sets.
$\text{CN}^-$ is a strong field ligand, so the crystal field splitting energy is greater than the pairing energy ($\Delta_\text{o} > P$).
This results in a low-spin complex where electrons preferentially pair up in the lower-energy $t_{2g}$ orbitals before occupying $e_g$ orbitals.

4. Electron distribution:
$$\text{Configuration} = t_{2g}^4\, e_g^0$$
The three $t_{2g}$ orbitals contain: one doubly occupied orbital and two singly occupied orbitals.

Therefore, the number of unpaired electrons is $2$.

Independent check: Mn oxidation state: x + 6(−1) = −3 → x = +3, so Mn³⁺ is d⁴. CN⁻ is a strong-field ligand → low spin: t₂g⁴ e_g⁰. Filling t₂g gives one paired orbital and two singly occupied → 2 unpaired electrons.
distractor_notes:
Option A (0): Arises from the misconception that any low-spin complex has all electrons paired (i.e. must be diamagnetic).
Option B (1): Arises from an oxidation state error, assuming $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($d^5$) instead of $\text{Mn}^{3+}$, which gives $t_{2g}^5\, e_g^0$ with 1 unpaired electron.
Option D (4): Arises from treating $\text{CN}^-$ as a weak field ligand (high-spin, $\Delta_\text{o} < P$), giving configuration $t_{2g}^3\, e_g^1$ with 4 unpaired electrons.

brief: Assign R/S configuration to a molecule drawn as a Fischer projection.
stem:
The absolute configuration of the chiral centers in the following Fischer projection is:
$$
\begin{array}{c}
\text{COOH} \\
| \\
\text{H}-\text{C}_2-\text{OH} \\
| \\
\text{HO}-\text{C}_3-\text{H} \\
| \\
\text{CH}_3
\end{array}
$$
working:
1. Configuration at $\text{C}_2$:
- Assign CIP priorities to the four groups attached to $\text{C}_2$:
  1: $-\text{OH}$ ($Z = 8$)
  2: $-\text{COOH}$ (carbon bonded to $(\text{O}, \text{O}, \text{O})$)
  3: $-\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$ ($\text{C}_3$, carbon bonded to $(\text{O}, \text{C}, \text{H})$)
  4: $-\text{H}$ ($Z = 1$)
  Since $(\text{O}, \text{O}, \text{O}) > (\text{O}, \text{C}, \text{H})$, priority order is: $-\text{OH} > -\text{COOH} > \text{C}_3 > -\text{H}$.
- On the Fischer projection, $-\text{OH}$ is on the right, $-\text{COOH}$ is at the top, and $\text{C}_3$ is at the bottom.
- Tracing $1 \to 2 \to 3$ gives a counter-clockwise path.
- Since the lowest priority group ($-\text{H}$) is on a horizontal bond, the apparent configuration is reversed: counter-clockwise corresponds to $R$.
- Thus, the configuration at $\text{C}_2$ is $2R$.

2. Configuration at $\text{C}_3$:
- Assign CIP priorities to the four groups attached to $\text{C}_3$:
  1: $-\text{OH}$ ($Z = 8$)
  2: $-\text{CH(OH)COOH}$ ($\text{C}_2$, carbon bonded to $(\text{O}, \text{C}, \text{H})$)
  3: $-\text{CH}_3$ (carbon bonded to $(\text{H}, \text{H}, \text{H})$)
  4: $-\text{H}$ ($Z = 1$)
  Priority order is: $-\text{OH} > \text{C}_2 > -\text{CH}_3 > -\text{H}$.
- On the Fischer projection, $-\text{OH}$ is on the left, $\text{C}_2$ is at the top, and $-\text{CH}_3$ is at the bottom.
- Tracing $1 \to 2 \to 3$ gives a clockwise path.
- Since the lowest priority group ($-\text{H}$) is on a horizontal bond, the apparent configuration is reversed: clockwise corresponds to $S$.
- Thus, the configuration at $\text{C}_3$ is $3S$.

Combining both centers gives $(2R, 3S)$.

Independent check: Compound is 2,3-dihydroxybutanoic acid. C2 priorities: OH > COOH [C(O,O,O)] > C3 [C(O,C,H)] > H. In Fischer, horizontal bonds point toward viewer; H is horizontal at C2, so reverse apparent rotation: OH(right)→COOH(up)→C3(down) appears CCW (S) → actual R. C3 priorities: OH > C2 [C(O,C,H)] > CH3 > H; H horizontal again: OH(left)→C2(up)→CH3(down) appears CW (R) → actual S. Verified by signed-volume (determinant) calculation with Fischer 3D geometry: C2 = R, C3 = S.
distractor_notes:
$(2R, 3R)$ arises from failing to invert the apparent clockwise direction at $\text{C}_3$ where $-\text{H}$ is horizontal.
$(2S, 3R)$ arises from neglecting the horizontal inversion rule at both centers (reading apparent counter-clockwise as $S$ and apparent clockwise as $R$).
$(2S, 3S)$ arises from failing to invert the apparent counter-clockwise direction at $\text{C}_2$, while correctly inverting at $\text{C}_3$.

brief: Match functional-group detection (Lassaigne's test: N, S, halogen) with correct observation/chemistry.
stem:
Match the element(s) detected in Lassaigne's test (List-I) with the characteristic species formed (List-II):

**List-I**
(P) Nitrogen only
(Q) Sulphur only
(R) Both Nitrogen and Sulphur
(S) Chlorine

**List-II**
(1) Violet complex, $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_5\text{NOS}]^{4-}$
(2) Prussian blue, $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]_3$
(3) Blood-red complex, $[\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})]^{2+}$
(4) White precipitate, $\text{AgCl}$
working:
In Lassaigne's test:
1. Nitrogen alone forms sodium cyanide ($\text{NaCN}$), which on reaction with $\text{FeSO}_4$ and acidification with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives ferric ferrocyanide (Prussian blue), $\text{Fe}_4[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_6]_3$. Thus, P $\to$ 2.
2. Sulphur alone forms sodium sulphide ($\text{Na}_2\text{S}$), which gives a violet colour with sodium nitroprusside due to the formation of $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_5\text{NOS}]^{4-}$. Thus, Q $\to$ 1.
3. When both Nitrogen and Sulphur are present, sodium thiocyanate ($\text{NaSCN}$) is formed, which reacts with $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ to give a blood-red complex, $[\text{Fe}(\text{SCN})]^{2+}$. Thus, R $\to$ 3.
4. Chlorine forms sodium chloride ($\text{NaCl}$), which gives a white precipitate of $\text{AgCl}$ with acidified $\text{AgNO}_3$. Thus, S $\to$ 4.

Matching: P-(2), Q-(1), R-(3), S-(4).

Independent check: Lassaigne's test: N only gives sodium ferrocyanide → Prussian blue Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 (P-2). S only gives Na2S → violet [Fe(CN)5NOS]4- with sodium nitroprusside (Q-1). Both N and S give NaSCN → blood-red [Fe(SCN)]2+ with Fe3+ (R-3). Cl gives AgCl white ppt soluble in NH4OH (S-4). Charges verified: nitroprusside-sulfide complex -4, FeSCN +2, Prussian blue neutral. Matches option (A).
distractor_notes:
Option B confuses the reagents/products for nitrogen (Prussian blue) and sulphur (nitroprusside test).
Option C confuses the test for nitrogen alone with the test when both nitrogen and sulphur are present.
Option D swaps the products formed in the nitrogen test with the sulphur and nitrogen combined test.

brief: Evaluate two statements on ionisation enthalpy trends across a period and down a group; pick the correct combination.
stem:
Given below are two statements regarding periodic trends in first ionisation enthalpy ($\Delta_i H_1$):

Statement I: Across the second period, the first ionisation enthalpy of boron is greater than that of beryllium.

Statement II: Down a group, the first ionisation enthalpy generally decreases with an increase in atomic radius.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
Statement I is correct, but Statement II is incorrect
Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct
working:
1. **Evaluation of Statement I:**
The ground-state electronic configurations are:
$$\text{Be}\ (Z = 4): 1s^2 2s^2$$
$$\text{B}\ (Z = 5): 1s^2 2s^2 2p^1$$
In beryllium, the outermost electron resides in a completely filled, penetrating $2s$ subshell. In boron, the electron to be removed is in a $2p$ subshell, which is at a higher energy level and is shielded from the nuclear charge by the inner $1s^2$ and $2s^2$ electrons. As a result, less energy is required to remove the $2p$ electron of boron than the $2s$ electron of beryllium:
$$\Delta_i H_1(\text{Be}) = 899\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} > \Delta_i H_1(\text{B}) = 801\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$
Thus, the first ionisation enthalpy of boron is less than that of beryllium. Statement I is incorrect.

2. **Evaluation of Statement II:**
Down a group, each successive element possesses an additional electron shell, leading to an increase in atomic radius. The increased distance of the valence electrons from the nucleus, combined with enhanced shielding by core electrons, outweighs the increase in nuclear charge. Consequently, the valence electrons are held less tightly, and the first ionisation enthalpy generally decreases. Statement II is correct.

Therefore, Statement I is incorrect, but Statement II is correct.

Independent check: IE1(B) ≈ 801 kJ/mol < IE1(Be) ≈ 899 kJ/mol because Be has a stable filled 2s² subshell while B loses a higher-energy 2p electron; hence Statement I is false. Down a group, atomic radius increases and IE1 generally decreases, so Statement II is true.
distractor_notes:
Option A: Mistakenly applies the general left-to-right period trend without considering the subshell stability and shielding anomaly between Be ($2s^2$) and B ($2p^1$).
Option B: Incorrectly assumes the group trend is also false, confusing the influence of increasing nuclear charge with effective nuclear attraction.
Option C: Commits both errors: assumes the general period trend holds strictly (believing B > Be) and assumes ionisation enthalpy increases down a group due to increasing nuclear charge.

brief: Order given alkyl halides by SN2 reactivity / leaving group ability and identify correct sequence.
stem: The correct decreasing order of reactivity of alkyl halides towards an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ reaction for a given alkyl group $R$ is:
working:
In an $	ext{S}_	ext{N}2$ reaction, the rate depends critically on the ability of the halide ion to depart (leaving group ability) as well as the carbon–halogen ($	ext{C}-	ext{X}$) bond strength.

1. Leaving group ability is inversely related to basicity. Since the conjugate acid strength is $	ext{HI} > 	ext{HBr} > 	ext{HCl} > 	ext{HF}$, the halide basicity order is $	ext{I}^- < 	ext{Br}^- < 	ext{Cl}^- < 	ext{F}^-$. The weaker the base, the better it serves as a leaving group. Hence, leaving group ability follows $	ext{I}^- > 	ext{Br}^- > 	ext{Cl}^- > 	ext{F}^-$.

2. The $	ext{C}-	ext{X}$ bond dissociation enthalpy decreases in the order: $	ext{C}-	ext{F} > 	ext{C}-	ext{Cl} > 	ext{C}-	ext{Br} > 	ext{C}-	ext{I}$. Thus, the $	ext{C}-	ext{I}$ bond is the weakest and easiest to break.

Both factors make the reactivity order for a given alkyl group:
$$R	ext{I} > R	ext{Br} > R	ext{Cl} > R	ext{F}$$

Independent check: SN2 rate depends on leaving-group ability, which follows C–X bond strength: C–I (213) < C–Br (285) < C–Cl (327) < C–F (485 kJ/mol). Weakest bond / best leaving group reacts fastest, so RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
distractor_notes:
Option A reverses the sequence by mistakenly assuming reactivity follows electronegativity or bond polarity of the C-X bond.
Option C incorrectly ranks bromide higher than iodide.
Option D incorrectly transposes chloride and bromide, violating the periodic trend in leaving group ability.

brief: Ask which of several triatomic/polyatomic species is non-polar despite polar bonds due to symmetric geometry (dipole moment zero).
stem: Which of the following molecules contains polar bonds but has a net dipole moment of zero due to its symmetrical geometry?
working:
A molecule has zero net dipole moment ($\mu = 0$) if the vector sum of all individual bond dipoles and lone pair moments cancels out symmetrically.

1. For $	ext{XeF}_4$:
- Central atom $	ext{Xe}$ has $8$ valence electrons.
- Forms $4$ single bonds with $	ext{F}$ and has $2$ lone pairs.
- Steric number $= 4 + 2 = 6$ ($sp^3d^2$ hybridisation).
- Geometry of electron pairs is octahedral, and molecular shape is square planar with the two lone pairs occupying axial positions ($180^\circ$ apart) to minimize repulsion.
- In the square plane, the four polar $	ext{Xe}-	ext{F}$ bond dipoles cancel out in opposite pairs ($180^\circ$ apart):
$$\vec{\mu}_{	ext{net}} = 0$$

2. For the other species:
- $	ext{SF}_4$: Steric number $= 4 + 1 = 5$ ($sp^3d$), see-saw shape; bond dipoles do not cancel ($\mu 
eq 0$).
- $	ext{NF}_3$: Steric number $= 3 + 1 = 4$ ($sp^3$), trigonal pyramidal shape; asymmetric ($\mu \approx 0.24\ 	ext{D} 
eq 0$).
- $	ext{ClF}_3$: Steric number $= 3 + 2 = 5$ ($sp^3d$), T-shaped; asymmetric ($\mu 
eq 0$).

Therefore, $	ext{XeF}_4$ is non-polar despite containing polar bonds.

Independent check: All four have polar bonds (F more electronegative). VSEPR: SF4 (4bp+1lp) seesaw → polar; XeF4 (4bp+2lp) square planar with lone pairs trans → bond dipoles cancel, μ=0; NF3 (3bp+1lp) trigonal pyramidal → polar; ClF3 (3bp+2lp) T-shaped → polar. Only XeF4 is symmetric with zero net dipole.
distractor_notes:
Distractor A: SF4 is mistakenly assumed to be a regular tetrahedral geometry (overlooking the equatorial lone pair), which would give zero dipole moment.
Distractor C: NF3 is confused with BF3; although its lone pair partially opposes the N-F bond moments, it is pyramidal and possesses a non-zero dipole moment.
Distractor D: ClF3 is incorrectly assumed to have a symmetrical planar shape like trigonal planar, ignoring the two lone pairs that cause a T-shaped asymmetric structure.

brief: Give the IUPAC name of a complex (e.g. [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2) or formula from name.
stem: The correct IUPAC name of the coordination compound $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$ is:
working:
1. Identify the ligands present in the coordination sphere and their alphabetical order:
- $\text{NH}_3$: ammine
- $\text{H}_2\text{O}$: aqua
- $\text{Cl}^-$: chlorido
Alphabetical order of ligands (ignoring numerical prefixes like tetra-): ammine precedes aqua, which precedes chlorido. Thus, the order is tetraammine, aqua, chlorido.

2. Determine the oxidation state of the central cobalt ion:
Let the oxidation state of $\text{Co}$ be $x$.
$x + 4(0) + 1(0) + 1(-1) + 2(-1) = 0 \implies x - 3 = 0 \implies x = +3$.
So, cobalt is in the $+3$ oxidation state, denoted as cobalt(III).

3. Since the complex cation $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})\text{Cl}]^{2+}$ carries a positive charge, the metal name remains 'cobalt' (not 'cobaltate').

4. The ionizable anion is chloride.

Combining these rules gives: Tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride.

Independent check: Complex ion charge = +2 (two outer Cl-). With NH3 and H2O neutral and coordinated Cl- = -1, Co oxidation state = +3. Ligands cited alphabetically: ammine < aqua < chlorido, giving tetraammineaquachloridocobalt(III) chloride. Cationic complex uses 'cobalt', not 'cobaltate'. Option A has wrong ligand order; B wrong oxidation state; D wrong suffix.
distractor_notes:
Option A: Mistakenly alphabetizes using the multiplying prefix 'tetra-', incorrectly placing 'aqua' before 'tetraammine'.
Option B: Uses an incorrect oxidation state of $+2$ for cobalt, typically caused by forgetting the coordinated chloride ion.
Option D: Incorrectly adds the suffix '-ate' to the metal name, which applies only to anionic complexes.

brief: Give electronic configuration of a transition metal ion (e.g. Cr2+, Mn2+) and its oxidation state/d-orbital occupancy.
stem: The electronic configuration of a divalent ion of a $3d$ transition metal is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^4$. The atomic number of the metal and the number of unpaired electrons in its ground-state neutral atom are, respectively:
working:
1. The divalent cation $M^{2+}$ has the electronic configuration $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^4$.
2. The number of electrons in $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^4$ is $18 + 4 = 22$.
3. Since the cation carries a $+2$ charge, the neutral atom $M$ has $22 + 2 = 24$ electrons. Thus, the atomic number of the metal is $Z = 24$ (Chromium, $\text{Cr}$).
4. Due to the extra stability of a half-filled $d$-subshell, the ground-state electronic configuration of neutral $\text{Cr}$ ($Z = 24$) is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$.
5. The number of unpaired electrons in neutral $\text{Cr}$ is $5$ (from the singly occupied $3d$ orbitals) $+ 1$ (from the singly occupied $4s$ orbital) $= 6$.

Therefore, the atomic number is $24$ and the number of unpaired electrons is $6$.

Independent check: M²⁺ = [Ar]3d⁴ has 22 electrons, so neutral atom Z = 24 (Cr). Ground-state Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹ (half-filled d stability), giving 5 + 1 = 6 unpaired electrons.
distractor_notes:
- $24$ and $4$: Assumes the standard Aufbau configuration $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^4 4s^2$ for Chromium, forgetting the anomalous half-filled $3d^5 4s^1$ configuration.
- $24$ and $5$: Recognizes the $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^1$ configuration but counts only the unpaired $d$-electrons, overlooking the unpaired electron in the $4s$ subshell.
- $25$ and $5$: Confuses the divalent ion with a trivalent ion (e.g., $\text{Mn}^{3+}$, which is also $3d^4$), leading to $Z = 25$ (Manganese, $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5 4s^2$) with $5$ unpaired electrons.

brief: Propose a two-step conversion of an alcohol/alkene to an ether via Williamson synthesis with correct alkyl halide choice.
stem: Which of the following reaction sequences is most suitable for the preparation of *tert*-butyl ethyl ether from 2-methylpropan-2-ol?
working:
Williamson ether synthesis operates via an $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ mechanism where an alkoxide ion attacks an alkyl halide. To prepare an unsymmetrical ether containing a tertiary alkyl group, the tertiary group must be supplied by the alkoxide, and the primary alkyl group must come from the alkyl halide:

1. Formation of alkoxide:
Aliphatic alcohols are weaker acids than water and cannot be deprotonated by $\text{NaOH}$. An active alkali metal like $\text{Na}$ is used:
$$2(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-OH} + 2\text{Na} \rightarrow 2(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-O}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{H}_2\uparrow$$

2. $\text{S}_\text{N}2$ ether synthesis:
$$(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-O}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{NaBr}$$
Because ethyl bromide is a primary halide, nucleophilic substitution dominates over elimination, giving *tert*-butyl ethyl ether in good yield.

Independent check: Williamson synthesis requires the bulky alkoxide + primary halide. (A) Na converts t-BuOH to t-BuO⁻Na⁺, which does SN2 on primary CH3CH2Br giving t-Bu-O-Et. (B) gives t-BuBr, and EtO⁻ (strong base) causes E2 with the 3° halide → isobutene. (C) NaOH cannot appreciably deprotonate t-BuOH (pKa ~18 > water 15.7). (D) conc. H2SO4/140 °C with a 3° alcohol gives dehydration and ether mixtures, not the target selectively.
distractor_notes:
Option B encodes using a tertiary alkyl halide with an alkoxide base: $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-Br} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa}$ undergoes exclusively E2 elimination to yield 2-methylpropene rather than ether.
Option C encodes the misconception that aqueous $\text{NaOH}$ can deprotonate aliphatic alcohols; water is more acidic than *tert*-butanol, so alkoxide formation is negligible and $\text{OH}^-$ simply hydrolyzes the alkyl halide to ethanol.
Option D encodes using acid-catalyzed bimolecular dehydration; tertiary alcohols rapidly undergo unimolecular dehydration to give 2-methylpropene, while any bimolecular condensation of ethanol gives diethyl ether.

brief: Show a substrate structure in a figure; ask which reagent (Lucas reagent sequence) distinguishes the given alcohols by rate/appearance.
stem: Which reagent distinguishes the alcohol shown in the figure from a primary alcohol by the rapid appearance of turbidity at room temperature?
working:
The compound shown in the figure is 2-methylpropan-2-ol ($tert$-butanol), which is a tertiary ($3^\circ$) alcohol. Lucas reagent is an equimolar mixture of concentrated $\text{HCl}$ and anhydrous $\text{ZnCl}_2$. Tertiary alcohols react via an $\text{S}_\text{N}1$ mechanism involving a stable tertiary carbocation intermediate, reacting almost instantaneously to produce an insoluble alkyl chloride: $$\text{(CH}_3)_3\text{C-OH} + \text{HCl} \xrightarrow{\text{anhyd. } \text{ZnCl}_2} \text{(CH}_3)_3\text{C-Cl}\downarrow + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ This insoluble alkyl chloride appears immediately as turbidity or cloudiness. In contrast, primary alcohols do not produce turbidity at room temperature under these conditions.

Independent check: Figure shows (CH3)3C–OH (tertiary alcohol). Lucas reagent = conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl2. Tertiary alcohols form a stable 3° carbocation (SN1) and give insoluble alkyl chloride as immediate turbidity at room temperature; primary alcohols show no turbidity. Only option A is the Lucas reagent.
distractor_notes:
Dilute HCl + anhydrous ZnCl2 incorrectly uses dilute acid, which provides insufficient hydronium and chloride activity to drive the conversion.
Conc. HCl + anhydrous AlCl3 confuses the Lucas reagent Lewis acid (ZnCl2) with the Lewis acid typically used in Friedel–Crafts alkylation/acylation.
Conc. H2SO4 + anhydrous ZnCl2 replaces hydrochloric acid with sulfuric acid, which lacks nucleophilic chloride ions and promotes alcohol dehydration rather than alkyl chloride precipitation.

brief: Ask why transition metal ions are coloured (d–d transition) and match a given ion with its colour.
stem: Transition metal ions in aqueous solution are coloured primarily due to \_\_\_\_\_\_, and the characteristic colour of $\text{Cu}^{2+}(\text{aq})$ is \_\_\_\_\_\_.
working:
The colour of transition metal ions in aqueous solution arises from the absorption of visible light that promotes an electron from a lower-energy $d$-orbital to a higher-energy $d$-orbital within the ligand-field split $d$-subshell; this phenomenon is termed a $d\text{--}d$ transition. The $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ion has a $3d^9$ electronic configuration (one unpaired electron). In aqueous solution, it forms the hydrated complex $[\text{Cu}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}$, which absorbs light in the red-orange region and transmits the complementary colour, appearing distinctly blue.

Independent check: Aqueous transition metal ions with partially filled d orbitals absorb visible light via d–d transitions (crystal field splitting). [Cu(H2O)6]2+ absorbs red/orange light and appears blue. Hence d–d transition; blue.
distractor_notes: Option A: Correctly identifies the $d\text{--}d$ transition mechanism but mistakes the colour of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ for green (which is typical of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ or $\text{Ni}^{2+}$). Option C: Correctly identifies the blue colour of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$, but confuses the cause of colour with charge transfer (which is responsible for colour in $d^0$ oxoanions like $\text{MnO}_4^-$). Option D: Both the mechanism (charge transfer) and colour (green) are incorrect.

brief: Given a set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, s), decide whether it is allowed for an electron; identify the invalid one.
stem: Which of the following sets of quantum numbers $(n, l, m, s)$ is not permissible for an electron in an atom?
working:
The rules governing the allowed values of quantum numbers are:
1. Principal quantum number: $n = 1, 2, 3, \dots$
2. Azimuthal quantum number: $l = 0, 1, 2, \dots, (n - 1)$
3. Magnetic quantum number: $m = -l, \dots, 0, \dots, +l$ (i.e., $|m| \le l$)
4. Spin quantum number: $s = \pm \dfrac{1}{2}$

Evaluating the options:
- For $3, 2, -2, +\dfrac{1}{2}$: $n = 3 \implies l \in \{0, 1, 2\}$. For $l = 2$, $m \in \{-2, -1, 0, +1, +2\}$, and $s = +\dfrac{1}{2}$. This is permissible ($3d$ orbital).
- For $4, 0, 0, -\dfrac{1}{2}$: $n = 4 \implies l = 0$ is valid, which gives $m = 0$, and $s = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. This is permissible ($4s$ orbital).
- For $3, 1, -2, +\dfrac{1}{2}$: Here $l = 1$. The allowed values of $m$ are $-1, 0, +1$. The given value $m = -2$ violates $|m| \le l$. Thus, this set is not permissible.
- For $2, 1, +1, -\dfrac{1}{2}$: $n = 2 \implies l = 1$ is valid, giving $m \in \{-1, 0, +1\}$, and $s = -\dfrac{1}{2}$. This is permissible ($2p$ orbital).

Therefore, the set in option C is not permissible.

Independent check: Rules: l = 0..n-1, m = -l..+l, s = ±1/2. (C) has l=1 but m=-2, which lies outside [-1, +1], so it is not permissible. A, B, D all satisfy the rules (verified numerically).
distractor_notes:
Option A: A student mistakenly considers $m = -2$ invalid because of the negative sign, forgetting that $m$ ranges from $-l$ to $+l$.
Option B: A student wrongly assumes $l = 0$ and $m = 0$ represents an unallowed or empty state, forgetting that $l = 0$ defines an $s$-orbital.
Option D: A student misremembers that $m = +1$ requires $l > 1$, falsely eliminating a standard $2p$ electron.

brief: Arrange given carbanions/radicals by stability with a stated reason (resonance, inductive effects).
stem: Considering resonance and inductive effects, what is the correct order of decreasing stability of the following carbanions: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^-$ (I), $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2^-$ (II), $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CH}^-$ (III), and $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^-$ (IV)?
working:
1. Resonance stabilization: In the benzyl carbanion, $	ext{C}_6	ext{H}_5	ext{CH}_2^-$ (I), the negative charge is delocalized over the ortho and para positions of the benzene ring through resonance (4 resonating structures). Delocalization significantly disperses the negative charge, making (I) the most stable carbanion among those given.
2. Inductive effect: In alkyl carbanions, alkyl groups exhibit an electron-donating inductive effect ($+I$). This $+I$ effect increases electron density on the already negatively charged carbon atom, thereby destabilizing the carbanion.
- Ethyl carbanion, $	ext{CH}_3	ext{CH}_2^-$ (II), has one $+I$ alkyl group ($1^\circ$).
- Isopropyl carbanion, $(	ext{CH}_3)_2	ext{CH}^-$ (III), has two $+I$ alkyl groups ($2^\circ$).
- $	ext{tert}$-Butyl carbanion, $(	ext{CH}_3)_3	ext{C}^-$ (IV), has three $+I$ alkyl groups ($3^\circ$).
Thus, among alkyl carbanions, stability decreases as the number of electron-donating alkyl groups increases: $1^\circ > 2^\circ > 3^\circ$, giving $	ext{II} > 	ext{III} > 	ext{IV}$.
Combining these effects gives the overall decreasing order of stability: $	ext{I} > 	ext{II} > 	ext{III} > 	ext{IV}$.

Independent check: Benzyl carbanion (I) is resonance-stabilized by delocalization into the phenyl ring, so it is most stable. Alkyl groups exert +I effect, intensifying the negative charge and destabilizing carbanions; more alkyl groups means less stability. Thus among II (1 alkyl), III (2 alkyls), IV (3 alkyls): II > III > IV. Overall: I > II > III > IV.
distractor_notes: Option B comes from correctly identifying the resonance stabilization of the benzyl carbanion but mistakenly applying the carbocation stability order (3° > 2° > 1°) to the alkyl carbanions.\nOption C comes from completely inverting the carbanion stability order by treating carbanions like carbocations or free radicals (3° > 2° > 1° > benzyl).\nOption D comes from correctly ordering the alkyl carbanions by the +I destabilizing effect but failing to recognize that resonance strongly stabilizes the benzyl carbanion.

archetype: volume from density then PV = nRT
brief: From gas density at given T and P, compute molar mass or volume via the ideal gas equation.
stem: The density of an ideal gas is $2.0\ \text{g L}^{-1}$ at $300\ \text{K}$ and $1.64\ \text{atm}$. What is the volume occupied by $15\ \text{g}$ of this gas at $400\ \text{K}$ and $0.82\ \text{atm}$? (Given: $R = 0.082\ \text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}$)
working:
Step 1: Determine the molar mass ($M$) of the gas using the density form of the ideal gas equation:
$$d = \dfrac{PM}{RT} \implies M = \dfrac{dRT}{P}$$
$$M = \dfrac{2.0\ \text{g L}^{-1} \times 0.082\ \text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} \times 300\ \text{K}}{1.64\ \text{atm}} = \dfrac{49.2}{1.64} = 30\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$$

Step 2: Calculate the number of moles ($n$) in $15\ \text{g}$ of the gas:
$$n = \dfrac{m}{M} = \dfrac{15\ \text{g}}{30\ \text{g mol}^{-1}} = 0.5\ \text{mol}$$

Step 3: Calculate the volume occupied by this amount of gas at $T = 400\ \text{K}$ and $P = 0.82\ \text{atm}$:
$$V = \dfrac{nRT}{P} = \dfrac{0.5\ \text{mol} \times 0.082\ \text{L atm K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1} \times 400\ \text{K}}{0.82\ \text{atm}} = \dfrac{16.4}{0.82} = 20\ \text{L}$$

Alternatively, find the initial volume $V_1 = \dfrac{m}{d_1} = \dfrac{15\ \text{g}}{2.0\ \text{g L}^{-1}} = 7.5\ \text{L}$, then apply the combined gas law:
$$V_2 = V_1 \left(\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\right)\left(\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}\right) = 7.5 \times \left(\dfrac{1.64}{0.82}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{400}{300}\right) = 7.5 \times 2 \times \dfrac{4}{3} = 20\ \text{L}.$$

Independent check: M = ρRT/P = 2.0×0.082×300/1.64 = 30 g/mol. n = 15/30 = 0.5 mol. V = nRT/P = 0.5×0.082×400/0.82 = 20 L.
distractor_notes:
$5\ \text{L}$: Inverting the pressure ratio ($P_2/P_1$ instead of $P_1/P_2$) in the combined gas law, giving $7.5 \times (0.82/1.64) \times (400/300) = 5\ \text{L}$.
$10\ \text{L}$: Forgetting the pressure change and using the initial pressure $1.64\ \text{atm}$ instead of $0.82\ \text{atm}$, yielding $V = 10\ \text{L}$.
$40\ \text{L}$: Calculating the molar volume for $1\ \text{mol}$ of gas ($V_m = RT/P = 40\ \text{L}$) without multiplying by $n = 0.5\ \text{mol}$.

brief: Compute electrode potential of a cell/concentration cell using the Nernst equation with given concentrations.
stem:
For the electrochemical cell at $298\text{ K}$:
$$\text{Ni}(s) \mid \text{Ni}^{2+}(aq,\, 0.01\text{ M}) \mid\mid \text{Ag}^+(aq,\, 0.01\text{ M}) \mid \text{Ag}(s)$$
the cell potential is:
(Given: $E^\circ_{\text{Ag}^+/\text{Ag}} = +0.80\text{ V}$, $E^\circ_{\text{Ni}^{2+}/\text{Ni}} = -0.25\text{ V}$, and $\dfrac{2.303 RT}{F} = 0.059\text{ V}$)
working:
1. Write the half-reactions and the balanced overall cell reaction:
Anode (oxidation): $\text{Ni}(s) \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^-$
Cathode (reduction): $2\text{Ag}^+(aq) + 2e^- \rightarrow 2\text{Ag}(s)$
Overall reaction: $\text{Ni}(s) + 2\text{Ag}^+(aq) \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)$
Number of electrons transferred, $n = 2$.

2. Compute the standard cell potential, $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$:
$$E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cathode}} - E^\circ_{\text{anode}} = +0.80\text{ V} - (-0.25\text{ V}) = +1.05\text{ V}$$

3. Determine the reaction quotient, $Q$:
$$Q = \dfrac{[\text{Ni}^{2+}]}{[\text{Ag}^+]^2} = \dfrac{0.01}{(0.01)^2} = \dfrac{10^{-2}}{10^{-4}} = 10^2$$
$$\log_{10} Q = \log_{10}(10^2) = 2$$

4. Apply the Nernst equation at $298\text{ K}$:
$$E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.059}{n} \log_{10} Q$$
$$E_{\text{cell}} = 1.05 - \dfrac{0.059}{2} \times 2 = 1.05 - 0.059 = 0.991\text{ V}$$

Independent check: Cell reaction: Ni + 2Ag+ → Ni2+ + 2Ag, n=2. E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.25) = 1.05 V. Q = [Ni2+]/[Ag+]² = 0.01/(0.01)² = 100. Nernst: E = 1.05 − (0.059/2)·log100 = 1.05 − 0.059 = 0.991 V.
distractor_notes:
Option A ($0.932\text{ V}$): Uses $n = 1$ instead of $n = 2$ in the Nernst equation ($1.05 - 0.059 \times 2 = 0.932\text{ V}$).
Option C ($1.050\text{ V}$): Forgets to square $[\text{Ag}^+]$ in the reaction quotient, giving $Q = 0.01/0.01 = 1$, $\log Q = 0$, and thus $E_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$.
Option D ($1.109\text{ V}$): Commits a sign error in the Nernst equation by adding the logarithmic term instead of subtracting it ($1.05 + 0.059 = 1.109\text{ V}$).

brief: Evaluate statements on aliphatic vs aromatic amine basicity in gas/aqueous phases and pick correct ones.
stem:
Consider the following statements regarding the basicity of amines:

I. In the gas phase, the basic strength of alkylamines decreases in the order: $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{NH}_3$.
II. In aqueous solution, trimethylamine is a stronger base than dimethylamine.
III. Aniline is less basic than aliphatic amines because the lone pair on nitrogen is delocalised over the benzene ring.

Which of the above statements are correct?
working:
Statement I is correct: In the gas phase, there are no solvation or steric effects. Basicity depends solely on the electron-donating inductive effect ($+I$) of the alkyl groups, which stabilizes the conjugate acid ($R_3\text{NH}^+$). Hence, the order is $3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{NH}_3$.

Statement II is incorrect: In aqueous solution, basicity is governed by an interplay of inductive effect, hydration enthalpy (solvation of the conjugate ammonium cation), and steric hindrance. For methyl-substituted amines, the order in aqueous medium is: $$(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{NH} > \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 > (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{N} > \text{NH}_3$$ Thus, dimethylamine is a stronger base than trimethylamine.

Statement III is correct: In aromatic amines such as aniline, the unshared pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom is in conjugation with the aromatic $\pi$-system and is delocalised into the ring through resonance (represented by five contributing canonical structures). This decreases the electron density on nitrogen, making aniline significantly less basic than aliphatic amines.

Therefore, statements I and III are correct.

Independent check: I: In gas phase only +I effect operates (no solvation), so 3° > 2° > 1° > NH3 — correct. II: In water, solvation/H-bonding of the ammonium ion and steric effects reverse part of the inductive trend; for methylamines pKb: (CH3)2NH 3.27 < CH3NH2 3.38 < (CH3)3N 4.22, so dimethylamine is stronger than trimethylamine — II is false. III: Aniline's lone pair is delocalised into the ring, lowering basicity vs aliphatic amines — correct. Hence I and III only.
distractor_notes:
