$\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+3\text{HCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}$. Nitrogen expands its octet during hydrolysis, whereas phosphorus does not.
$\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+3\text{HCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+5\text{HCl}$. The phosphorus oxidation states decrease during hydrolysis.
solution:
In $\text{NCl}_3$, N is $\text{N}^{4-}$, so hydrolysis gives $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{HOCl}$; in phosphorus chlorides, P is $\text{P}^{4+}$ and forms P–O bonds.
$$
\text{NCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\to\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl};\quad \text{PCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\to\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+3\text{HCl};\quad \text{PCl}_5+4\text{H}_2\text{O}\to\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}.
$$
Thus the products and bond-polarity explanation match (A).
working:
$\text{NCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl}$
$\text{PCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+3\text{HCl}$
$\text{PCl}_5+4\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}$
$\text{N}^{\delta-}\! -\!\text{Cl}^{\delta+};\quad \text{P}^{\delta+}\! -\!\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$

Independent check: NCl3 + 3H2O -> NH3 + 3HOCl (N is the negative end of N–Cl, so N gets H and Cl gets OH). PCl3 + 3H2O -> H3PO3 + 3HCl and PCl5 + 4H2O -> H3PO4 + 5HCl (P is the positive end, so P forms P–OH bonds, Cl leaves as HCl). All equations balance. Option A has correct products and correct rationale. B has wrong NCl3 products; C has correct products but a false explanation (N cannot expand its octet); D swaps the phosphorus acids and claims reduction, but hydrolysis is not redox.
distractor_notes: B assumes the chlorine in $\text{NCl}_3$ forms HCl. C gives the correct products but incorrectly claims nitrogen expands its octet. D interchanges the phosphorus oxyacids and gives an incorrect oxidation-state explanation.

brief: Figure shows an alcohol and a target ether; choose the best halide–alkoxide combination and conditions for a high-yield Williamson synthesis.
stem: For the conversion shown in the figure, which reagent pair and conditions are best for a high-yield Williamson synthesis?
options: $\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$ and sodium ethoxide in dry acetone
tert-Butyl bromide and sodium methoxide in dry acetone
$\text{CH}_3\text{Br}$ and sodium tert-butoxide in dry acetone
Ethyl bromide and sodium tert-butoxide in dry acetone
solution:
Williamson synthesis proceeds by an $S_N2$ reaction; methyl bromide is ideal, while tert-butoxide supplies the bulky alkoxide.
$$\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CO}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{Br} \longrightarrow \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{COCH}_3$$
Thus, methyl tert-butyl ether is obtained in high yield using methyl bromide and sodium tert-butoxide in dry acetone.
working:
The target ether has a tert-butyl group and a methyl group bonded to oxygen.
Use the bulky tert-butoxide as the alkoxide and methyl bromide as the primary halide.
$\text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{CO}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{Br}\rightarrow \text{(CH}_3\text{)}_3\text{COCH}_3$

Independent check: The product is methyl tert-butyl ether. Williamson synthesis forms it by SN2 attack of tert-butoxide on methyl bromide; tertiary halides favor elimination instead.
distractor_notes: B: a tertiary halide favors elimination; C: forms methyl ethyl ether; D: forms ethyl tert-butyl ether rather than the target.

brief: For a first-order reaction, find the time for a stated fraction of reactant to decompose, or the fraction left after a given number of half-lives.
stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of $20$ min. How long does it take for $\dfrac{7}{8}$ of the reactant to decompose?
solution:
The fraction remaining is $1-\frac{7}{8}=\frac{1}{8}=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^3$, so $3$ half-lives elapse.
$$t=3(20\,\text{min})=60\,\text{min}$$
working:
Fraction remaining $=1-\dfrac{7}{8}=\dfrac{1}{8}=\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3$.
Thus, $3$ half-lives elapse.
$t=3(20\ \text{min})=60\ \text{min}$.

Independent check: A remaining fraction of 1/8 equals (1/2)^3, so 3 half-lives are needed: 3 × 20 = 60 min.
distractor_notes: A: counts one half-life; B: counts two half-lives; D: counts four half-lives.

brief: From boiling-point elevation or freezing-point depression of a weak electrolyte solution with known molality, compute the van 't Hoff factor and then the degree of dissociation.
stem: A weak electrolyte $\text{ACl}_2$ dissociates as $\text{ACl}_2\rightleftharpoons\text{A}^{2+}+2\text{Cl}^-$. A $0.25\ \text{mol kg}^{-1}$ aqueous solution has $\Delta T_f=0.93\ \text{K}$. Given $K_f(\text{water})=1.86\ \text{K kg mol}^{-1}$, find its degree of dissociation.
solution:
The van’t Hoff factor is $i=\dfrac{\Delta T_f}{K_fm}=\dfrac{0.93}{1.86\times0.25}=2$.
For $\mathrm{ACl_2\rightleftharpoons A^{2+}+2Cl^-}$, $i=1+2\alpha$.
$$\alpha=\frac{i-1}{2}=\frac{1}{2}$$
working:
$i=\dfrac{\Delta T_f}{K_f m}=\dfrac{0.93}{1.86(0.25)}=2$.
For $\text{ACl}_2\rightleftharpoons\text{A}^{2+}+2\text{Cl}^-$, $i=1+2\alpha$.
$\alpha=\dfrac{i-1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

Independent check: Van’t Hoff factor: $i=\Delta T_f/(K_f m)=0.93/(1.86\times0.25)=2$. For $\text{ACl}_2\to\text{A}^{2+}+2\text{Cl}^-$, $i=1+2\alpha$, so $\alpha=1/2$.
distractor_notes: A: Uses an incorrect coefficient of $3$ for the dissociation contribution to $i$.\nC: Uses $i/3$ as the degree of dissociation.\nD: Omits the stoichiometric factor of $2$ in $i=1+2\alpha$.

brief: A complex with two different ligands and counter-ions is described; pick its fully correct IUPAC name with ligands in alphabetical order.
stem: The name of $[\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5\text{Cl}]\text{Cl}_2$ is
solution:
The complex ion has charge $+2$. If the oxidation state of Co is $x$, then $x-1=+2$, so $x=+3$.
The ligands are named alphabetically as ammine and chlorido; the counter-ion is chloride.
Hence, the name is pentaamminechloridocobalt(III) chloride.
working:
Complex charge $=+2$; hence $x-1=+2$, so cobalt is in oxidation state $+3$.\nLigands in alphabetical order: ammine, chlorido.\nThe two outer-sphere chloride ions are named collectively as chloride.

Independent check: The two outer Cl⁻ ions make the complex cation 2+. Since NH₃ is neutral and coordinated Cl is −1, Co is +3. Ligand names are ordered alphabetically: ammine before chlorido.
distractor_notes: B: places ligands out of alphabetical order.\nC: assigns the wrong oxidation state to cobalt.\nD: incorrectly prefixes the counter-ion name with a numerical prefix.

brief: For a xenon fluoride (e.g. XeF4), determine the number of lone pairs on xenon, its hybridisation and the shape of the molecule.
stem: For $\text{XeF}_4$, the number of lone pairs on xenon, its hybridisation and the molecular shape are
solution:
Xe has $8$ valence electrons; in $\text{XeF}_4$, four Xe–F bonds leave two lone pairs on xenon.
$$\text{Steric number}=4+2=6\;\Rightarrow\;sp^3d^2$$
The two lone pairs occupy opposite positions, giving a square-planar molecular shape.
working:
Xe has $8$ valence electrons; four Xe–F bonds leave $4$ nonbonding electrons on Xe.\nThus Xe has $2$ lone pairs and steric number $6$.\nHybridisation: $sp^3d^2$; shape: square planar.

Independent check: Xe has 8 valence electrons. Four Xe–F bonds leave 2 lone pairs on Xe, giving 6 electron domains: sp³d² hybridisation and square-planar molecular shape.
distractor_notes: B: counts one lone pair and assigns the corresponding wrong shape.\nC: uses the wrong steric number and geometry.\nD: overcounts the lone pairs and assigns the wrong shape.

brief: Given limiting molar conductivities of a strong electrolyte pair, assemble the limiting molar conductivity of a weak acid (or base) by addition and subtraction of the values.
stem: At the same temperature, $\Lambda_m^\circ$ for $\text{HCl}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ and $\text{NaCl}$ are $426.0$, $91.0$ and $126.4\ \text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$, respectively. What is $\Lambda_m^\circ$ for $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$?
solution:
By Kohlrausch’s law, $\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{CH_3COOH})=\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{HCl})+\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{CH_3COONa})-\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{NaCl})$.
$$\Lambda_m^\circ=426.0+91.0-126.4=390.6\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}$$
working:
By Kohlrausch's law, $\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})=\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl})+\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa})-\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl})$.\n$=426.0+91.0-126.4=390.6\ \text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Independent check: By Kohlrausch’s law, Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH₃COONa) − Λ°(NaCl) = 426.0 + 91.0 − 126.4 = 390.6 S cm² mol⁻¹.
distractor_notes: A: omits the contribution from sodium acetate.\nC: uses an incorrect sign in the ionic-conductivity combination.\nD: adds all three given values instead of subtracting the sodium ion contribution.

brief: Figure shows a disubstituted benzene with one activating and one deactivating group; predict the major mononitration product considering the stronger director.
stem: On mononitration with concentrated $\text{HNO}_3/\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ of the compound as shown in the figure, which product is favoured?
solution: The $-CHO$ group directs nitration meta, while $-CH_3$ directs ortho/para; both groups therefore favour substitution at C3 and C5. C5 is para to methyl and less sterically hindered than C3, which is ortho to methyl. Hence the favoured product is 2-methyl-5-nitrobenzaldehyde.
working:
The methyl group directs to C3 and C5; the aldehyde group directs meta to itself, also to C3 and C5.
C5 is para to methyl, whereas C3 is ortho to methyl.
The less hindered para product is favoured: 2-methyl-5-nitrobenzaldehyde.

Independent check: CHO directs nitration meta; methyl directs ortho/para. Both favor positions 3 and 5. Position 5 is less sterically hindered than position 3, so the favoured product is 2-methyl-5-nitrobenzaldehyde.
distractor_notes: A: Selects the ortho-to-methyl site rather than the less hindered para site.\nB: Places nitro para to the deactivating aldehyde group.\nD: Selects a site ortho to the deactivating aldehyde and meta to methyl.

brief: Figure shows Fischer projections of similar molecules; assign R/S at each stereocentre and classify pairs as identical, enantiomers or diastereomers.
stem: For Fischer projections I–III shown in the figure, select the correct configurations and pairwise relationships.
options: I: $(2S,3S)$; II: $(2R,3R)$; III: $(2R,3R)$; I–II and I–III are enantiomers, while II–III are identical.
I: $(2S,3S)$; II: $(2R,3R)$; III: $(2R,3S)$; I–II are enantiomers, and I–III and II–III are diastereomers.
I: $(2S,3S)$; II: $(2R,3R)$; III: $(2S,3R)$; I–II are enantiomers, and I–III and II–III are diastereomers.
I: $(2S,3S)$; II: $(2R,3R)$; III: $(2S,3S)$; I–II and II–III are enantiomers, while I–III are identical.
solution:
At C2, priorities are $\mathrm{OH>CHO>C3\ chain>H}$; at C3, $\mathrm{OH>C2\ chain>CH_3>H}$. Since horizontal groups in a Fischer projection point towards the viewer, invert the observed order when H is horizontal.
Thus, I is $(2S,3S)$, II is $(2R,3R)$, and III is $(2S,3R)$.
I–II differ at both stereocentres and are enantiomers; I–III and II–III differ at one centre and are diastereomers.
working:
At C2: OH > CHO > C3 chain > H; at C3: OH > C2 chain > CH3 > H.
In a Fischer projection, horizontal groups point towards the viewer; reverse the order when H is horizontal.
I: $(2S,3S)$; II: $(2R,3R)$; III: $(2S,3R)$.
I–II differ at both centres: enantiomers.
I–III and II–III differ at one centre: diastereomers.

Independent check: At C2, priorities are OH > CHO > lower chain > H; at C3, OH > upper chain > CH3 > H. In each Fischer projection, H is horizontal (toward), so the observed sense is inverted. This gives I (2S,3S), II (2R,3R), and III (2S,3R). I–II are enantiomers; the other pairs are diastereomers.
distractor_notes: B: swaps the configurations assigned to the two centres in III. C: assigns III the same configuration as II, then classifies those two as identical. D: assigns III the same configuration as I, then classifies those two as identical.

brief: Write the balanced combustion equation of a gaseous fuel, count Δng, and convert the given ΔH to ΔU (or vice versa) using ΔngRT.
stem: For complete combustion of $1$ mol of propane, with water formed as a liquid, find $\\Delta U$ at $300$ K if $\Delta H=-2200$ kJ mol$^{-1}$. Take $R=8.0$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
solution:
For the combustion reaction, $[?][?]$; hence $[?][?]$.
Using $[?][?]$ and $[?][?]$,
$$\Delta U=\Delta H-\Delta n_gRT=-2200-(-3)(2.4)=-2192.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}.$$
working:
$\text{C}_3\text{H}_8(g)+5\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow3\text{CO}_2(g)+4\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$
$\Delta n_g=3-6=-3$
$RT=(8.0)(300)=2400$ J mol$^{-1}=2.4$ kJ mol$^{-1}$
$\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT$
$\Delta U=-2200-(-3)(2.4)=-2192.8$ kJ mol$^{-1}$

Independent check: C₃H₈ + 5O₂ → 3CO₂ + 4H₂O(l), so Δn_gas = 3 − 6 = −3. Using ΔH = ΔU + Δn_gasRT, ΔU = −2200 − (−3)(8)(300)/1000 = −2192.8 kJ mol⁻¹.
distractor_notes: A: reverses the sign when rearranging the relation. B: miscounts $\Delta n_g$ as $-1$. C: overlooks one mole of gaseous $\text{O}_2$ when counting $\Delta n_g$.

brief: Sentence split into parts (a/b/c/d) with a subject-verb agreement error (collective noun / distance-expression treated as singular); one option 'No error'.
stem:
Identify the part that contains an error, if any.

(a) The fleet of research vessels
(b) are expected to reach the harbour
(c) before the onset of the monsoon,
(d) according to the latest forecast.
solution: “Fleet” is a singular collective noun and takes the singular verb “is.” Therefore, “are expected” should be “is expected,” so the error is in (b).
working:
The subject is the singular collective noun “fleet”; it requires “is expected,” not “are expected.” The error is in (b). Parts (a) and (c) contain no agreement error; the sentence is not error-free.

Independent check: “Fleet” is a singular collective noun, so the verb should be “is,” not “are.”
distractor_notes: A: The singular collective noun is correctly formed in (a). C: The time phrase in (c) does not create an agreement error. D: Incorrect because “are expected” disagrees with the singular subject “fleet”.

archetype: para jumble (5 sentences, find the first sentence)
brief: Four sentence options given for the opening of a short paragraph on a general topic; pick the most coherent opener.
stem:
Arrange the following sentences into a coherent paragraph. Which sentence should come first?

P. As a result, many households now grow herbs and vegetables in containers.
Q. Urban gardening has become a practical way to bring greenery into crowded neighbourhoods.
R. Even a small balcony can provide enough room for a few pots.
S. These plants can also make fresh ingredients readily available.
T. With regular watering and sunlight, they are easy to maintain.
solution: Q introduces the broad topic of urban gardening, while the other sentences provide examples or refer back to plants and pots introduced later.
working:
Q introduces the topic. R gives a specific example; T’s “they” refers to the pots/plants, followed by P’s “As a result” and S’s “These plants”. Q is the only broad introductory sentence.

Independent check: Q introduces the topic; the other sentences depend on ideas or references introduced later.
distractor_notes:
P: “As a result” requires an earlier cause.
R: “Even” makes it a supporting example, not an introduction.
S: “These plants” requires an earlier reference.

brief: Single blank in a simple sentence; choose the word that fits context, options being near-synonyms of everyday level.
stem: The guide gave a ______ explanation of the route, so none of the hikers took a wrong turn.
solution: “None of the hikers took a wrong turn” indicates that the route was easy to understand; therefore, the explanation was **clear**.
working:
“None ... took a wrong turn” indicates the explanation was easy to understand: clear.

Independent check: A clear explanation would help hikers follow the route without taking a wrong turn.
distractor_notes:
Vague: means unclear, contrary to the outcome.
Complex: describes difficulty, not helpful clarity.
Lengthy: describes duration or extent, not how understandable it was.
critic_notes: [minor] The item is too trivial for BITSAT since 'vague', 'complex' and 'lengthy' are all obviously incompatible with 'none of the hikers took a wrong turn'; use closer distractors such as 'meticulous', 'succinct' or 'cursory' to raise the discrimination.

brief: Pick the nearest meaning of a common NCERT-level word like 'obsolete' or 'candid' from four options.
stem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to **candid**.
solution: “Candid” means honest and straightforward; its nearest synonym is “frank.”
working:
“Candid” means truthful and straightforward; “frank” is the nearest synonym.

Independent check: “Candid” means frank or honest; (A) is the nearest synonym.
distractor_notes:
Careless: means inattentive or negligent.
Timid: means lacking confidence or courage.
Formal: means following established conventions.

brief: Give the meaning of an idiom like 'to let the cat out of the bag' used in a short sentence.
stem: When Meera asked about the surprise farewell, Arun **beat around the bush** instead of answering directly. What does the idiom mean?
options: Avoid discussing the main point directly
Make a difficult task seem simple
Criticise someone in a roundabout way
solution: “Beat around the bush” means avoiding the main point rather than answering directly. Hence, it means to avoid discussing the main point directly.
working:
To beat around the bush is to avoid addressing the main point directly. The other options describe revealing, simplifying, or criticising.

Independent check: “Beat around the bush” means avoiding the main point instead of speaking directly.
distractor_notes: B: Confuses evasion with disclosure. C: Describes simplifying a task. D: Adds criticism, which is not part of the idiom.

brief: Choose the opposite of a moderately common word such as 'abundant' or 'transparent'.
stem: Choose the word opposite in meaning to **SCARCE**.
solution: “Scarce” means available in small quantities; “plentiful” means available in abundance, so it is the opposite.
working:
Scarce means available in small quantities; plentiful means available in abundance. The other options are similar to scarce.

Independent check: “Scarce” means limited or insufficient; its opposite is “plentiful.”
distractor_notes: A: Near-synonym of scarce. C: Near-synonym of scarce. D: Near-synonym of scarce.

brief: Underlined phrase with a tense inconsistency in a time-clause sentence (e.g., 'after he will finish'); pick the grammatically correct improvement.
stem: Choose the best improvement for the underlined phrase: We will begin the meeting <u>as soon as the director will arrive</u>.
options: as soon as the director arrived
as soon as the director arrives
as soon as the director is arriving
as soon as the director had arrived
solution: In a future time clause introduced by “as soon as,” use the simple present: “as soon as the director arrives.”
working:
In a future time clause introduced by “as soon as,” use the simple present: “the director arrives.” The other options use an unsuitable tense or aspect.

Independent check: In a future time clause introduced by “as soon as,” use the present simple: “the director arrives.”
distractor_notes: B: Uses past tense despite a future meeting. C: Uses an unnecessary progressive form. D: Uses past perfect, inconsistent with the future context.

brief: Complete an analogy pair like 'Doctor : Hospital :: Teacher : ?' with four options at a moderate difficulty level.
stem: COMPASS : DIRECTION :: THERMOMETER : ?
solution: A compass indicates direction; similarly, a thermometer measures temperature. Hence the matching relationship is with temperature.
working:
A compass indicates direction; a thermometer indicates temperature. The other options are associated concepts or materials, not the quantity indicated.

Independent check: A compass indicates direction; a thermometer measures temperature.
distractor_notes: B: Weather is a context in which temperature is measured. C: Mercury may be a thermometer's contents. D: Names the general activity, not the indicated quantity.
critic_notes: [minor] The item is tagged 'Sentence Completion (vocabulary)' but is actually a word-analogy question, so the label (and the duplicate tag shared with q63) should be corrected to 'Analogy'.

stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Urban trees are often praised for making streets more attractive, but their importance extends beyond appearance. By casting shade, trees reduce the amount of heat absorbed by pavements and buildings. They also release water vapour through their leaves, a process that can cool the surrounding air. Together, these effects can make a tree-lined street more comfortable during hot weather.

The benefits, however, are not distributed evenly. In many cities, some neighbourhoods have abundant tree cover while others have few trees and extensive paved surfaces. Residents in the latter areas may face greater exposure to heat, particularly when they have limited access to air-conditioned indoor spaces. Planting trees can help, but it is not an instant remedy: young trees provide less shade, and they need suitable soil, water, and care to survive.

For this reason, urban planners increasingly treat tree cover as part of public infrastructure rather than as decoration. They can map where shade is scarce, select species suited to local conditions, and plan for long-term maintenance. Such measures do not eliminate the need for other responses to extreme heat, but they can make neighbourhoods cooler and more liveable over time. The success of a planting programme, therefore, depends not simply on how many trees are planted, but also on where they grow and whether they are supported as they mature.

What is the central idea of the passage?
options: Urban trees improve city life when they are planned and maintained as useful infrastructure.
Urban trees are mainly valuable because they make streets visually attractive.
Planting trees can immediately eliminate the effects of extreme heat in cities.
Every city neighbourhood benefits equally from having the same number of trees.
solution: The passage explains that trees cool urban areas, but their benefits depend on where they are planted and how they are maintained. Thus, trees are most effective when planned and supported as useful infrastructure.
working: The passage describes how trees cool streets and stresses that their benefits depend on equitable placement and long-term care. It concludes that tree cover should be treated as infrastructure.
distractor_notes: B reduces the benefits to appearance; C exaggerates what tree planting can achieve; D contradicts the passage's point about uneven distribution.

stem: According to the passage, what helps cool the air around trees?
options: The growth of young trees without regular care
The absorption of water by nearby paved surfaces
The release of water vapour through their leaves
The replacement of all other heat responses by tree cover
solution: Trees cool the surrounding air by releasing water vapour through their leaves.
working: The passage states that trees release water vapour through their leaves, which can cool the surrounding air.
distractor_notes: B reverses the passage's explanation; C is not identified as a cooling process; D contradicts the passage's statement that other heat responses remain necessary.

brief: Give five similar-looking words and ask which one comes third when arranged as in a dictionary; brief the author to include words sharing first two letters so third-letter comparison matters.
stem: Arrange these words in dictionary order: **cab, cabin, cable, cactus, cadence**. Which word comes third?
solution: Compare letters alphabetically: “cab” comes first as a prefix, followed by “cabin” and then “cable” since $i<l$. Thus, the third word is cable.
working:
Order: cab, cabin, cable, cactus, cadence. “cab” comes first as a prefix; cabin precedes cable because i precedes l. The third word is cable.

Independent check: Alphabetically: cab, cabin, cable, cactus, cadence. The third word is cable.
distractor_notes: A: Places cabin after cable. C: Overlooks that both b-words precede c-words. D: Overlooks that cactus precedes cadence.
critic_notes: [minor] The five words are already printed in correct dictionary order, so the "third" word can be read straight off the list without any sorting; shuffle the presentation order.

brief: A word is coded by shifting each letter a fixed number of positions forward; provide the coded form of one word and ask for the code of a second word at moderate difficulty.
stem: If each letter is replaced by the letter two places after it in the alphabet, MANGO is coded as **OCPIQ**. How will RIVER be coded by the same rule?
solution: Shift each letter forward by 2 places: $R\to T,\ I\to K,\ V\to X,\ E\to G,\ R\to T$. Thus, RIVER is coded as $\boxed{\text{TKXGT}}$.
working:
Shift every letter forward by 2: R→T, I→K, V→X, E→G, R→T. Hence RIVER → TKXGT.

Independent check: Shift each letter forward by 2: R→T, I→K, V→X, E→G, R→T, giving TKXGT.
distractor_notes: B: Shifts V by only one place. C: Shifts letters backward. D: Shifts the final R by three places.

brief: Simple increasing series with a single constant pattern (e.g. add fixed number or alternate small steps); ask for the next term at the easiest level.
stem: Find the next term in the series: 7, 12, 17, 22, ____.
solution:
Each term increases by $5$.
$$22+5=27$$
working:
Each term increases by 5: 22 + 5 = 27.

Independent check: Each term increases by 5, so the next term is 22 + 5 = 27.
distractor_notes: A: Adds 4. C: Adds 6. D: Adds 7.

brief: Pair of numbers related by a simple operation (e.g. square/cube, digit sum, or multiply-and-add constant); give one pair and a single number, ask for the analogous partner.
stem: Select the number related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first: $18 : 9 :: 26 : ?$
solution:
Add the digits of each number: $1+8=9$, so apply the same rule to $26$.
$$2+6=8$$
working:
Add the digits of each number: $1+8=9$, so $2+6=8$. The other options do not equal the digit sum of 26.

Independent check: 18 → 1+8=9; therefore 26 → 2+6=8.
distractor_notes: B: Uses the difference of the digits. C: Doubles the digit sum. D: Uses the difference of the digits in reverse order.

brief: First pair maps a word/letter set to a numeric code using letter positional values combined with rearrangement of letters; candidate must decode the hidden two-step rule and apply it to a new word at highest difficulty.
stem: In a letter-number code, CLOUD is written as 21151243. By the same rule, how is TRACE written?
solution:
Arrange the letters in descending alphabetical order and write their A1Z26 values consecutively.
$$\text{TRACE} \to \text{TRECA} \to 20|18|5|3|1 = 2018531$$
working:
Arrange the letters in reverse alphabetical order, then replace each by its A1Z26 value: CLOUD → UOLDC → 21|15|12|4|3. TRACE → TRECA → 20|18|5|3|1 = 2018531.

Independent check: CLOUD has letter positions 3, 12, 15, 21, 4; arranging them in descending order gives 21, 15, 12, 4, 3. TRACE gives 20, 18, 1, 3, 5, which in descending order is 20, 18, 5, 3, 1 = 2018531.
distractor_notes: B uses alphabetical rather than reverse alphabetical order; C misorders the values for E and C; D keeps TRACE in its original order.
critic_notes: [minor] The unsegmented code 21151243 forces the candidate to guess both the parsing and the unstated rule (letters taken in descending alphabetical order, then converted to positions), so add hyphens as in Q87 or give a second worked example.

stem: Select the figure which is different from the other three.
solution: Three of the figures are rotations of the same figure; figure (D) is its mirror image, which cannot be obtained by rotation.
working: Three of the figures are rotations of the same figure; figure (D) is its mirror image, which cannot be obtained by rotation.

brief: Two straightforward universal/affirmative statements (All A are B, All B are C) with two conclusions; ask which conclusions definitely follow, keeping it at beginner level with no negatives or possibilities.
stem:
**Statements:**
All cedars are trees.
All trees are plants.

**Conclusions:**
I. All cedars are plants.
II. All plants are cedars.
solution: Since cedars are trees and trees are plants, cedars are plants; hence conclusion I follows. The inclusion cannot be reversed, so conclusion II does not follow.
working:
Cedars ⊆ trees ⊆ plants, so conclusion I follows. The inclusion need not reverse; conclusion II does not follow.

Independent check: Cedars ⊆ trees and trees ⊆ plants, so cedars ⊆ plants. The statements do not imply plants ⊆ cedars.
distractor_notes: B: Reverses the inclusion chain. C: Assumes plants must be cedars. D: Misses the direct transitive inclusion.

brief: Series of letter groups where each term shifts forward by a fixed/increasing number of positions; ask for the next term, difficulty 2 with a mildly varying shift.
stem: Find the next term in the letter-group series: **BC, EF, JK, QR, ____**
solution: The first letters advance by $+3,+5,+7$, so the next advances by $+9$: $B,E,J,Q,Z$. Each pair consists of consecutive letters, wrapping after $Z$; hence the next pair is $ZA$.
working:
The first letters advance by +3, +5, +7, then +9: B, E, J, Q, Z. The paired second letter is always the next alphabet letter, giving ZA.

Independent check: First-letter positions are 2, 5, 10, 17, increasing by 3, 5, 7; next increase is 9, giving position 26 (Z). Each pair has consecutive letters, wrapping after Z, so the next pair is ZA.
distractor_notes: B: Uses an incorrect final shift. C: Wraps to A rather than advancing from Q by nine. D: Reverses the order of the final pair.

brief: Statements with one negative or particular statement (Some A are not B type); conclusions include one definite deduction and one 'possibility' conclusion; ask which conclusions follow.
stem:
**Statements:**
All limes are citrus fruits.
Some fruits are not citrus fruits.

**Conclusions:**
I. Some fruits are not limes.
II. Some citrus fruits may be limes.
solution: Since all limes are citrus fruits, any fruit that is not a citrus fruit cannot be a lime; hence some fruits are not limes. The statements also allow some citrus fruits to be limes, so both conclusions follow.
working:
The fruits that are not citrus cannot be limes, so I follows. Limes can be included within citrus fruits without contradiction, so II is possible.

Independent check: Since all limes are citrus, the stated non-citrus fruits are not limes, so I follows. The statements do not rule out some citrus fruits being limes, so II is possible and follows.
distractor_notes: A: Misses the compatible possibility in II. B: Misses the definite deduction in I. D: Rejects both a definite deduction and a compatible possibility.
critic_notes: [minor] Conclusion II's "may be" phrases a definitely-true relation as a mere possibility, which makes the key convention-dependent; state it plainly as "Some citrus fruits are limes" so that C is unambiguously correct.

brief: Give a medium-length word and four options; ask which option word can be formed using only the letters of the given word, each letter used at most as many times as it appears.
stem: Which of the following words can be formed from the letters of **NOTEBOOKS**, using each letter no more often than it occurs in the given word?
solution:
NOTEBOOKS contains $B$, $K$, and $S$ once each, and has at least one $O$.
Thus $BOOKS$ can be formed using the available letters.
working:
NOTEBOOKS has O twice; N, T, E, B, K and S once each.
BOOKS uses available letters.
STOOP needs three Os; BONNET needs two Ns; TOOT needs two Ts.

Independent check: NOTEBOOKS contains B, K, S once each and O three times, so BOOKS can be formed. The other options require a missing P or a repeated N or T.
distractor_notes: B: Uses three Os, but only two are available. C: Uses two Ns, but only one is available. D: Uses two Ts, but only one is available.

brief: Four letter/number pairs where three share the same internal relation (e.g. same difference or product between pair members); pick the pair that does not follow, at moderate difficulty with a non-obvious common rule.
stem: Three of the following letter-number pairs follow the same rule. Select the odd pair out.
solution:
Using alphabet position $n$, the rule is number $=n^2-1$. For $B,D,F$, this gives $2^2-1=3$, $4^2-1=15$, and $6^2-1=35$.
For $H$, the number should be $8^2-1=63$, not $65$.
working:
For each letter with alphabet position n, the number is n² − 1: B → 2²−1=3; D → 4²−1=15; F → 6²−1=35. H should give 8²−1=63, not 65.

Independent check: Letter positions are 2, 4, 6, 8. The first three numbers equal position² − 1; for H, the number should be 63, not 65.
distractor_notes: A follows position²−1; B follows position²−1; C follows position²−1.

brief: Simple direct letter coding: show a word written as a group of number codes and ask for the code of another word using the same letter-number mapping, kept easy with a short word.
stem: If **LAMP** is coded as **12-1-13-16**, what is the code for **MAP**?
solution: Each letter is coded by its position in the alphabet: $M=13$, $A=1$, and $P=16$. Hence, MAP is coded as $13-1-16$.
working:
Each letter is replaced by its position in the alphabet: M=13, A=1, P=16. Hence MAP = 13-1-16.

Independent check: Use each letter’s position in the alphabet: M=13, A=1, P=16.
distractor_notes: B: Uses L's code for M. C: Reverses the codes for M and A. D: Uses O's code for P.

stem: Find the missing number in the given figure.
solution: In each row, the third number is twice the sum of the first two: 2, 9 → 22; 8, 3 → 22. So, 5, 8 → 26.
working: In each row, the third number is twice the sum of the first two: 2, 9 → 22; 8, 3 → 22. So, 5, 8 → 26.

brief: Pointing-type question: a person says 'he is the son of my grandfather's only son/daughter' style single-step chain; ask how the pointed person is related to the speaker, using a short two-link chain.
stem: A woman points to a boy and says, “He is the son of my paternal grandfather’s only son, who is my father.” How is the boy related to her?
solution: Her paternal grandfather’s only son is her father. The boy is her father’s son, so he is her brother.
working:
Her paternal grandfather’s only son is her father. The boy is her father’s son, so he is her brother.
B: He is not her child; C: no sibling’s parent is stated; D: the paternal line is specified.

Independent check: Her paternal grandfather’s only son is her father. The boy is her father’s son, so he is her brother.
distractor_notes: B: Mistakes the boy for her own son. C: Assumes he is her sibling’s child. D: Treats the specified paternal line as an unspecified branch.
critic_notes: [minor] The appositive "who is my father" hands over the entire relationship chain, reducing the puzzle to a one-step reading exercise; delete that clause.

brief: Total number of students in a row and a student's position from one end is given; ask their position from the other end or how many are between two given ranks — keep it a one- or two-clause easy question.
stem: There are 32 students standing in a row. Mira is 11th from the left. What is her position from the right?
solution:
Position from the right $= 32 - 11 + 1 = 22$.
Mira is $22$nd from the right.
working:
Position from right = 32 − 11 + 1 = 22.

Independent check: Position from right = 32 − 11 + 1 = 22nd.
distractor_notes: A: Subtracts without adding 1. C: Adds one too many. D: Uses an incorrect subtraction.

subtopic: Image of a point in a line
brief: Find the image of a point in a given line and construct the equation of the line joining the point to its image.
stem: The image of $P(2,-1)$ in the line $3x+4y+23=0$ and the equation of the line joining $P$ to its image are, respectively,
solution:
For reflection across $ax+by+c=0$, $P'=P-\dfrac{2f}{a^2+b^2}(a,b)$, where $f=3(2)+4(-1)+23=25$.
$$P'=(2,-1)-2(3,4)=(-4,-9).$$
The joining line is perpendicular to the mirror line, so it has normal $(4,-3)$ and passes through $(2,-1)$: $4(x-2)-3(y+1)=0$, or $4x-3y-11=0$.
working:
$f=3(2)+4(-1)+23=25$, $3^2+4^2=25$.
$P'=P-\dfrac{2f}{25}(3,4)=(-4,-9)$.
The joining line is perpendicular to the mirror line, so its normal is $(4,-3)$.
$4(x-2)-3(y+1)=0\Rightarrow 4x-3y-11=0$.

Independent check: For P(2,-1), the line expression is 25 and the normal has squared length 25. Reflection gives P'=P-2(3,4)=(-4,-9). The line through P and P' is 4x-3y-11=0.
distractor_notes: B uses the opposite sign for the reflection displacement; C gives the mirror line itself; D uses a line parallel to the mirror instead of perpendicular to it.

brief: Count arrangements of words where certain letters are never adjacent (complementary counting).
stem: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of COMPUTER have the letters C and O not adjacent?
solution:
All 8 letters are distinct, so total arrangements are $8!$. Treating C and O as one block gives $2\cdot7!$ arrangements with them adjacent.
$$8!-2\cdot7!=40320-10080=30240$$
working:
All letters are distinct: $8!=40320$.
With C and O adjacent: $2\cdot7!=10080$.
Required count $=8!-2\cdot7!=30240$.

Independent check: All 8 letters are distinct. Total arrangements: 8! = 40320. With C and O adjacent: 2 × 7! = 10080. Thus nonadjacent: 40320 − 10080 = 30240.
distractor_notes: B ignores the restriction; C counts only arrangements with C and O adjacent; D subtracts only one ordering of the adjacent pair.

brief: Find the condition on the radius/centre so that a circle is tangent to both coordinate axes or a given line.
stem: A circle has centre $(p,9-p)$, where $0<p<9$. If it is tangent to both coordinate axes, what is its radius?
solution:
Tangency to both coordinate axes gives $r=p=9-p$.
$$2p=9\Rightarrow p=4.5,\qquad r=4.5.$$
working:
Tangency to the axes gives $r=p=9-p$.\n$2p=9\Rightarrow r=4.5$.

Independent check: Tangency to both axes requires the radius to equal both positive coordinates: $p=9-p$. Thus $p=4.5$ and the radius is $4.5$.
distractor_notes: A: Uses half the coordinate sum incorrectly.\nC: Rounds the radius to the nearest integer.\nD: Uses the sum of the coordinates as the radius.

subtopic: Cross product and angle between vectors
brief: Use the cross product of two vectors to find the sine of the angle between them, given their dot product.
stem: For $\vec a=\hat i+2\hat j+2\hat k$ and $\vec b=2\hat i+\hat j+2\hat k$, given that $\vec a\cdot\vec b=8$, the sine of the angle between them is
solution:
Using $\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\vec a\times\vec b|}{|\vec a||\vec b|}$, with $|\vec a|=|\vec b|=3$ and $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\sqrt{17}$,
$$\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{17}}{3\cdot3}=\frac{\sqrt{17}}{9}.$$
working:
$\vec a\times\vec b=2\hat i+2\hat j-3\hat k$, so $|\vec a\times\vec b|=\sqrt{17}$.
$|\vec a|=|\vec b|=3$.
$\sin\theta=\dfrac{|\vec a\times\vec b|}{|\vec a||\vec b|}=\dfrac{\sqrt{17}}{9}$.

Independent check: |a|=|b|=3 and a·b=8, so cos θ=8/9. Thus sin θ=√(1−64/81)=√17/9.
distractor_notes: B gives the cosine from the dot product; C divides by the sum of the magnitudes; D introduces an extra factor of $2$ in the denominator.

brief: Find the equation of a line through the intersection of two given lines and passing through another point (family of lines).
stem: The equation of the line through the intersection of $x+2y-8=0$ and $3x-y-3=0$, and through $(5,0)$, is
solution:
Solving the two lines gives their intersection $(2,3)$. The slope through $(2,3)$ and $(5,0)$ is $-1$, so
$$y-3=-(x-2)\quad\Rightarrow\quad x+y-5=0.$$
working:
From $3x-y-3=0$, $y=3x-3$.
Substitution gives $x+2(3x-3)-8=0$, hence $(x,y)=(2,3)$.
Through $(2,3)$ and $(5,0)$, the slope is $-1$.
$y-3=-(x-2)\Rightarrow x+y-5=0$.

Independent check: Solving the two equations gives intersection (2,3). The line through (2,3) and (5,0) is x+y-5=0.
distractor_notes: B uses an incorrect slope through the intersection; C uses slope $1$; D uses slope $-3$.

brief: Evaluate a limit of the form (1 + kx)^(a/x) or (f(x))^g(x) reducing to e.
stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle \lim_{x\to0}(1+2x)^{\dfrac{3}{x}}(1-x)^{\dfrac{2}{x}}$.
solution:
Let $L$ denote the limit. Taking logarithms and using $\lim_{x\to0}\frac{\ln(1+ax)}{x}=a$,
$$\ln L=3\cdot2+2\cdot(-1)=4.$$
Hence $L=e^4$.
working:
$\ln L=\lim_{x\to0}\left[\dfrac{3}{x}\ln(1+2x)+\dfrac{2}{x}\ln(1-x)\right]=6-2=4,\quad L=e^4.$

Independent check: Taking logarithms, the exponent is \(\frac{3}{x}\ln(1+2x)+\frac{2}{x}\ln(1-x)\to 6-2=4\). Thus the limit is \(e^4\).
distractor_notes: A: omits the coefficient $3$ in the first exponent, making the contributions cancel.\nC: ignores the second factor.\nD: uses the wrong sign for $\ln(1-x)\sim -x$.

brief: Find the domain of a function involving a square root of a quadratic expression using sign analysis.
stem: The domain of $f(x)=\sqrt{-2x^2+7x-3}$ is
solution:
For the square root to be defined, $-2x^2+7x-3\ge 0$. Its roots are $\frac12$ and $3$, and the quadratic opens downward.
$$-2x^2+7x-3\ge 0\quad\text{for }\frac12\le x\le 3$$
Hence the domain is $[\frac12,3]$.
working:
$-2x^2+7x-3=0$ has roots $x=\dfrac{1}{2},3$.\\
Since the quadratic opens downward, $-2x^2+7x-3\ge 0$ between and including the roots.\\
Domain: $[\dfrac{1}{2},3]$.

Independent check: Solve −2x²+7x−3 ≥ 0. Its roots are 1/2 and 3, and the quadratic is nonnegative between them, inclusive.
distractor_notes: A: Reverses the sign interval. C: Excludes the roots, although the square root is defined there. D: Makes a sign error when finding the smaller root.

brief: Given a small frequency/univariate table, compute the mean deviation about the median.
stem: The table gives a data set with frequencies. Find its mean deviation about the median. $$\begin{array}{c|cccc}x_i&1&3&5&8\\f_i&2&3&2&2\end{array}$$
solution:
The total frequency is $N=9$, so the median is $m=3$. Hence,
$$\text{Mean deviation about median}=\frac{\sum f_i|x_i-m|}{N}=\frac{2|1-3|+3|3-3|+2|5-3|+2|8-3|}{9}=2.$$
working:
$N=9,\quad m=3$\n$\text{MD}=\dfrac{2|1-3|+3|3-3|+2|5-3|+2|8-3|}{9}=\dfrac{18}{9}=2.$

Independent check: There are 9 observations, so the median is 3. The mean deviation is \(\frac{2|1-3|+3|3-3|+2|5-3|+2|8-3|}{9}=\frac{18}{9}=2\).
distractor_notes: B: treats the distinct data values as unweighted when finding the median.\nC: divides by $N-1$ instead of $N$.\nD: omits division by the total frequency.

brief: Given a determinant with entries involving x, factorise it into linear factors using row/column operations.
stem: Using row operations, factorise the determinant: $$\begin{vmatrix}x-2&-1&1\\x&x-3&-1\\x&-2&x-2\end{vmatrix}$$
solution:
Apply $R_2\to R_2-R_1$ and $R_3\to R_3-R_1$; these operations leave the determinant unchanged:
$$D=\begin{vmatrix}x-2&-1&1\\2&x-2&-2\\2&-1&x-3\end{vmatrix}=(x-2)\big[(x-2)(x-3)-2\big].$$
Hence, $D=(x-2)(x-1)(x-4)$.
working:
$R_2\to R_2-R_1,\ R_3\to R_3-R_1$ gives $D=\begin{vmatrix}x-2&-1&1\\2&x-2&-2\\2&-1&x-3\end{vmatrix}.$\n$D=(x-2)[(x-2)(x-3)-2]=(x-2)(x-1)(x-4).$

Independent check: Expanding along the first row gives \(D=(x-2)(x^2-5x+4)+(x^2-x)+(-x^2+x)=(x-2)(x-1)(x-4)\).
distractor_notes: B: gives the first factor the wrong sign.\nC: gives the second factor the wrong sign.\nD: gives the third factor the wrong sign.

brief: Find the combined standard deviation of two groups given their sizes, means, and standard deviations.
stem: Two groups of $20$ observations have means $10$ and $14$, and standard deviations $1$ and $3$, respectively. Find the combined standard deviation.
working:
$\bar{x}=12$\n$\sigma^2=\dfrac{20[1^2+(10-12)^2]+20[3^2+(14-12)^2]}{40}=9,\quad \sigma=3.$

Independent check: The combined mean is 12. The combined variance is the average of the within-group variances plus the squared offsets from 12: [(1²+2²)+(3²+2²)]/2 = 9. Thus the combined standard deviation is 3.
distractor_notes: A: uses only the groups' mean offsets and ignores within-group variation.\nB: combines within-group variances but ignores the difference between the means.\nD: adds average standard deviation and half the difference between means.

brief: Use differentials to estimate the approximate value of a root of a number or a function at a nearby point.
stem: Using differentials, the approximate value of $\sqrt{101}$ is
solution:
For $f(x)=\sqrt{x}$, use $dy\approx f'(x)\,dx$ near $x=100$, where $f(100)=10$ and $f'(100)=\dfrac{1}{20}$.
$$\sqrt{101}\approx 10+\dfrac{1}{20}(1)=10.05$$
distractor_notes: A: Uses an extra factor of $10$ in the differential.\nC: Doubles the differential.\nD: Uses an incorrect change in the input.

brief: Sum an arithmetico-geometric series to n terms by multiplying by the common ratio and subtracting.
stem: The sum of the first $n$ terms of $3+\dfrac{5}{3}+\dfrac{7}{3^2}+\cdots$ is
solution:
Let $S_n=3+\dfrac53+\cdots+\dfrac{2n+1}{3^{n-1}}$. Then
$$\frac23S_n=3+2\left(\frac13+\cdots+\frac1{3^{n-1}}\right)-\frac{2n+1}{3^n}=4-\frac{2n+4}{3^n}.$$
Hence $S_n=6-\dfrac{n+2}{3^{n-1}}$.
working:
Let $S_n=3+\dfrac{5}{3}+\cdots+\dfrac{2n+1}{3^{n-1}}$. Then
$\dfrac{2}{3}S_n=3+2\left(\dfrac13+\cdots+\dfrac1{3^{n-1}}\right)-\dfrac{2n+1}{3^n}$
$=3+\left(1-\dfrac1{3^{n-1}}\right)-\dfrac{2n+1}{3^n}$
$S_n=6-\dfrac{n+2}{3^{n-1}}$.

Independent check: The kth term is (2k+1)/3^(k−1). Summing this arithmetic-geometric series gives S_n = 6 − (n+2)/3^(n−1), matching option B.
distractor_notes:
A: Incorrect end-term contribution in the subtraction.
C: Off-by-one error in the final power of $3$.
D: Incorrect coefficient when simplifying the end terms.

brief: Use inclusion–exclusion to count the number of onto/surjective functions from one finite set to another.
stem: How many onto functions are there from a set with $4$ elements to a set with $3$ elements?
solution:
By inclusion–exclusion, subtract functions that omit at least one element of the codomain:
$$3^4-\binom31 2^4+\binom32 1^4=81-48+3=36.$$
working:
By inclusion–exclusion: $3^4-\binom{3}{1}2^4+\binom{3}{2}1^4$\n$=81-48+3=36$.

Independent check: By inclusion–exclusion, the number of onto functions is 3^4 - 3(2^4) + 3(1^4) = 36.
distractor_notes: A: Counts arrangements of three selected domain elements instead.\nB: Omits the final inclusion–exclusion correction.\nD: Counts all functions, not just onto functions.

brief: Use z·z̄ = |z|² to simplify an expression involving conjugates and quotients into a real or simple form.
stem: If $z+\bar z=4$ and $z\bar z=5$, find $\dfrac{z^2+\bar z^2}{z\bar z}$.
solution:
$z^2+\bar z^2=(z+\bar z)^2-2z\bar z=4^2-2(5)=6$.\\
Hence, $\displaystyle \frac{z^2+\bar z^2}{z\bar z}=\frac{6}{5}$.
working:
$z^2+\bar z^2=(z+\bar z)^2-2z\bar z=16-10=6$
$\therefore\ \dfrac{z^2+\bar z^2}{z\bar z}=\dfrac65$.

Independent check: Use (z+bar z)^2 - 2z bar z = z^2 + bar z^2, giving 16 - 10 = 6. Divide by z bar z = 5 to get 6/5.
distractor_notes:
A: Uses $(z+\bar z)^2$ without subtracting $2z\bar z$.
C: Subtracts $2z\bar z$ but omits the squared sum.
D: Takes the reciprocal of the required ratio.

brief: Solve a first-order linear ODE with a non-standard coefficient of dy/dx using the integrating factor method.
stem: For $(1+x^2)\dfrac{dy}{dx}+2xy=x$, with $y(0)=1$, find $y(1)$.
solution:
Dividing by $1+x^2$, the integrating factor is $1+x^2$, so $
\dfrac{d}{dx}\big[(1+x^2)y\big]=x.
$Using $y(0)=1$, $(1+x^2)y=1+\dfrac{x^2}{2}$; hence $y(1)=\dfrac{1+\frac12}{2}=\dfrac34$.
working:
$y'+\dfrac{2x}{1+x^2}y=\dfrac{x}{1+x^2}$; integrating factor $=1+x^2$
$\dfrac{d}{dx}[(1+x^2)y]=x$
$(1+x^2)y=\dfrac{x^2}{2}+C$; $y(0)=1\Rightarrow C=1$
$y(1)=\dfrac{1+\frac12}{2}=\dfrac34$.

Independent check: The integrating factor is 1+x², giving d[(1+x²)y]/dx = x. Applying y(0)=1 yields (1+x²)y = 1 + x²/2, so y(1)=3/4.
distractor_notes:
A: Drops the integration constant fixed by the initial condition.
B: Omits the contribution from the initial value when evaluating at $x=1$.
D: Inverts the final value.

brief: Determine k so that a piecewise function is continuous, then check differentiability at the joining point.
stem: Let $f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{e^{kx}-1}{x},&x<0,\\1+2x,&x\geq 0.\end{cases}$ Choose $k$ so that $f$ is continuous at $0$, then determine its differentiability there.
solution:
For continuity at $0$, $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac{e^{kx}-1}{x}=k=f(0)=1$, so $k=1$.
$$f'_-(0)=\lim_{h\to0^-}\frac{(e^h-1)/h-1}{h}=\frac12,\qquad f'_+(0)=2.$$$\nSince$ the one-sided derivatives are unequal, $f$ is continuous but not differentiable at $0$.
working:
$f(0)=1$; $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac{e^{kx}-1}{x}=k$, so continuity requires $k=1$.
For $k=1$, $f'_-(0)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0^-}\frac{(e^h-1)/h-1}{h}=\frac12$.
$f'_+(0)=2$; hence $f$ is not differentiable at $0$.

Independent check: As x→0−, (e^{kx}−1)/x→k, so continuity requires k=1. Then the left derivative is 1/2, while the right derivative is 2; hence f is not differentiable at 0.
distractor_notes:
B: Assumes continuity guarantees matching one-sided derivatives.
C: Sets $k$ equal to the right-hand derivative instead of the left-hand limit.
D: Overlooks that the left-hand limit can be matched by choosing $k=1$.

brief: Given |f(x)| and g(x) counts for two sets, find the cardinality of the union or of a difference using Venn-style reasoning with three sets.
stem: Let finite sets $A,B,C$ satisfy $|A|=34$, $|B|=33$, $|C|=33$, $|A\cup B|=59$, $|B\cup C|=60$, $|C\cup A|=61$ and $|A\cap B\cap C|=4$. Find $|(A\cup B)\setminus C|$.
solution: $|A\cap B|=34+33-59=8$ and $|A\cap C|=|B\cap C|=6$. Thus $|(A\cup B)\cap C|=6+6-4=8$, so $$|(A\cup B)\setminus C|=59-8=51.$$
distractor_notes: A: subtracts both overlaps with $C$ but does not restore the triple intersection.\nC: subtracts only one overlap with $C$.\nD: does not remove elements lying in $C$.

brief: Solve a trigonometric equation of the form a cos x + b sin x = c or a sum-to-product type and write the general solution.
stem: The general solution, for real $x$, of $\cos 3x+\cos x=\sin 2x$ is:
solution:
Using $\\cos 3x+\\cos x=2\\cos 2x\\cos x$, the equation becomes
$$2\\cos x(\\cos 2x-\\sin x)=0.$$
Thus $\\cos x=0$ gives $x=\\frac{\\pi}{2}+k\\pi$. Otherwise, $1-2\\sin^2x=\\sin x$, so $\\sin x=\\frac12$ or $-1$; these give $x=\\frac{\\pi}{6}+2k\\pi$, $\\frac{5\\pi}{6}+2k\\pi$, with $\\sin x=-1$ already included above.
working:
$\cos 3x+\cos x=2\cos 2x\cos x$, so $2\cos x(\cos 2x-\sin x)=0$.
$\cos x=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}+k\pi$.
$\cos 2x=\sin x\Rightarrow 1-2\sin^2x=\sin x\Rightarrow (2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)=0$.
$\sin x=\dfrac12\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{\pi}{6}+2k\pi$ or $\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+2k\pi$; $\sin x=-1$ is already included.

Independent check: Use cos 3x + cos x = 2 cos 2x cos x. Then cos x(cos 2x − sin x) = 0. Thus cos x = 0, or with sin x = t, 1 − 2t² = t, giving t = 1/2 or −1. These yield exactly the solutions in (A).
distractor_notes: B: omits the roots from $\sin x=\dfrac12$ in the second quadrant.\nC: omits the $\cos x=0$ roots with odd multiples of $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.\nD: gives period $\pi$ to roots that have period $2\pi$, adding extraneous solutions.

brief: Use symmetry about the axis and the property ∫₀ᵃ f(x)dx with f(a−x) to evaluate a nontrivial definite integral without full antiderivatives.
stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{\sin^4 x+2\sin^2x\cos^2x}{\sin^4x+\cos^4x+4\sin^2x\cos^2x}\,dx$.
solution:
Let $f(x)$ denote the integrand. Under $x\mapsto \frac{\pi}{2}-x$, its numerator becomes $\cos^4x+2\sin^2x\cos^2x$; the two numerators sum to the denominator, so $f(x)+f\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=1$.
By reflection, both integrals equal $I$, hence $$2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\frac{\pi}{2}\quad\Rightarrow\quad I=\frac{\pi}{4}.$$
working:
Let $f(x)$ be the integrand. Then $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-xight)$ has numerator $\cos^4x+2\sin^2x\cos^2x$.
$f(x)+f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-xight)=1$.
By reflection, $\int_0^{\pi/2} f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-xight)dx=I$.
$2I=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\Rightarrow I=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

Independent check: Let f(x) be the integrand. Then f(x)+f(π/2−x)=1, since the two numerators sum to the denominator. Hence 2I=π/2 and I=π/4.
distractor_notes: A: divides the interval length by an extra factor of $2$.\nC: uses an incorrect reflected numerator when adding the integrands.\nD: takes the value of $2I$ as the value of $I$.

brief: Set up and compute the area bounded by a parabola/line pair or two curves with a simple intersection.
stem: Find the area enclosed by the parabola $y=4x-x^2$ and the line $y=2x$.
solution:
The curves intersect where $4x-x^2=2x$, giving $x=0,2$. Between these points, the parabola lies above the line.
$$\text{Area}=\int_0^2\big[(4x-x^2)-2x\big]dx=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\frac{4}{3}\text{ square units}.$$
working:
$4x-x^2=2x\Rightarrow x=0,2$.\n$\text{Area}=\displaystyle\int_0^2\big[(4x-x^2)-2x\big]dx=\left[x^2-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\dfrac{4}{3}$.

Independent check: Intersections: 4x − x² = 2x gives x = 0, 2. The area is ∫₀²(2x − x²) dx = 4/3.
distractor_notes: A: underestimates the integral by a factor of $2$.\nC: treats the average vertical gap as $1$ over the interval.\nD: integrates the parabola alone and omits the line.

brief: Find the work done / projection of one vector on another using dot product with given magnitudes and angle.
stem: Vectors of magnitudes $8$ and $5$ make an angle of $60^\\circ$. What is the scalar projection of the first vector on the second?
solution:
The scalar projection of the first vector on the second is $|\vec a|\cos\theta$.
$$8\cos60^\circ=8\left(\frac12\right)=4$$
working:
Scalar projection $=|\vec a|\cos\theta=8\cos60^\circ=4$.

Independent check: Scalar projection = |a| cos 60° = 8 × 0.5 = 4.
distractor_notes: A: uses the second vector's magnitude for the projection. C: omits the cosine factor. D: calculates the dot product instead of the scalar projection.
critic_notes: [minor] The angle is typeset as `$60^\\circ$` (double backslash), which will print as a broken/undefined control sequence rather than 60°.

brief: Bayes' theorem word problem: given prior probabilities and conditional probabilities, find the posterior probability of a cause.
stem: Machines $A,B,C$ are used with probabilities $\frac12,\frac13,\frac16$. Two checks are conditionally independent given the machine; their pass probabilities are $(\frac12,\frac12)$ for $A$, $(\frac23,\frac34)$ for $B$, and $(\frac34,p)$ for $C$. If both checks pass with probability $\frac{17}{48}$, find the probability the item came from $C$, given both checks passed.
solution:
By conditional independence and total probability,
$$\frac12\cdot\frac14+\frac13\cdot\frac12+\frac16\cdot\frac34p=\frac{17}{48},\qquad p=\frac12.$$
Hence, by Bayes’ theorem,
$$P(C\mid\text{both pass})=\frac{(1/6)(3/4)(1/2)}{17/48}=\frac{3}{17}.$$
working:
$$\frac12\cdot\frac14+\frac13\cdot\frac12+\frac16\cdot\frac34p=\frac{17}{48}\quad\Rightarrow\quad p=\frac12$$
$$P(C\mid\text{both pass})=\frac{\frac16\cdot\frac34\cdot\frac12}{\frac{17}{48}}=\frac{3}{17}$$

Independent check: By total probability, \(\frac18+\frac16+\frac p8=\frac{17}{48}\), so \(p=\frac12\). Thus \(P(C\mid\text{both pass})=\frac{(1/6)(3/4)(1/2)}{17/48}=\frac3{17}\).
distractor_notes:
A: Uses only the first pass probability for $C$ and omits normalization.
C: Normalizes by the evidence contribution from $A$ and $B$ alone.
D: Assumes $p=1$ instead of recovering it from the given marginal probability.

brief: Integrate a product (e.g., log or inverse trig function times polynomial/power) using integration by parts, possibly applied twice.
stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle\int x^2e^x\,dx$.
solution:
Using integration by parts twice,
$$\int x^2e^x\,dx=x^2e^x-2\int xe^x\,dx=e^x(x^2-2x+2)+C.$$
working:
$$\int x^2e^x\,dx=x^2e^x-2\int xe^x\,dx$$
$$=x^2e^x-2(xe^x-e^x)+C=e^x(x^2-2x+2)+C$$

Independent check: Integrating by parts twice gives \(\int x^2e^x\,dx=e^x(x^2-2x+2)+C\).
distractor_notes:
B: Sign error in the terms produced by integration by parts.
C: Omits the final $2e^x$ contribution.
D: Fails to reduce the coefficient of $x^2$ after factoring out $e^x$.

brief: Solve a trigonometric equation involving multiple angles (e.g., tan 2x = cot 3x) and select the number of solutions in an interval or list the general solution.
stem: How many solutions does $\tan 3x=\cot 2x$ have in $0<x<2\pi$?
solution:
Since $\\cot 2x=\\tan(\\frac{\\pi}{2}-2x)$, equality of tangents gives
$$3x=\\frac{\\pi}{2}-2x+k\\pi \\quad\\Rightarrow\\quad x=\\frac{\\pi}{10}+\\frac{k\\pi}{5}.$$
The interval $0<x<2\\pi$ gives $k=0,1,\\ldots,9$. For $k=2,7$, both sides are undefined; hence the number of solutions is $10-2=8$.
working:
$$3x=\frac{\pi}{2}-2x+k\pi\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=\frac{\pi}{10}+\frac{k\pi}{5}$$
$$0<x<2\pi\Rightarrow k=0,1,\ldots,9$$
$$\tan 3x\text{ or }\cot 2x\text{ is undefined when }k\equiv2\pmod5$$
$$10-2=8$$

Independent check: Since \(\cot 2x=\tan(\frac{\pi}{2}-2x)\), equality gives \(x=\frac{\pi}{10}+\frac{k\pi}{5}\). The interval allows \(k=0,\ldots,9\), but \(k=2,7\) make both sides undefined. Thus there are 8 solutions.
distractor_notes:
A: Excludes too many candidate values at the undefined points.
C: Excludes only one of the two invalid candidates in the interval.
D: Counts every value from the tangent identity without checking the original domains.

brief: Form 4-digit numbers from given digits satisfying a divisibility or repetition restriction, counting case by case.
stem: How many four-digit numbers can be formed from $0,1,2,3,5$ without repetition that are divisible by $5$?
solution:
A number divisible by $5$ must end in $0$ or $5$.
If the last digit is $0$, the remaining three places can be filled in $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$ ways; if it is $5$, the first digit has $3$ choices, followed by $3\cdot2$ choices.
$$24+3\cdot3\cdot2=24+18=42$$
working:
Last digit $0$: $4\cdot3\cdot2=24$. Last digit $5$: $3\cdot3\cdot2=18$. Total $=24+18=42$.

Independent check: If the last digit is 0: 4×3×2=24. If it is 5: 3×3×2=18. Total = 42.
distractor_notes: A: counts only numbers ending in $5$. B: counts only numbers ending in $0$. D: allows $0$ in the first position when counting both cases.

brief: For a matrix A satisfying a given quadratic matrix equation, express Aⁿ as a linear combination of A and I using repeated bookkeeping.
stem: Let $A$ be a square matrix satisfying $A^2-5A+6I=0$. Then $A^5$ is
working:
$$A^2=5A-6I$$
$$A^3=19A-30I,\quad A^4=65A-114I$$
$$A^5=65A^2-114A=211A-390I$$

Independent check: From A² = 5A − 6I, reduce powers: A³ = 19A − 30I, A⁴ = 65A − 114I, and A⁵ = 211A − 390I.
distractor_notes:
B: Sign error on the constant-matrix term.
C: Uses $3^5+2^5$ instead of $3^5-2^5$ and omits a weighted term.
D: Uses $2^5-3^5$ as the constant coefficient, omitting the interpolation weights.

brief: Use the scalar triple product/determinant condition to test whether three points or two lines and a point are coplanar, or find the shortest distance between skew lines.
stem: The lines $\mathbf r=(0,0,3)+s(1,2,0)$ and $\mathbf r=(-1,3,2)+t(2,-1,1)$ intersect. If $P=(2,0,k)$ is coplanar with them, find $k$.
solution:
The lines intersect at $C=(1,2,3)$. Coplanarity requires the scalar triple product to vanish:
$$\bigl((1,2,0)\times(2,-1,1)\bigr)\cdot(1,-2,k-3)=0.$$
Since $(1,2,0)\times(2,-1,1)=(2,-1,-5)$, we get $19-5k=0$, hence $k=\dfrac{19}{5}$.
working:
At $s=t=1$, the intersection is $C=(1,2,3)$.
$\vec u=(1,2,0),\quad \vec v=(2,-1,1),\quad \overrightarrow{CP}=(1,-2,k-3)$.
$\vec u	imes\vec v=(2,-1,-5)$.
$\overrightarrow{CP}\cdot(\vec u	imes\vec v)=2+2-5(k-3)=19-5k=0$.
$k=\dfrac{19}{5}$

Independent check: The lines intersect at (1,2,3). Coplanarity requires (1,2,0)×(2,-1,1) · (P−(1,2,3)) = 0, giving 19−5k=0, so k=19/5.
distractor_notes: A: Sign error when solving the determinant condition.\nB: Omits the $-3$ in the displacement component $k-3$.\nC: Arithmetic error in evaluating the scalar triple product.

brief: Find the equation of a parabola (or its focus/directrix/latus rectum) from given vertex and axis information.
stem: A parabola has vertex $(1,2)$, axis parallel to the $x$-axis, and passes through $(5,6)$. Its equation is:
solution:
For a parabola with vertex $(h,k)$ and axis parallel to the $x$-axis, $(y-k)^2=4p(x-h)$. Substituting $(h,k)=(1,2)$ and the point $(5,6)$:
$$16=4p(4)\Rightarrow p=1.$$
Hence, $(y-2)^2=4(x-1)$.
working:
$(y-2)^2=4a(x-1)$.\n$(6-2)^2=4a(5-1)\Rightarrow16=16a\Rightarrow a=1$.\n$(y-2)^2=4(x-1)$

Independent check: For a horizontal-axis parabola, (y−2)² = 4p(x−1). Substituting (5,6) gives 16 = 16p, so p = 1.
distractor_notes: B: Uses the wrong sign for the vertex's $x$-coordinate.\nC: Takes the axis parallel to the $y$-axis.\nD: Omits the factor $4$ in the standard form.

brief: Solve a homogeneous differential equation dy/dx = f(y/x) using the substitution y = vx.
stem: Solve $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=1+\dfrac{y}{x}$, where $x\ne0$.
solution:
Set $y=vx$. Then $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1+v$, giving $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac1x$.
$$v=\ln|x|+C \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y=x(\ln|x|+C).$$
working:
Set $y=vx$: $v+x\dfrac{dv}{dx}=1+v$. Thus $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=\dfrac1x$, so $v=\ln|x|+C$. Hence $y=x(\ln|x|+C)$.

Independent check: Rewrite as \(y'-\frac{y}{x}=1\). Then \(\left(\frac{y}{x}\right)'=\frac1x\), so \(y=x(\ln|x|+C)\).
distractor_notes: A: omits the factor $x$ when returning from $v=y/x$. B: uses the wrong sign when integrating. C: fails to multiply the logarithmic term by $x$.

brief: Convert a composite like sin⁻¹(x) expressed via tan⁻¹ into a single inverse trig value using the triangle method.
stem: Evaluate $\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3}{5}\right)+\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)$.
solution:
Let $A=\tan^{-1}(3/4)$, since $\tan(\\sin^{-1}(3/5))=3/4$. Then
$$\tan\left(A+\tan^{-1}(1/7)\right)=\frac{3/4+1/7}{1-(3/4)(1/7)}=1.$$
Both angles are positive and their sum is less than $\pi/2$, so the result is $\tan^{-1}(1)$.
working:
Let $A=\sin^{-1}(3/5)=	an^{-1}(3/4)$, using a $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle.
$	an(A+	an^{-1}(1/7))=\dfrac{3/4+1/7}{1-(3/4)(1/7)}=1$.
Both angles are positive and their sum is less than $\pi/2$.
$A+	an^{-1}(1/7)=	an^{-1}(1)=\dfrac{\pi}{4}$

Independent check: Let α = sin⁻¹(3/5), so tan α = 3/4. Then tan(α + tan⁻¹(1/7)) = ((3/4) + (1/7))/(1 − 3/28) = 1. The sum is in the principal range, so it equals tan⁻¹(1).
distractor_notes: A: Adds the inverse tangent arguments directly.\nB: Uses the numerator of the tangent addition formula but omits its denominator.\nD: Reverses the opposite and adjacent sides when converting the inverse sine.

brief: Find the direction cosines of a line joining two points, then the angle it makes with an axis, or the distance of a point from an axis.
stem: The directed line from $P=(1,-2,0)$ to $Q=(k,4,8)$ makes equal acute angles with the positive $x$- and $y$-axes. Find its cosine with the positive $z$-axis.
solution:
The direction vector is $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(k-1,6,8)$. Equal acute angles with the positive $x$- and $y$-axes imply $k-1=6$, so $\overrightarrow{PQ}=(6,6,8)$.
$$|\overrightarrow{PQ}|=\sqrt{6^2+6^2+8^2}=2\sqrt{34},\qquad \cos\gamma=\frac{8}{2\sqrt{34}}=\frac{4}{\sqrt{34}}$$
working:
$\overrightarrow{PQ}=(k-1,6,8)$. Equal acute angles with the positive $x$- and $y$-axes give $k-1=6$, so $k=7$.\n$|\overrightarrow{PQ}|=\sqrt{6^2+6^2+8^2}=2\sqrt{34}$.\n$\cos\gamma=\dfrac{8}{2\sqrt{34}}=\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{34}}$

Independent check: The direction vector is $(k-1,6,8)$. Equal acute angles with the positive $x$- and $y$-axes give $k-1=6$, so the vector is $(6,6,8)$. Its magnitude is $2\sqrt{34}$, hence its cosine with the positive $z$-axis is $8/(2\sqrt{34})=4/\sqrt{34}$.
distractor_notes: A: Uses the $x$- or $y$-direction cosine instead of the $z$-direction cosine.\nC: Gives $\sin\gamma$ rather than $\cos\gamma$.\nD: Omits one of the equal component squares when normalizing.
critic_notes: [minor] "Find its cosine with the positive $z$-axis" is unidiomatic; rewrite as "find the cosine of the angle it makes with the positive $z$-axis".

brief: Related rates: rate of change of volume/area given the rate of change of a length (sphere/cone/cube scenario).
stem: A conical vessel has liquid depth $h$ and surface radius $r=\dfrac{h}{3}$. If $h$ is increasing at $2$ cm s$^{-1}$, find the rate at which its volume increases when $h=6$ cm.
solution:
Using $V=\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$ and $r=\frac{h}{3}$, we get $V=\frac{\pi h^3}{27}$.
$$\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{\pi h^2}{9}\frac{dh}{dt}=\frac{\pi(6)^2}{9}(2)=8\pi\ \text{cm}^3\,\text{s}^{-1}$$
working:
$V=\dfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2h=\dfrac{\pi h^3}{27}$
$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{\pi h^2}{9}\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{\pi(6)^2}{9}(2)=8\pi\ \text{cm}^3\,\text{s}^{-1}$

Independent check: V=(1/3)πr²h=πh³/27, so dV/dt=(πh²/9)(dh/dt). At h=6 and dh/dt=2, dV/dt=8π cm³ s⁻¹.
distractor_notes:
A: Uses $dV/dh$ without multiplying by $dh/dt$.
C: Makes a coefficient error while differentiating the cubic volume.
D: Uses the cylinder volume formula instead of the cone volume formula.

brief: Binomial distribution: find the probability of exactly/at least r successes, or recover the parameters given two probabilities.
stem: A binomial random variable $X$ satisfies $P(X=0)=\dfrac{1}{16}$ and $P(X=1)=\dfrac{1}{4}$. Find $P(X\ge 2)$.
solution:
Since $X$ is integer-valued, $P(X\ge2)=1-P(X=0)-P(X=1)$. Thus
$$P(X\ge2)=1-\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{4}=\boxed{\frac{11}{16}}.$$
working:
$\dfrac{P(X=1)}{P(X=0)}=\dfrac{np}{1-p}=4$, and $(1-p)^n=\dfrac{1}{16}$.
Thus $p=\dfrac{4}{n+4}$ and $\left(\dfrac{n}{n+4}\right)^n=\dfrac{1}{16}$, giving $n=4$, $p=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$P(X\ge2)=1-P(X=0)-P(X=1)=1-\dfrac{1}{16}-\dfrac{1}{4}=\dfrac{11}{16}$.

Independent check: P(X\ge 2)=1-P(X=0)-P(X=1)=1-\frac{1}{16}-\frac{1}{4}=\frac{11}{16}.
distractor_notes:
A: Gives the probability of exactly two successes.
B: Gives the probability of more than two successes.
D: Gives the probability of at least one success.

brief: Use the general term of (a + bx)ⁿ to find the coefficient of a specific power of x, or the term independent of x.
stem: The coefficient of $x^3$ in the expansion of $(1+2x)^6$ is
solution:
By the binomial theorem, the $x^3$ term corresponds to $r=3$:
$$\binom{6}{3}(2x)^3=160x^3.$$
Hence, the coefficient is $160$.
working:
$T_{r+1}=\binom{6}{r}(2x)^r$. For $x^3$, $r=3$: coefficient $=\binom{6}{3}2^3=160$.

Independent check: The coefficient of x^3 is \(\binom{6}{3}2^3=20\cdot8=160\).
distractor_notes: A: uses $2$ instead of $2^3$. B: uses $2^2$ instead of $2^3$. C: uses $\binom{6}{2}$ instead of $\binom{6}{3}$.

brief: Identify the centre and radius of a circle by completing the square in its general equation.
stem: The centre and radius of the circle $x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0$ are respectively:
solution:
Completing squares:
$$x^2+y^2-6x+4y-12=0\Rightarrow (x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=25.$$
Comparing with $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$, the centre is $(3,-2)$ and radius is $5$.
working:
$(x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=25$\nCentre $(3,-2)$; radius $5$.

Independent check: Completing squares gives $(x-3)^2+(y+2)^2=25$, so the centre is $(3,-2)$ and the radius is $5$.
distractor_notes: B: Reverses the signs of both centre coordinates. C: Takes the square root of the constant incorrectly. D: Gets the sign of the $y$-coordinate wrong.

brief: Determine intervals where a polynomial/rational function is increasing or decreasing by sign analysis of f′(x).
stem: The function $f(x)=x^3-3x^2+1$ is decreasing on:
solution:
A function is decreasing where $f'(x)<0$. Here,
$$f'(x)=3x(x-2)<0 \quad\text{for }0<x<2.$$
Hence, $f$ is decreasing on $(0,2)$.
working:
$f'(x)=3x(x-2)$\n$f'(x)<0$ for $0<x<2$.

Independent check: f'(x)=3x(x-2)<0 for 0<x<2, so f is decreasing on (0,2).
distractor_notes: A: Chooses an interval where the derivative is positive. C: Chooses an interval where the derivative is positive. D: Includes an interval where the derivative is positive.

brief: Definite integral of a rational/trigonometric function where a substitution (t = tan x or x → 1/x) or symmetry simplifies it dramatically.
stem: Evaluate $\displaystyle I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\sin^2x\cos^2x}$.
solution:
Let $t=\tan x$; then $I=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{1+t^2}{t^4+3t^2+1}\,dt$. Set $u=t-\frac1t$, so $du=\frac{1+t^2}{t^2}\,dt$ and $t^4+3t^2+1=t^2(u^2+5)$. Thus
$$I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{du}{u^2+5}=\frac{\pi}{\sqrt5}.$$
working:
$t=\tan x:\quad I=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\dfrac{1+t^2}{t^4+3t^2+1}\,dt$.
Let $J=\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\dfrac{dt}{t^4+3t^2+1}$. The substitution $t\mapsto1/t$ gives $\displaystyle\int_0^\infty\dfrac{t^2\,dt}{t^4+3t^2+1}=J$, so $I=2J$.
With $u=t-1/t$, $du=\dfrac{1+t^2}{t^2}dt$ and $t^4+3t^2+1=t^2(u^2+5)$.
$I=\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\dfrac{du}{u^2+5}=\dfrac{\pi}{\sqrt{5}}$.

Independent check: Let t=tan x. Then I=∫₀∞ (1+t²)/(t⁴+3t²+1) dt. Set u=t−1/t, so du=(1+t²)dt/t² and t⁴+3t²+1=t²(u²+5). Thus I=∫₋∞∞ du/(u²+5)=π/√5.
distractor_notes:
A: Misses the factor of two from the reciprocal symmetry.
C: Uses an incorrect quadratic coefficient after the substitution.
D: Introduces an extra factor of two in the final integral.
critic_notes: [minor] This duplicates q109 in skill and format (a symmetric rational trig integrand over $[0,\pi/2]$ evaluated by reflection/standard reduction), and is the more time-consuming of the pair; replace one of them with a different integration technique.

brief: Classify a given relation (reflexive/symmetric/transitive/equivalence) on a small set and, if it is an equivalence, count equivalence classes.
stem: Let $A=\{0,1,2,3,4\}$ and define $R$ on $A$ by $xRy$ iff $x^2\equiv y^2\pmod 5$. Which statement is correct?
options: $R$ is an equivalence relation with $3$ equivalence classes.
$R$ is reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive.
$R$ is symmetric and transitive, but not reflexive.
$R$ is reflexive and transitive, but not symmetric.
solution:
The values of $x^2\pmod 5$ are $0$ for $x=0$, $1$ for $x=1,4$, and $4$ for $x=2,3$. Hence $R$ is equality of these residues, so it is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.
Its equivalence classes are $\{0\}$, $\{1,4\}$, and $\{2,3\}$; therefore, there are $3$ classes.
working:
$x^2\bmod 5$ has values $0$ for $x=0$, $1$ for $x=1,4$, and $4$ for $x=2,3$.
Thus $R$ is equality of these residues, so it is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.
Its classes are $\{0\}$, $\{1,4\}$ and $\{2,3\}$: $3$ classes.

Independent check: Since congruence modulo 5 is an equivalence relation, equality of the squares modulo 5 makes R reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. The classes are {0}, {1,4}, and {2,3}.
distractor_notes:
A: Incorrectly denies transitivity of equality of residues.
C: Incorrectly denies reflexivity.
D: Incorrectly denies symmetry.

brief: Given a 3×3 matrix relationship between A, adj A and |A|, recover the missing determinant value, possibly with a diagonal or simple structured matrix.
stem: If $A$ is a nonsingular $3\times3$ matrix and $\operatorname{adj}A=2A$, then $|A|$ is:
solution:
For a nonsingular $3\times3$ matrix, $|\operatorname{adj}A|=|A|^2$. Let $|A|=d\ne0$; taking determinants of $\operatorname{adj}A=2A$ gives
$$d^2=|2A|=2^3d=8d.$$
Hence $d=8$.
working:
Let $|A|=d\ne0$. Then $|\operatorname{adj}A|=d^2=|2A|=8d$.\nHence $d=8$.

Independent check: Let d=|A|. For a nonsingular 3×3 matrix, |adj A|=d². Taking determinants of adj A=2A gives d²=8d; since d≠0, d=8.
distractor_notes: A: Uses the $2\times2$ adjugate determinant power. C: Applies the scalar factor to the determinant incorrectly. D: Introduces an unsupported negative sign.

brief: Use Vieta's relations (sum/product of roots) of one quadratic to construct another quadratic whose roots are transformed (e.g., reciprocal or doubled roots).
stem: If $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are the roots of $x^2-5x+6=0$, the quadratic equation whose roots are $2\alpha$ and $2\beta$ is:
solution:
By Vieta’s formulas, $\alpha+\beta=5$ and $\alpha\beta=6$. Hence the new roots have sum $2\alpha+2\beta=10$ and product $(2\alpha)(2\beta)=24$.
$$x^2-10x+24=0$$
working:
$\alpha+\beta=5$, $\alpha\beta=6$.\n$2\alpha+2\beta=10$, $(2\alpha)(2\beta)=24$.\nRequired equation: $x^2-10x+24=0$.

Independent check: The original roots have sum 5 and product 6. Doubling both gives sum 10 and product 24, so the equation is x² − 10x + 24 = 0.
distractor_notes: B: Leaves the sum of the roots unchanged. C: Leaves the product of the roots unchanged. D: Doubles the product instead of multiplying it by $4$.

brief: Two balls thrown vertically from the same point one after another meet at a common height; find the time interval between throws or the meeting height.
stem: A ball is thrown vertically upward at $15\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. One second later, another is thrown upward from the same point at $25\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. If $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, at what height do they meet?
solution:
Taking $t$ from the first throw, the heights are $y_1=15t-5t^2$ and $y_2=25(t-1)-5(t-1)^2$.
$$y_1=y_2\Rightarrow t=1.5\text{ s},\qquad y=15(1.5)-5(1.5)^2=11.25\text{ m}$$
working:
Let $t$ be measured from the first throw: $y_1=15t-5t^2$, $y_2=25(t-1)-5(t-1)^2$.
$y_1=y_2\Rightarrow t=1.5$ s.
$y=15(1.5)-5(1.5)^2=11.25$ m.

Independent check: Let t be the time (s) after the first throw. Equating heights, 15t−5t² = 25(t−1)−5(t−1)² gives t=1.5 s. Their height is 15(1.5)−5(1.5)² = 11.25 m.
distractor_notes:
A: uses the second ball's flight time for the first ball's height.
C: neglects gravity during the second ball's flight.
D: neglects gravity for the first ball.

brief: A car decelerating uniformly covers the last half of a distance in a given time; find total time or initial velocity using two kinematic equations.
stem: A car decelerates uniformly to rest after travelling $80$ m. If it covers the last $40$ m in $4$ s, what is its total stopping time?
solution: For the last $4$ s, the car comes to rest, so $40=\frac12 a(4)^2$, giving $a=5\,\text{m s}^{-2}$$.\nFor$ the full stopping distance, $80=\frac12 aT^2$, hence $T=\sqrt{\frac{160}{5}}=4\sqrt2\,\text{s}$.
working:
For the last $40$ m, ending at rest: $40=\dfrac{1}{2}a(4)^2\Rightarrow a=5$ m s$^{-2}$.\nFor the full journey, $80=\dfrac{1}{2}aT^2$.\n$T=\sqrt{\dfrac{160}{5}}=4\sqrt{2}$ s.

Independent check: In the last 4 s, the average speed is 2a, so 40 = 8a and a = 5 m/s². From 80 = ½aT², T = 4√2 s.
distractor_notes: A: Uses the final-segment time as the total time. C: Omits the factor of $\sqrt{2}$ when relating the times. D: Doubles the correct total time.

brief: Coulomb-force analogy question: two protons repel with a given force; ask for force at a new separation or force between alpha particles at the same separation.
stem: Two protons separated by a distance $r$ repel with a force of $3.0\times10^{-8}$ N. What is the repulsive force between two $\alpha$ particles separated by the same distance?
solution:
By Coulomb’s law, at fixed separation $F\propto q_1q_2$. Each $\alpha$ particle has charge $+2e$, so
$$F_{\alpha\alpha}=4F_{pp}=4(3.0\times10^{-8})=1.2\times10^{-7}\,\text{N}.$$
working:
$F\propto q_1q_2$ at fixed separation.\nEach alpha particle has charge $2e$, so $F_{\alpha\alpha}=\dfrac{(2e)(2e)}{e^2}F_{pp}=4(3.0\times10^{-8})=1.2\times10^{-7}$ N.

Independent check: By Coulomb’s law, force scales with the product of the charges. Each alpha particle has charge +2e, so the force is 4 times as large: 4(3.0×10⁻⁸ N) = 1.2×10⁻⁷ N.
distractor_notes: A: Assumes the force is unchanged. B: Scales for only one doubled charge. D: Applies an extra factor of $2$.

brief: A body starts from rest with constant acceleration; use v-u relation plus displacement relation to find distance in a particular second or velocity at a marked point.
stem: A body starts from rest and moves with constant acceleration $2$ m s$^{-2}$. What distance does it travel during the fourth second?
solution:
For motion from rest with constant acceleration, $s(t)=\frac{1}{2}at^2$. Thus, the distance during the fourth second is
$$s(4)-s(3)=\frac{1}{2}(2)(4^2-3^2)=7\text{ m}.$$
working:
$s(t)=\dfrac{1}{2}at^2=t^2$.\nDistance during the fourth second: $s(4)-s(3)=16-9=7$ m.

Independent check: Distance in the fourth second: s_4-s_3 = \frac{a}{2}(2\cdot4-1)=7\text{ m}.
distractor_notes: A: Uses half the acceleration times the second number. B: Uses $a(n-1)$ for the distance in the $n$th second. D: Uses $an$ for the distance in the $n$th second.

subtopic: de Broglie wavelength of accelerated particles
brief: Compare de Broglie wavelengths of an electron and a proton accelerated through the same potential difference.
stem: An electron and a proton, initially at rest, each gain the same kinetic energy in an accelerator. If $m_p/m_e=1840$, what is the ratio of the proton’s de Broglie wavelength to the electron’s?
solution:
For a particle with kinetic energy $K$, $4\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$.
Since $K_p=K_e$,
$$\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_e}=\sqrt{\dfrac{m_e}{m_p}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1840}}.$$
working:
$\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mK}}$ for kinetic energy $K$.\\
$\dfrac{\lambda_p}{\lambda_e}=\sqrt{\dfrac{m_eK_e}{m_pK_p}}=\sqrt{\dfrac{m_e}{m_p}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1840}}$.

Independent check: For equal kinetic energy in the nonrelativistic regime, p = √(2mK) and λ = h/p. Hence λₚ/λₑ = √(mₑ/mₚ) = 1/√1840.
distractor_notes: A: uses the mass ratio directly. C: takes the reciprocal ratio. D: uses the reciprocal mass ratio directly.

brief: Projectile given range and maximum height; solve the two trajectory equations to find launch speed and angle of projection.
stem: A projectile is launched from level ground and lands at the same level. Its range is $60$ m and its maximum height is $20$ m. Taking $g=10$ m s$^{-2}$, its launch speed and angle of projection are
solution:
From $H=\dfrac{u_y^2}{2g}$, $u_y=\sqrt{2gH}=20\,\text{m s}^{-1}$. Thus $T=\dfrac{2u_y}{g}=4\,\text{s}$ and $u_x=\dfrac{R}{T}=15\,\text{m s}^{-1}$.\\
$$u=\sqrt{u_x^2+u_y^2}=25\,\text{m s}^{-1},\qquad \theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{u_y}{u_x}\right)=53.1^\circ.$$
working:
$H=\dfrac{u_y^2}{2g}\Rightarrow u_y=20$ m s$^{-1}$.
$T=\dfrac{2u_y}{g}=4$ s; hence $u_x=\dfrac{R}{T}=15$ m s$^{-1}$.
$u=\sqrt{u_x^2+u_y^2}=25$ m s$^{-1}$; $\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{20}{15}\right)=53.1^\circ$.

Independent check: From H = u_y²/(2g), u_y = 20 m s⁻¹. Flight time = 2u_y/g = 4 s, so u_x = 60/4 = 15 m s⁻¹. Thus speed = 25 m s⁻¹ and angle = tan⁻¹(20/15) ≈ 53.1°.
distractor_notes:
B: Uses the vertical component as the launch speed.
C: Takes the complementary angle, measured from the vertical.
D: Incorrectly combines the range and height to find speed and angle.

brief: A block slides from rest down a curved frictionless track onto a rough horizontal stretch; use energy conservation plus work-energy theorem to find where it stops.
stem: A block starts from rest and descends through a vertical height of $5$ m along a frictionless curved track. It then crosses a horizontal rough stretch whose first $4$ m has coefficient of friction $0.25$, followed by a portion with coefficient $0.5$. Taking $g=10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$, how far from the start of the rough stretch does it stop?
solution:
By conservation of energy, the kinetic energy per unit mass at the rough stretch is $gh=10(5)=50\,\text{J kg}^{-1}$. The first $4$ m dissipates $\mu g d=0.25(10)(4)=10\,\text{J kg}^{-1}$, leaving $40\,\text{J kg}^{-1}$.
$$d_2=\frac{40}{0.5(10)}=8\,\text{m},\qquad d=4+8=12\,\text{m}.$$
working:
Energy per unit mass at entry: $gh=50$ J kg$^{-1}$.
Work per unit mass over first $4$ m: $0.25(10)(4)=10$ J kg$^{-1}$.
Remaining energy: $40$ J kg$^{-1}$; distance in second portion $=40/[0.5(10)]=8$ m.
Total distance $=4+8=12$ m.

Independent check: The block reaches the rough stretch with 50 J/kg of kinetic energy. The first 4 m dissipates 0.25×10×4 = 10 J/kg, leaving 40 J/kg. At μ = 0.5, friction dissipates 5 J/kg per metre, so it travels 8 m further. Total distance = 12 m.
distractor_notes:
A: reports only the distance in the second portion.
B: uses $\mu=0.5$ over the entire rough stretch.
