$$\text{Cl}\boldsymbol{\cdot}+\text{O}_3\rightarrow\text{ClO}\boldsymbol{\cdot}+\text{O}_2,\qquad \text{ClO}\boldsymbol{\cdot}+\text{O}\rightarrow\text{Cl}\boldsymbol{\cdot}+\text{O}_2.$$
The chlorine radical is regenerated; the net reaction is $\text{O}_3+\text{O}\rightarrow2\text{O}_2$.
working:
$\text{Cl}\boldsymbol{\cdot}+\text{O}_3\rightarrow\text{ClO}\boldsymbol{\cdot}+\text{O}_2$
$\text{ClO}\boldsymbol{\cdot}+\text{O}\rightarrow\text{Cl}\boldsymbol{\cdot}+\text{O}_2$
Net: $\text{O}_3+\text{O}\rightarrow2\text{O}_2$; $\text{Cl}\boldsymbol{\cdot}$ is regenerated.

Independent check: Cl· reacts with O₃ to form ClO· and O₂; ClO· then reacts with O to regenerate Cl· and produce another O₂. Net: O₃ + O → 2O₂.
distractor_notes: A: CFCs release chlorine radicals through ultraviolet photolysis, not mainly by tropospheric reaction with water. B: The chlorine radical is regenerated in the catalytic cycle. C: CFC photolysis is driven by ultraviolet, not visible, light.

brief: Compare cloudiness appearance time for a primary, secondary and tertiary alcohol with Lucas reagent; ask which reacts immediately and why.
stem: On adding Lucas reagent to primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, which one gives immediate cloudiness, and why?
options: Primary alcohol; it forms the most stable carbocation
Secondary alcohol; it forms the most stable carbocation
Tertiary alcohol; it reacts by an $S_{N2}$ mechanism
Tertiary alcohol; it forms the most stable carbocation
solution:
Lucas reaction proceeds mainly by the $S_N1$ mechanism, whose rate depends on carbocation stability:
$$3^\circ > 2^\circ > 1^\circ$$
Tertiary alcohol forms the most stable carbocation and reacts fastest, giving immediate cloudiness.
working:
Lucas reaction proceeds mainly by $\text{S}_\text{N}1$.\
Carbocation stability: tertiary $>$ secondary $>$ primary.\
Thus a tertiary alcohol gives immediate cloudiness.

Independent check: Tertiary alcohols form the most stable carbocations, so they react fastest by the SN1 pathway and give immediate cloudiness.
distractor_notes: A: reverses the carbocation stability order.\nB: assigns the fastest reaction to a secondary alcohol.\nD: gives the right alcohol but the wrong mechanism.

brief: Give a Fischer projection of a two-chiral-centre molecule in the figure; ask students to rank/identify the correct R/S assignment and enantiomer/diastereomer relation among drawn structures.
stem: For the three Fischer projections of 2,3-dibromopentane shown, which option correctly gives their configurations and the relationships of I–II and I–III?
options: I: $(2R,3S)$; II: $(2S,3S)$; III: $(2S,3R)$; I–II are enantiomers and I–III are diastereomers.
I: $(2R,3S)$; II: $(2S,3S)$; III: $(2S,3R)$; I–II are diastereomers and I–III are enantiomers.
I: $(2S,3R)$; II: $(2R,3R)$; III: $(2R,3S)$; I–II are diastereomers and I–III are identical.
I: $(2R,3R)$; II: $(2S,3R)$; III: $(2S,3S)$; I–II are identical and I–III are enantiomers.
solution: At C2, priorities are $\text{Br}>\text{C3 chain}>\text{CH}_3>\text{H}$; at C3, they are $\text{Br}>\text{C2 chain}>\text{C}_2\text{H}_5>\text{H}$. Accounting for horizontal groups pointing toward the viewer gives I $(2R,3S)$, II $(2S,3S)$, and III $(2S,3R)$. I and II differ at one stereocentre, so they are diastereomers; I and III differ at both, so they are enantiomers. (B)
working:
At C2: $\text{Br}>\text{C3 chain}>\text{CH}_3>\text{H}$; at C3: $\text{Br}>\text{C2 chain}>\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3>\text{H}$. Horizontal $\text{H}$ is toward the viewer: I is $(2R,3S)$, II is $(2S,3S)$, III is $(2S,3R)$. I–II differ at one centre; I–III invert both.

Independent check: 2,3-Dibromopentane has two distinct stereocenters (CH3 vs C2H5 ends), so no meso form: inverting both centers gives enantiomers, inverting one gives diastereomers. Checking each option's stated relationships against its own configurations: (A) (2R,3S)/(2S,3S) differ at one center → diastereomers ✓; (2R,3S)/(2S,3R) differ at both → enantiomers ✓. B, C, D all misstate these relationships (B swaps them; C calls enantiomers identical; D calls diastereomers identical). Only A is internally consistent, so it must be the intended answer even though the figure fails to show projections I–III.
distractor_notes: B: Reverses the enantiomer/diastereomer relationships. C: Assigns the configurations incorrectly and treats an enantiomeric pair as identical. D: Misassigns all three projections and their relationships.
critic_notes: [minor] Only option A gives relationships that are consistent with its own stated configurations (B, C and D are internally contradictory), so the item can be answered without ever looking at the Fischer projections — make the distractors self-consistent so the figure is actually needed.

brief: State the geometry and hybridisation of XeF4 (square planar) among options; simple structure identification.
stem: What are the geometry and hybridisation of the central atom in $\text{XeF}_4$?
solution:
Xe has 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs, so there are 6 electron domains around the central atom.
$$\text{Hybridisation}=sp^3d^2$$
The two lone pairs occupy opposite positions in an octahedral arrangement, leaving a square-planar molecular geometry.
working:
$\text{XeF}_4$: 4 bond pairs and 2 lone pairs around Xe.\
Six electron domains give $sp^3d^2$ hybridisation; the two lone pairs occupy opposite positions.\
Molecular geometry: square planar.

Independent check: Xe has 4 Xe–F bonds and 2 lone pairs: 6 electron domains give an octahedral arrangement. The two lone pairs are opposite, leaving a square-planar molecular geometry; the conventional hybridisation is sp³d².
distractor_notes: A: counts only four electron domains.\nC: uses the wrong molecular geometry and electron-domain count.\nD: gives the geometry but an incorrect hybridisation.

brief: Mixture of two non-reacting gases in a vessel: given masses and molar masses, find total pressure at a given temperature using partial pressures and PV = nRT.
stem: A $12.3\ \text{L}$ vessel at $300\ \text{K}$ contains $4.0\ \text{g}$ of helium and $14.0\ \text{g}$ of nitrogen. Find the total pressure. Take $R=0.082\ \text{L atm mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, $M(\text{He})=4.0\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$ and $M(\text{N}_2)=28.0\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$.
solution:
The total number of moles is $n=\frac{4.0}{4.0}+\frac{14.0}{28.0}=1.50\ \text{mol}$. Using the ideal gas equation,
$$P=\frac{nRT}{V}=\frac{(1.50)(0.082)(300)}{12.3}=3.0\ \text{atm}.$$
distractor_notes: A: Uses only the nitrogen partial pressure. B: Uses only the helium partial pressure. D: Does not convert both gas masses to moles correctly.

brief: Rank a set of cyclic/acyclic species (including an antiaromatic ion and an aromatic ion) by stability using Hückel's rule.
stem: Select the decreasing order of stability of the following anions, considering resonance and cyclic conjugation.
options: Cyclopentadienyl anion ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_5^-$) > allyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_5^-$) > propyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^-$) > cyclopropenyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_3^-$)
Cyclopentadienyl anion ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_5^-$) > cyclopropenyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_3^-$) > allyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_5^-$) > propyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^-$)
Allyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_5^-$) > cyclopentadienyl anion ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_5^-$) > propyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^-$) > cyclopropenyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_3^-$)
Cyclopropenyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_3^-$) > cyclopentadienyl anion ($\text{C}_5\text{H}_5^-$) > allyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_5^-$) > propyl anion ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_7^-$)
solution: Cyclopentadienyl anion has $6\pi$ electrons and is aromatic; the allyl anion is resonance-stabilized, whereas the propyl anion is localized. The cyclopropenyl anion has $4\pi$ electrons in a cyclic conjugated system and is antiaromatic, so it is least stable. Hence the decreasing order is cyclopentadienyl $>$ allyl $>$ propyl $>$ cyclopropenyl.
working:
Cyclopentadienyl anion: $6\pi$ electrons, aromatic. Allyl anion: resonance-delocalized; propyl anion: localized. Cyclopropenyl anion: $4\pi$ electrons in a cyclic conjugated system, antiaromatic. Hence the order is cyclopentadienyl $>$ allyl $>$ propyl $>$ cyclopropenyl.

Independent check: Cyclopentadienyl anion is aromatic with 6 π electrons; allyl anion is resonance-stabilized; propyl anion is localized. The cyclopropenyl anion has 4 π electrons in cyclic conjugation and is antiaromatic, making it least stable. Thus the order is Cp > allyl > propyl > cyclopropenyl.
distractor_notes: B: Treats the $4\pi$ cyclopropenyl anion as more stable than the acyclic resonance-stabilized anion. C: Underestimates aromatic stabilization of the cyclopentadienyl anion. D: Treats the antiaromatic cyclopropenyl anion as the most stable.

brief: Compare [Fe(CN)6]4− and [Fe(H2O)6]2+ for hybridisation and magnetic nature (diamagnetic vs paramagnetic); pick the correct pairing.
stem: Which pairing correctly describes $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$ and $[\text{Fe(H}_2\text{O)}_6]^{2+}$, respectively?
solution:
Fe$^{2+}$ has configuration $3d^6$. CN$^-$ is a strong-field ligand, so the complex is low-spin and uses inner $d^2sp^3$ hybridisation; all electrons are paired.
H$_2$O is a weak-field ligand, giving a high-spin $sp^3d^2$ complex with four unpaired electrons.
Thus, the pair is $d^2sp^3$, diamagnetic; $sp^3d^2$, paramagnetic.
working:
$\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is $d^6$.\
$\text{CN}^-$ is strong-field: low-spin $d^6$, $d^2sp^3$, 0 unpaired electrons.\
$\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is weak-field: high-spin $d^6$, $sp^3d^2$, 4 unpaired electrons.

Independent check: Fe²⁺ is d⁶. CN⁻ gives a low-spin inner-orbital complex (d²sp³), diamagnetic; H₂O gives a high-spin outer-orbital complex (sp³d²), paramagnetic.
distractor_notes: B: interchanges the ligands' field strengths and properties.\nC: assigns paramagnetism to the low-spin complex and diamagnetism to the high-spin one.\nD: reverses the hybridisation and magnetic behaviour of both complexes.

brief: Show an asymmetric ether (figure) treated with excess HI; identify both products and note why the cleavage occurs at the bond giving the stable carbocation/SN1 path.
stem: The ether shown is treated with excess HI. Which pair of organic products forms, and what accounts for the cleavage?
options: 2-Iodo-2-methylpropane and iodoethane; cleavage proceeds via the stable tertiary carbocation
1-Iodo-2-methylpropane and iodoethane; cleavage proceeds via a primary carbocation
2-Iodo-2-methylpropane and ethanol; the alcohol is not further cleaved by excess HI
1-Iodopropane and iodomethane; cleavage occurs at both sides of the oxygen
solution:
Protonation of the ether is followed by C–O cleavage at the tertiary side via the stable tert-butyl carbocation:
$$ (CH_3)_3C-O-CH_2CH_3 \xrightarrow{HI} (CH_3)_3C-I + CH_3CH_2OH $$
Excess HI converts ethanol to iodoethane, giving 2-iodo-2-methylpropane and iodoethane.
working:
$(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{HI}$ cleaves at the tertiary side via $\text{S}_\text{N}1$.\
$(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-I} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ form initially.\
Excess HI converts ethanol to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I}$; final organic products: tert-butyl iodide and iodoethane.

Independent check: The ether is ethyl tert-butyl ether. HI cleaves the C–O bond on the tertiary side via a stable tertiary carbocation; excess HI converts the resulting ethanol to iodoethane. The products are 2-iodo-2-methylpropane and iodoethane.
distractor_notes: B: puts iodine on the primary carbon of the tert-butyl group.\nC: overlooks further conversion of ethanol by excess HI.\nD: incorrectly cleaves the carbon skeleton into smaller alkyl groups.

brief: Four options giving electron gain enthalpy orders across halogens/chalcogens/N–O pair; pick the incorrect one, testing the Cl > F exception and S > O anomaly.
stem: Taking more negative electron gain enthalpy as higher in the order, which sequence is incorrect?
solution:
More negative electron gain enthalpy ranks higher. Since $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{O})=-141\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$ and $\Delta_{eg}H(\text{N})=+7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$,
$$\text{O} > \text{N}$$
Hence the sequence $\text{N} > \text{O}$ is incorrect.
working:
$\text{Cl}(-349)>\text{F}(-328)$; $\text{S}(-200)>\text{O}(-141)$; $\text{O}(-141)>\text{N}(+7)$ (values in $\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$; $>$ denotes more negative).

Independent check: More negative electron gain enthalpy ranks higher. The values give Cl > F > Br > I and S > Se > Te > O; O also ranks above N. Thus only N > O is incorrect.
distractor_notes: A: Correct halogen order, including the Cl–F exception. B: Correct chalcogen order, including the S–O anomaly. C: Correctly places O above N.
critic_notes: [minor] Options C and D are exact reverses of the same two-species comparison, which cues that the answer lies in that pair; replace one of them with a four-species sequence of the same form as A and B.

brief: Use limiting molar conductivities of two known strong electrolytes to compute Λ°m of a third (e.g., acetic acid from HCl, NaCl, CH3COONa).
stem: Given $\Lambda_m^\circ$ values of $\text{HCl}$, $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ as $426$, $126$ and $91$ $\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$, respectively, calculate $\Lambda_m^\circ$ of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$.
solution:
By Kohlrausch’s law,
$$\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})=\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl})+\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa})-\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl})$$
$=426+91-126=391\ \text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$.
working:
$\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})=\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{HCl})+\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{CH}_3\text{COONa})-\Lambda_m^\circ(\text{NaCl})$
$=426+91-126=391\ \text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}$ Independent check: By Kohlrausch’s law, Λ°(CH₃COOH) = Λ°(HCl) + Λ°(CH₃COONa) − Λ°(NaCl) = 426 + 91 − 126 = 391 S cm² mol⁻¹.
distractor_notes: A: Adds the wrong pair of electrolyte contributions; B: Subtracts sodium acetate instead of sodium chloride; D: Adds the two given conductivities without subtracting sodium chloride.

brief: Ratio of Bohr radii or energies of He+ vs H for the same n, or energy of an n-th level of a hydrogen-like ion; single scaling formula.
stem: The energy of the $n=2$ level of hydrogen is $-3.4$ eV. What is the energy of the $n=2$ level of $\text{He}^+$?
solution:
For a hydrogen-like ion, $E_n\propto -\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}$. At the same $n$, He$^+$ has $Z=2$, so
$$E_2(\text{He}^+)=2^2E_2(\text{H})=4(-3.4)=-13.6\ \text{eV}.$$
working:
$E_n\propto -\dfrac{Z^2}{n^2}$
At the same $n$: $E_n(\text{He}^+)=4E_n(\text{H})$
$=4(-3.4)=-13.6\ \text{eV}$ Independent check: For a hydrogen-like ion, energy scales as Z² at fixed n. He⁺ has Z=2, so E₂=4(−3.4 eV)=−13.6 eV.
distractor_notes: A: Uses the reciprocal scaling factor; B: Ignores the change in nuclear charge; C: Applies a factor of two instead of four.

brief: Identify shapes of simple species like ClF3 / SO2 / NH3 from VSEPR lone-pair counting; pick correct shape set from options.
stem: Which option gives the shapes of $\text{ClF}_3$, $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{NH}_3$, respectively?
solution: By VSEPR theory, $\text{ClF}_3$ is $AX_3E_2$ and T-shaped, $\text{SO}_2$ is $AX_2E$ and bent, while $\text{NH}_3$ is $AX_3E$ and trigonal pyramidal.
working:
$\text{ClF}_3$: $AX_3E_2$, T-shaped
$\text{SO}_2$: $AX_2E$, bent
$\text{NH}_3$: $AX_3E$, trigonal pyramidal Independent check: VSEPR: ClF₃ is T-shaped (AX₃E₂), SO₂ is bent, and NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal.
distractor_notes: A: Assigns shapes without accounting for lone pairs; C: Confuses molecular shape with electron-pair geometry; D: Omits the lone pairs on sulfur and nitrogen.
critic_notes: [minor] This tests exactly the same VSEPR shape-prediction skill as q48 (XeF4 geometry/hybridisation), so one of the two should be swapped for a different bonding topic (e.g. MO/bond order or dipole moment).

brief: Given spin-only magnetic moment of a transition metal ion, back-calculate the number of unpaired electrons and identify the metal ion.
stem: A transition-metal ion has a spin-only magnetic moment of $\sqrt{15}\ \text{BM}$. Which ion can it be?
solution:
The spin-only magnetic moment is $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}\,\text{BM}$.
$$15=n(n+2)\Rightarrow n=3$$
$\text{V}^{2+}$ has configuration $[\text{Ar}]3d^3$, with three unpaired electrons.
working:
$\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$; $15=n(n+2)\Rightarrow n=3$; $\text{V}^{2+}:[\text{Ar}]3d^3$.

Independent check: For spin-only moment, μ = √[n(n+2)] BM. √15 BM gives n = 3 unpaired electrons. V²⁺ has configuration 3d³, with three unpaired electrons.
distractor_notes: A: Ti$^{3+}$ has one unpaired electron. C: Cr$^{2+}$ has four unpaired electrons. D: Ni$^{2+}$ has two unpaired electrons.

brief: Convert aniline to a target substituted arene (figure shows starting amine and product, e.g., to m-bromophenol); choose the correct reagent sequence involving diazotisation and substitution.
stem: For the conversion shown in the figure, choose the correct sequence of reagents.
solution:
Aniline undergoes diazotization, then the diazonium group is replaced by $\text{CN}$ using $\text{CuCN}$; acidic hydrolysis of the nitrile gives benzoic acid.
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\xrightarrow[273\text{–}278\,\text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}}\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-\xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}}\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN}\xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+,\ heat}\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$$
working:
$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2\xrightarrow[273\text{–}278\,\text{K}]{\text{NaNO}_2/\text{HCl}}\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^-\xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}}\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN}\xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+,\ heat}\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$.

Independent check: Diazotization of aniline followed by CuCN replaces the diazonium group with CN; acidic hydrolysis on heating converts the nitrile to benzoic acid. This is option A.
distractor_notes: B: CuCl gives chlorobenzene instead of the nitrile. C: Hydrogenation reduces the nitrile rather than hydrolysing it. D: KI gives iodobenzene.

brief: Products and structures on hydrolysis of PCl5 / SiCl4 / NCl3 with balanced outcomes; ask which hydrolysis gives a specific oxide acid set — high-difficulty, multi-product reasoning.
stem: On complete hydrolysis in excess water, which set gives the balanced equations for $\text{PCl}_5$, $\text{SiCl}_4$, and $\text{NCl}_3$, respectively?
solution:
Complete hydrolysis of $\text{PCl}_5$ and $\text{SiCl}_4$ gives phosphoric acid and silica, respectively; $\text{NCl}_3$ hydrolyses to ammonia and hypochlorous acid.
$$\text{PCl}_5+4\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl},\quad \text{SiCl}_4+2\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{SiO}_2+4\text{HCl}$$
$$\text{NCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{NH}_3+3\text{HClO}$$
These equations correspond to (D).
working:
$\text{PCl}_5+4\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}$; $\text{SiCl}_4+2\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{SiO}_2+4\text{HCl}$; $\text{NCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{NH}_3+3\text{HClO}$.

Independent check: Complete hydrolysis gives H₃PO₄ and HCl from PCl₅, SiO₂ and HCl from SiCl₄, and NH₃ and HClO from NCl₃. These balanced equations are all in (A).
distractor_notes: B: Gives the partial hydrolysis product POCl₃. C: Incorrectly changes P(V) to phosphorous acid and adds oxygen. D: Gives an intermediate partial hydrolysis product of NCl₃.

subtopic: Diagonal relationship of Li and Mg
brief: Which properties of Li resemble Mg rather than other alkali metals (nitride formation, carbonate decomposition); pick the correct set of shared properties.
stem: Which statements correctly describe similarities between lithium and magnesium? I. Both form nitrides on direct combination with nitrogen. II. Both carbonates decompose on heating to the oxide and carbon dioxide. III. Both hydroxides are highly soluble in water. IV. Both form superoxides on reaction with oxygen.
solution:
Both combine directly with nitrogen to form nitrides: Li₃N and Mg₃N₂.
$$\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Li}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2,\qquad \text{MgCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{MgO}+\text{CO}_2$$
Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble, and neither metal forms a superoxide; hence only I and II are correct.
working:
$\text{Li}_3\text{N}$ and $\text{Mg}_3\text{N}_2$ form by direct combination with $\text{N}_2$.
$\text{Li}_2\text{CO}_3\xrightarrow{\Delta}\text{Li}_2\text{O}+\text{CO}_2$; $\text{MgCO}_3\xrightarrow{\Delta}\text{MgO}+\text{CO}_2$.
III and IV are false. Independent check: Li and Mg both form nitrides directly with nitrogen, and both carbonates decompose on heating to the oxide and CO₂. Mg(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble, and neither forms a superoxide with oxygen. Thus I and II are correct.
distractor_notes: B: Includes the false claim that both hydroxides are highly soluble; C: Includes the false claim that both form superoxides; D: Includes both false claims.

brief: For a combustion reaction with given ΔU, compute ΔH using Δng of gases; direct substitution with R in appropriate units.
stem: For the combustion reaction $2\text{CO}(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightarrow2\text{CO}_2(g)$ at $250$ K, $\Delta U=-560$ kJ mol$^{-1}$ for the reaction as written. Take $R=8.0$ J mol$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$. Find $\Delta H$.
solution: For gaseous reactions, $[?]$
working:
$\Delta n_g=2-(2+1)=-1$\n$\Delta H=\Delta U+\Delta n_gRT$\n$=-560+\dfrac{(-1)(8.0)(250)}{1000}=-562$ kJ mol$^{-1}$

Independent check: For the reaction as written, Δn_g = 2 − 3 = −1. Thus ΔH = ΔU + Δn_gRT = −560 kJ mol⁻¹ − (8.0 × 250 / 1000) kJ mol⁻¹ = −562 kJ mol⁻¹.
distractor_notes: A: Uses $\Delta n_g=-2$.\nC: Omits the $\Delta n_gRT$ correction.\nD: Uses the wrong sign for the correction.

brief: Ask which compound is obtained when a Grignard reagent reacts with a specified substrate (water/CO2/methanol) or which reagent destroys a Grignard reagent; simple product identification.
stem: What is formed after hydrolysis of the product obtained by reacting $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{MgBr}$ with $\text{CO}_2$?
solution:
Grignard reagents react with $\text{CO}_2$ to form a carboxylate with one additional carbon atom.
$$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{MgBr}+\text{CO}_2\rightarrow\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{MgBr}\xrightarrow{\text{hydrolysis}}\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$$
The product is propanoic acid.
working:
$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{MgBr}+\text{CO}_2\rightarrow\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{CO}_2\text{MgBr}$\nHydrolysis gives $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$ (propanoic acid).

Independent check: C₂H₅MgBr reacts with CO₂ to form a carboxylate with one extra carbon; hydrolysis gives CH₃CH₂COOH, propanoic acid.
distractor_notes: A: Does not account for the carbon added from $\text{CO}_2$.\nC: Adds two carbons instead of one.\nD: Gives the wrong carbon skeleton.

brief: Which of the given ions is colourless in aqueous solution (d0 or d10 ion like Cu+/Zn2+/Sc3+); single-concept recall.
stem: Which of the following ions is colourless in aqueous solution?
solution: Scandium(III) has the configuration $\text{Sc}^{3+}:[\text{Ar}]3d^0$. With no $d$ electrons, $d$–$d$ transitions are not possible, so the ion is colourless in aqueous solution.
working:
$\text{Sc}^{3+}: [\text{Ar}]$ ($d^0$)\nNo $d$–$d$ transition is possible; the ion is colourless.

Independent check: Sc³⁺ has a d⁰ configuration, so it has no d–d transitions and is colourless. The other ions have partially filled d orbitals.
distractor_notes: B: $\text{Ti}^{3+}$ has a partially filled $d$ subshell.\nC: $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ has a partially filled $d$ subshell.\nD: $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ has a partially filled $d$ subshell.

brief: Identify which aldehyde undergoes Cannizzaro reaction and why (no α-hydrogen); could include a mild computation of the mole ratio of alcohol to acid formed.
stem: Among propanal, butanal, 2-methylpropanal and benzaldehyde, which undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction because it has no α-hydrogen? On complete reaction of $0.40$ mol in concentrated aqueous NaOH, followed by acidification, what amounts of alcohol and acid are formed?
options: Propanal; $0.20$ mol propan-1-ol and $0.20$ mol propanoic acid
Benzaldehyde; $0.40$ mol benzyl alcohol and $0.40$ mol benzoic acid
Benzaldehyde; $0.20$ mol benzyl alcohol and $0.20$ mol benzoic acid
solution:
Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen, so it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction.
$$2\,\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}+\mathrm{OH^-}\rightarrow\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2OH}+\mathrm{C_6H_5COO^-}$$
Thus, $0.40$ mol benzaldehyde forms $0.20$ mol benzyl alcohol and, after acidification, $0.20$ mol benzoic acid.
working:
$2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}+\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}+\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COO}^-$
$0.40/2=0.20$ mol each of alcohol and acid after acidification.
Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen.

Independent check: Only benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogen. Cannizzaro stoichiometry is 2 mol aldehyde → 1 mol alcohol + 1 mol carboxylate; acidification gives 0.20 mol each from 0.40 mol benzaldehyde.
distractor_notes: A: Propanal has an α-hydrogen, so it does not undergo Cannizzaro reaction. C: 2-methylpropanal has an α-hydrogen. D: Uses the aldehyde-to-product ratio as 1:1 instead of 2:1.

brief: For an exothermic equilibrium like N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, predict the effect of increasing pressure/temperature/addition of inert gas at constant volume on yield.
stem: For the exothermic equilibrium $\text{N}_2(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NH}_3(g)$, which change increases the equilibrium yield of $\text{NH}_3$?
options: Increasing the pressure at constant temperature
Increasing the temperature at constant pressure
Adding an inert gas at constant volume
solution:
By Le Chatelier’s principle, increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer gaseous moles.
$$4\text{ mol reactants} > 2\text{ mol NH}_3$$
Hence, the equilibrium yield of NH₃ increases.
working:
Reactant side: $4$ mol gaseous species; product side: $2$ mol.\nIncreasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward fewer gas moles: $\text{NH}_3$ yield increases.

Independent check: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas moles: 2 mol NH₃ versus 4 mol reactants. Thus NH₃ yield increases.
distractor_notes: B: Higher temperature shifts an exothermic equilibrium toward reactants.\nC: Adding inert gas at constant volume does not change the reacting gases' partial pressures.\nD: A catalyst changes the rate, not the equilibrium composition.

brief: Give log(x/m) vs log P data/plot; extract the slope and intercept, state what slope = 1 means, and interpret adsorption behaviour — includes a subtle point about saturation limiting the isotherm.
stem: For the Freundlich isotherm, $\log\dfrac{x}{m}=\log k+\dfrac{1}{n}\log P$. Common-log data give $(\log P,\log(x/m))=(0,-1)$ and $(1,0)$. Which interpretation is correct?
options: $n=1$, $k=0.1$, and $\dfrac{x}{m}=0.1P$; the model predicts a finite saturation plateau at high $P$.
$n=1$, $k=10$, and $\dfrac{x}{m}=10P$; the model has no finite saturation plateau and must fail at sufficiently high $P$.
$n=1$, $k=0.1$, and $\dfrac{x}{m}=0.1P$; the model has no finite saturation plateau and must fail at sufficiently high $P$.
solution:
The slope is $1/n$, and the intercept is $\log k$:
$$\frac{1}{n}=\frac{0-(-1)}{1-0}=1,\qquad \log k=-1$$
Hence $n=1$, $k=0.1$, so $\dfrac{x}{m}=0.1P$. The Freundlich isotherm has no finite saturation plateau and must fail at sufficiently high $P$.
working:
$\text{slope}=\dfrac{0-(-1)}{1-0}=1=\dfrac{1}{n}\Rightarrow n=1$
$\text{intercept}=\log k=-1\Rightarrow k=0.1$
$\dfrac{x}{m}=0.1P$; Freundlich does not include a saturation limit.

Independent check: The slope is 1/n = (0 - (-1))/(1 - 0) = 1, so n = 1. The intercept is log k = -1, so k = 0.1. Thus x/m = 0.1P, which has no finite saturation plateau.
distractor_notes: B: Treats $\log k=-1$ as $k=10$. C: Incorrectly assigns a saturation plateau to the Freundlich model. D: Inverts the pressure dependence.

brief: Compare de Broglie wavelength of an electron vs an alpha particle accelerated through the same potential difference (or same kinetic energy); derive the ratio from mass and charge.
stem: An electron and an α-particle are accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. Take $m_\alpha=4m_p$, $m_p=1836m_e$, and their charges as $e$ and $2e$, respectively. Neglect relativistic effects. What is $\lambda_e: \lambda_\alpha$?
solution:
For a particle accelerated through potential difference $V$, $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2mqV}$.
$$\frac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_\alpha}=\sqrt{\frac{m_\alpha(2e)}{m_e e}}=\sqrt{8\times1836}=12\sqrt{102}$$
Hence, $\lambda_e: \lambda_\alpha=12\sqrt{102}:1$. (B)
working:
$\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$
$\dfrac{\lambda_e}{\lambda_\alpha}=\sqrt{\dfrac{m_\alpha(2e)}{m_e e}}=\sqrt{8\times1836}$
$\sqrt{14688}=12\sqrt{102}$

Independent check: For the same potential difference, \(\lambda=h/\sqrt{2mqV}\). Thus \(\lambda_e/\lambda_\alpha=\sqrt{m_\alpha(2e)/(m_e e)}=\sqrt{14688}=12\sqrt{102}.\)
distractor_notes: A: Takes the reciprocal ratio. B: Omits the factor of $2$ in the α-particle charge. D: Uses $4e$ instead of $2e$ for the α-particle charge.

brief: Which statements about Hess's law / state functions / enthalpy being path independent are correct; simple true-false style multi-statement option.
stem: Consider the statements: (I) Enthalpy is a state function. (II) The enthalpy change is independent of the path. (III) Hess's law follows from this. (IV) Heat is a state function. Which are correct?
solution: Enthalpy is a state function, so $[?]$
working:
Enthalpy is a state function, so $\Delta H$ depends only on the initial and final states.\nHess's law follows; heat $q$ is path-dependent.\nCorrect: I, II and III.

Independent check: Enthalpy is a state function, so its change depends only on initial and final states; Hess’s law follows. Heat is path-dependent, not a state function.
distractor_notes:
A: Omits the consequence of path independence, Hess's law.
C: Incorrectly treats heat as a state function and omits I and III.
D: Incorrectly treats heat as a state function.

brief: Rank given ligands (CN−, F−, H2O, I−) by crystal field splitting strength using the spectrochemical series; straightforward ordering.
stem: Arrange the ligands in increasing order of crystal field splitting strength: $\text{I}^-$, $\text{F}^-$, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{CN}^-$.
solution:
According to the spectrochemical series, ligand field splitting strength increases in the order
$$\text{I}^- < \text{F}^- < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{CN}^-$$
working:
Spectrochemical series: $\text{I}^- < \text{F}^- < \text{H}_2\text{O} < \text{CN}^-$.

Independent check: From the spectrochemical series, the splitting strength increases as I⁻ < F⁻ < H₂O < CN⁻.
distractor_notes:
B: Reverses the relative strengths of iodide and fluoride.
C: Places water above fluoride.
D: Reverses the overall weak-to-strong ordering.

brief: In a spinel-like or NaCl-type arrangement, determine the fraction of octahedral voids occupied or the formula of the compound given occupancy.
stem: Anions $\text{X}^-$ form a cubic close-packed array. If $\text{M}^{2+}$ ions occupy half the octahedral voids, what is the formula of the solid?
solution:
For $N$ close-packed $\text{X}^-$ ions, the number of octahedral voids is $N$; half occupied gives $N/2$ $\text{M}^{2+}$ ions.
Thus, $n(\text{M}):n(\text{X})=N/2:N=1:2$, so the formula is $\text{MX}_2$.
working:
For $N$ close-packed anions, there are $N$ octahedral voids.\nOccupied voids $=N/2$, so $n(\text{M}):n(\text{X})=N/2:N=1:2$.\nFormula: $\text{MX}_2$.

Independent check: For N X⁻ ions in a cubic close-packed array, there are N octahedral voids. Half are occupied, so there are N/2 M²⁺ ions. The ratio M:X is 1:2.
distractor_notes:
A: Assumes all octahedral voids are occupied.
C: Reverses the cation-to-anion ratio.
D: Uses an incorrect void-occupancy ratio.

brief: Rank C–O bond lengths / bond orders in species like CO, CO2, CO3^2−, HCOOH using resonance structures and formal bond order counting.
stem: Arrange the indicated C–O bonds in increasing order of bond length: in $\text{CO}$, $\text{CO}_2$, $\text{HCOO}^-$ and $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$.
solution:
Bond length decreases as bond order increases. The average C–O bond orders are $3$ in CO, $2$ in CO₂, $1.5$ in HCOO⁻ and $4/3$ in CO₃²⁻.
Hence, in increasing order of bond length: $\text{CO} < \text{CO}_2 < \text{HCOO}^- < \text{CO}_3^{2-}$.
working:
Average C–O bond orders: $\text{CO}=3$, $\text{CO}_2=2$, $\text{HCOO}^-=1.5$, $\text{CO}_3^{2-}=4/3$.\nBond length increases as bond order decreases.\nThus: $\text{CO} < \text{CO}_2 < \text{HCOO}^- < \text{CO}_3^{2-}$.

Independent check: Bond orders decrease in the sequence CO (3), CO₂ (2), HCOO⁻ (1.5 average), CO₃²⁻ (4/3 average); lower bond order corresponds to greater bond length.
distractor_notes:
B: Reverses the relative bond lengths of CO and CO₂.
C: Reverses the relative bond lengths of formate and carbonate.
D: Orders the species largely by bond length in the opposite direction.

brief: Draw an alkene (figure, e.g., a cyclic diene) and ask for the dicarbonyl product(s) after ozonolysis with Zn/H2O; requires identifying both cleavage sites.
stem: The compound shown in the figure is subjected to ozonolysis followed by reductive work-up with Zn/H$_2$O. Which products are formed?
options: One molecule each of ethanedial and butane-1,4-dial
solution:
Reductive ozonolysis cleaves both C=C bonds, converting each alkene carbon into a carbonyl group. Cleavage of the ring gives two identical three-carbon fragments:
$$\text{C}_1=\text{C}_2-\text{C}_3-\text{C}_4=\text{C}_5-\text{C}_6-\text{C}_1 \xrightarrow[\text{Zn}/\text{H}_2\text{O}]{\text{O}_3} 2\,\text{OHC-CH}_2\text{-CHO}$$
Thus, two molecules of propane-1,3-dial are formed.
working:
$\text{C}_1=\text{C}_2-\text{C}_3-\text{C}_4=\text{C}_5-\text{C}_6-\text{C}_1$
$\xrightarrow[\text{Zn}/\text{H}_2\text{O}]{\text{O}_3}2\,\text{OHC-CH}_2\text{-CHO}$

Independent check: Reductive ozonolysis cleaves both C=C bonds. Each cleavage opens the ring into two three-carbon fragments, each OHC–CH₂–CHO (propane-1,3-dial).
distractor_notes: A: Treats the diene as if only one double bond were cleaved. C: Uses the fragments expected from a 1,3-cyclohexadiene. D: Gives only one of the two identical products.

brief: For PCl5 ⇌ PCl3 + Cl2 at given total pressure and α, set up ICE table and compute Kp; single-equation numerical.
stem: For the equilibrium $\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g)+\text{Cl}_2(g)$, the degree of dissociation is $0.5$ at a total pressure of $2$ atm. Find $K_p$.
solution:
For initial $1$ mol, equilibrium moles are $1-\alpha,\alpha,\alpha$, with total $1+\alpha$.
$$K_p=\frac{p_{\text{PCl}_3}p_{\text{Cl}_2}}{p_{\text{PCl}_5}}=\frac{\alpha^2P}{1-\alpha^2}=\frac{(0.5)^2(2)}{1-(0.5)^2}=\frac{2}{3}\text{ atm}$$
working:
Initially $1$ mol: equilibrium moles are $1-\alpha,\alpha,\alpha$; total $1+\alpha$.\n$p_{\text{PCl}_5}=\dfrac{1-\alpha}{1+\alpha}P$, $p_{\text{PCl}_3}=p_{\text{Cl}_2}=\dfrac{\alpha}{1+\alpha}P$.\n$K_p=\dfrac{p_{\text{PCl}_3}p_{\text{Cl}_2}}{p_{\text{PCl}_5}}=\dfrac{\alpha^2P}{1-\alpha^2}=\dfrac{(0.5)^2(2)}{1-(0.5)^2}=\dfrac{2}{3}$ atm.

Independent check: Starting with 1 mol PCl₅, α = 0.5 gives equilibrium amounts 0.5 mol PCl₅, 0.5 mol PCl₃, and 0.5 mol Cl₂. Each has partial pressure 2/3 atm, so Kₚ = (2/3)(2/3)/(2/3) = 2/3 atm.
distractor_notes: A: Omits a factor of 2 in the pressure expression; C: Uses $K_p=\alpha^2P/(1-\alpha)$; D: Uses $K_p=\alpha P/(1-\alpha^2)$.

brief: Rank acidity of terminal alkyne vs alkene vs alkane, or identify which alkynyl anion forms with NaNH2; conceptual comparison with reagent recognition.
stem: Arrange these compounds in decreasing order of acidity: ethyne, ethene and ethane.
solution:
Greater $s$-character stabilises the conjugate base: $sp > sp^2 > sp^3$.
Thus, the acidity order is ethyne $>$ ethene $>$ ethane, giving (C).
working:
Greater $s$-character stabilises the conjugate base: $sp > sp^2 > sp^3$.\nThus acidity: ethyne $>$ ethene $>$ ethane.

Independent check: Acidity increases as pKa decreases: ethyne (pKa ≈ 25) > ethene (≈ 44) > ethane (≈ 50).
distractor_notes: B: Reverses the acidity trend; C: Places the $sp^2$ compound above the $sp$ compound; D: Places the $sp^3$ compound above the $sp^2$ compound.

brief: Rank a set of given radicals (benzylic, allylic, tertiary, methyl) by stability; straightforward compare-and-rank with resonance reasoning.
stem: Arrange the following free radicals in decreasing order of stability: benzyl, allyl, tert-butyl and methyl.
solution:
Resonance stabilisation makes benzylic and allylic radicals more stable; benzyl has greater delocalisation. Among alkyl radicals, stability increases with substitution due to hyperconjugation.
$$\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2^\cdot > \text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2^\cdot > (\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}^\cdot > \text{CH}_3^\cdot$$
working:
Benzylic and allylic radicals are resonance-stabilised; benzyl has greater delocalisation.\nAmong alkyl radicals, stability increases with substitution: $3^\circ > 1^\circ > \text{methyl}$.\nOrder: benzyl $>$ allyl $>$ tert-butyl $>$ methyl.

Independent check: Benzyl and allyl radicals are resonance-stabilized, with benzyl more stable; tert-butyl is more stable than methyl due to hyperconjugation. Thus benzyl > allyl > tert-butyl > methyl.
distractor_notes: B: Reverses the relative stability of benzyl and allyl; C: Puts the tertiary radical above resonance-stabilised radicals; D: Puts the tertiary radical above the allyl radical.

brief: Evaluate statements on NH3, PH3, AsH3 regarding thermal stability, reducing character and bond angle trends down the group; pick the correct combination.
stem: Consider the following statements about Group 15 hydrides: I. Thermal stability follows $\text{NH}_3>\text{PH}_3>\text{AsH}_3$. II. Reducing character follows $\text{NH}_3>\text{PH}_3>\text{AsH}_3$. III. Bond angle follows $\text{NH}_3>\text{PH}_3>\text{AsH}_3$. Which statements are correct?
solution: Thermal stability decreases down Group 15, so $\text{NH}_3>\text{PH}_3>\text{AsH}_3$; I is true. Reducing character increases down the group, making II false, while bond angle decreases down the group, so III is true. Hence, I and III only.
working:
Thermal stability decreases down the group: $\text{NH}_3>\text{PH}_3>\text{AsH}_3$. Reducing character increases down the group, so II is false. Bond angle decreases down the group: $\text{NH}_3>\text{PH}_3>\text{AsH}_3$. Hence I and III only.

Independent check: Thermal stability decreases down the group, so I is true. Reducing character increases down the group, so II is false. Bond angle decreases from NH₃ to AsH₃, so III is true.
distractor_notes: A: misses the correct bond-angle trend; B: treats the reducing-character trend as correct; D: includes false statement II and omits true statement I.

brief: Identify which hydride is ionic / which reacts with water liberating H2; simple classification of NaH, CH4, HCl type species.
stem: Which hydride is ionic and liberates hydrogen gas when it reacts with water?
solution:
Ionic hydrides react with water to liberate hydrogen gas. For sodium hydride,
$$\text{NaH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{NaOH}+\text{H}_2\uparrow$$
Hence, $\text{NaH}$ is the required hydride.
working:
$\text{NaH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{NaOH}+\text{H}_2\uparrow$

Independent check: NaH is an ionic hydride and reacts with water: NaH + H₂O → NaOH + H₂.
distractor_notes: B: Methane is a covalent hydride; C: Hydrogen chloride is covalent and does not liberate hydrogen with water; D: Ammonia is a covalent hydride.

brief: Match/use of artificial sweeteners (aspartame, sucralose, alitame, saccharin) — identify the sweetener usable by a phenylketonuria patient or match sweetener to property/use.
stem: Which artificial sweetener should be avoided by a person with phenylketonuria because digestion can release phenylalanine?
solution: Aspartame contains phenylalanine and releases it on digestion. Therefore, it should be avoided by people with phenylketonuria.
working:
Aspartame is a methyl ester of a dipeptide that contains phenylalanine. Its digestion releases phenylalanine, so it should be avoided in phenylketonuria.

Independent check: Aspartame is metabolized to release phenylalanine, so it should be avoided in phenylketonuria.
distractor_notes: B: confuses a chlorinated sugar sweetener with the phenylalanine-containing one; C: selects another peptide-based sweetener; D: selects a sulfonimide sweetener without phenylalanine.

brief: Compare change in conductivity and molar conductivity with dilution for strong vs weak electrolyte; pick the correct trend explanation.
stem: On dilution, how do conductivity and molar conductivity change for strong and weak electrolytes?
options: Conductivity decreases for both; molar conductivity increases slightly for a strong electrolyte and sharply for a weak one.
Conductivity increases for both; molar conductivity increases slightly for a strong electrolyte and sharply for a weak one.
Conductivity decreases for both; molar conductivity increases sharply for a strong electrolyte and slightly for a weak one.
Conductivity decreases for both; molar conductivity decreases for both.
solution: On dilution, the number of ions per unit volume decreases, so conductivity decreases for both electrolytes. Since $\Lambda_m=\dfrac{\kappa}{c}$, molar conductivity increases slightly for strong electrolytes and sharply for weak electrolytes due to increased ionisation.
working:
On dilution, fewer ions occupy a unit volume, so conductivity decreases for both.
$\Lambda_m=\dfrac{\kappa}{c}$ increases on dilution.
The increase is modest for strong electrolytes and pronounced for weak electrolytes due to increased ionisation.

Independent check: On dilution, conductivity decreases for both electrolytes because there are fewer ions per unit volume. Molar conductivity increases slightly for strong electrolytes and sharply for weak electrolytes due to increased ionization.
distractor_notes: B: assumes conductivity rises as the solution is diluted. C: reverses the relative size of the molar-conductivity increase. D: assumes molar conductivity decreases on dilution.

brief: Given percentage composition of an organic compound and molar mass, find the molecular formula; simple ratio simplification to empirical formula.
stem: An organic compound contains $41.4\%$ carbon, $3.4\%$ hydrogen and $55.2\%$ oxygen. If its molar mass is $58\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, find its molecular formula. Use atomic masses C = 12, H = 1 and O = 16.
solution:
For $100\,\text{g}$, the mole ratio is $\frac{41.4}{12}:\frac{3.4}{1}:\frac{55.2}{16}=1:1:1$, so the empirical formula is $\text{CHO}$ (molar mass $29\,\text{g mol}^{-1}$).
$$n=\frac{58}{29}=2,\qquad \text{Molecular formula}=(\text{CHO})_2=\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2.$$
working:
For $100$ g: $n_C=\dfrac{41.4}{12}=3.45$, $n_H=3.4$, $n_O=\dfrac{55.2}{16}=3.45$.
Ratio $C:H:O=1:1:1$; empirical formula $=\text{CHO}$.
Empirical formula mass $=29$; multiplier $=\dfrac{58}{29}=2$.
Molecular formula $=\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_2$.

Independent check: For 100 g: C:H:O = 41.4/12 : 3.4/1 : 55.2/16 ≈ 1:1:1, so the empirical formula is CHO (29 g mol⁻¹). The multiplier is 58/29 = 2, giving C₂H₂O₂.
distractor_notes: A: gives the empirical formula instead of the molecular formula. C: assigns too many hydrogen atoms. D: uses a multiplier of four instead of two.

subtopic: Active to Passive Voice – present perfect/continuous tenses
brief: Ask the student to pick the correct passive transformation of a present perfect sentence (e.g., 'has completed'); distractors with wrong auxiliary or participle forms.
stem: Change the voice: The research team has submitted the final report to the director.
options: The final report has been submitted to the director by the research team.
The final report have been submitted to the director by the research team.
The final report has submitted to the director by the research team.
The final report had been submitted to the director by the research team.
solution: Present perfect active changes to passive as $has/have + been + past participle$. Since “report” is singular, the passive form is “has been submitted.”
working:
Present perfect passive: has/have + been + past participle. “Report” is singular, so use “has been submitted.”

Independent check: Present perfect active (“has submitted”) becomes present perfect passive (“has been submitted”).
distractor_notes: B uses a plural auxiliary with a singular subject. C omits “been” and leaves the active-form verb. D changes the tense to past perfect.

subtopic: Sentence rearrangement (PQRS) – argumentative paragraph with fixed first and last sentences
brief: Give a fixed opening and closing sentence on an abstract topic (e.g., technology and society) with four jumbled middle sentences P–Q–R–S that must be ordered using pronoun and connector clues; hard because of subtle linkages.
stem:
Arrange the four sentences P, Q, R and S between the fixed opening and closing sentences to form a coherent paragraph.

**Opening:** Digital tools can widen access to public knowledge, but access alone does not make a society better informed.

**Middle sentences:**
P. This apparent abundance, however, can obscure the difference between information that is merely available and evidence that has been carefully tested.
Q. The latter requires institutions that explain how claims are checked, corrected and placed in context.
R. Without such institutions, users may mistake repetition for confirmation, especially when a claim is repeated across several platforms.
S. For this reason, expanding access must be accompanied by habits and institutions that help people judge what they encounter.

**Closing:** A well-informed society therefore depends not only on the circulation of knowledge, but also on the means to assess it.

Which is the correct sequence?
solution: P contrasts available information with carefully tested evidence. Q explains what the latter requires, and R shows the risk when those institutions are absent. S then draws the conclusion: access must be paired with ways to judge information.
working:
P introduces the distinction between available information and tested evidence; “the latter” in Q refers to tested evidence. R’s “such institutions” refers to Q, and S’s “For this reason” draws the conclusion. Hence P–Q–R–S.

Independent check: P follows the opening by referring to the abundance of information. Q explains what carefully tested evidence requires; R describes what happens without those institutions; S draws the resulting conclusion.
distractor_notes: B: “The latter” in Q has no preceding distinction. C: R refers to institutions introduced in Q. D: S draws a conclusion before R supplies the supporting consequence.
critic_notes: [minor] P opens with "This apparent abundance", which has no antecedent in the fixed opening sentence (it speaks only of widened access, not abundance), so add a reference to the volume of information available in the opening line.

brief: Sentence with a collective/indefinite subject (e.g., 'each of the players') where the verb disagrees; one part contains the error, other parts are clean.
stem: Find the part of the sentence that contains an error. **(A)** Each of the applicants **(B)** have submitted the required documents **(C)** before the stated deadline **(D)** without any reminder.
solution: “Each” takes a singular verb, so “have submitted” should be “has submitted.” The error is in part (B).
working:
“Each” takes a singular verb: “Each of the applicants has submitted.” The error is in (B).

Independent check: “Each” is singular, so “have submitted” should be “has submitted.” The error is in part (B).
distractor_notes: A contains the correctly formed subject phrase. C is grammatically correct. D is grammatically correct.

brief: Blank for the correct preposition in a fixed expression (e.g., 'comply ___', 'preface ___'); distractors are common near-miss prepositions.
stem: The chairperson asked the members to refrain ___ making personal remarks during the discussion.
solution: The verb “refrain” takes the preposition “from” followed by a gerund: “refrain from making.”
working:
The fixed expression is “refrain from” + gerund: “refrain from making.”

Independent check: The standard construction is “refrain from” + gerund: “refrain from making.”
distractor_notes: B is not used with “refrain” in this expression. C is not used with “refrain” in this expression. D is not used with “refrain” in this expression.

subtopic: Sentence rearrangement – identify the first sentence
brief: Four jumbled short sentences of a simple narrative/event; the student must identify which sentence logically opens the passage (e.g., the one introducing the setting/person without pronoun reference).
stem:
Four sentences from a short passage are given below. Which sentence should come first?
1. At dawn, Mira arrived at the village railway station carrying a small parcel.
2. She handed it to the stationmaster, who promised to keep it safe.
3. He placed it in the locked office.
4. By noon, she had returned to collect it.
solution: Sentence 1 introduces Mira, the village station and the parcel. The other sentences refer back to these details, while “He” in sentence 3 refers to the stationmaster introduced in sentence 2.
working:
Sentence 1 introduces Mira, the station and the parcel. Sentences 2 and 4 refer to Mira and the parcel; sentence 3 begins with “He,” referring to the stationmaster introduced in sentence 2.

Independent check: Sentence 1 introduces Mira and the parcel; the other sentences refer back to them.
distractor_notes: B: “She” and “it” lack antecedents. C: “He” and “it” lack antecedents. D: “she” and “it” lack antecedents.

brief: Sentence using a future tense in a 'when/after/until' clause incorrectly (e.g., 'when he will arrive'); student must choose the corrected simple-present version.
stem: Choose the correct replacement for the underlined part of the sentence: We will begin the inspection <u>after the supervisor will arrive</u>.
options: after the supervisor has been arriving
solution: In a future time clause introduced by “after,” use the simple present: “after the supervisor arrives.”
working:
In a future time clause introduced by “after,” use the simple present: “after the supervisor arrives.”

Independent check: In a future time clause beginning with “after,” use the present simple: “after the supervisor arrives.”
distractor_notes: B uses past tense; C uses an unsuitable continuous form; D retains the future tense error.

brief: Sentence testing gerund form after a preposition (e.g., 'insisted on going'); design it so the sentence is actually correct – 'No error' is the right option, with distractor parts tempting misidentification.
stem:
Find the part of the sentence which contains an error.

(A) The manager objected
(B) to changing the schedule
(C) without consulting the team.
(D) No error
solution: “Objected to” is followed by the gerund “changing,” and “without consulting” is also grammatically correct. The sentence contains no error.
working:
In “objected to changing,” “to” is a preposition and correctly takes the gerund “changing.” “Without consulting” is also correct; neither phrase contains an error.

Independent check: “Objected to” is correctly followed by the gerund “changing”; the sentence has no grammatical error.
distractor_notes: A: The subject and verb are correctly used. B: “To” is a preposition here, so the gerund is correct. C: “Without” correctly takes the gerund “consulting.”

brief: Fill the blank in an everyday sentence with the correct phrasal verb (e.g., 'call off / call up / call for') based on context meaning.
stem: The organisers had to ______ the outdoor concert because of the heavy rain.
solution: “Put off” means to postpone, which fits delaying the outdoor concert because of heavy rain.
working:
“Put off” means postpone, which fits the cancellation of the concert due to rain.

Independent check: “Put off” means postpone, which fits cancelling or delaying the concert due to heavy rain.
distractor_notes: B means accommodate or tolerate; C means extinguish; D means connect by telephone.

brief: Give a moderately common descriptive adjective (e.g., 'arduous') in a short context sentence; options are near-synonyms, only one precise match.
stem: After the long journey, the usually <u>gregarious</u> traveller welcomed the company of fellow passengers. Choose the word closest in meaning to the underlined adjective.
solution: “Gregarious” means fond of the company of others; the closest meaning is “sociable.”
working:
“Gregarious” means fond of the company of others; “sociable” is the precise match.

Independent check: “Gregarious” means sociable or fond of company. The closest option is (A).
distractor_notes: B describes a tendency to speak a lot; C means polite; D means lively or vigorous.

brief: Single-blank sentence where the surrounding context (e.g., 'despite his illness, he remained ___') fixes the meaning; four plausible adjectives, one fits.
stem: Despite the repeated setbacks, the team remained _____ and continued working towards its goal.
solution: “Despite the repeated setbacks” shows the team remained determined; <u>resolute</u> means determined. Indifferent means unconcerned, hesitant means uncertain, and careless means inattentive.
working:
The team continued despite setbacks, so it was resolute (determined). Indifferent means unconcerned; hesitant means uncertain; careless means inattentive.

Independent check: “Despite the repeated setbacks” suggests the team remained determined; “resolute” means determined.
distractor_notes: B suggests lack of concern; C suggests reluctance; D suggests lack of care.

brief: Ask for the antonym of a straightforward abstract word (e.g., 'frugal' or 'candid'); options include a wrong-direction synonym as a trap.
stem: Choose the word opposite in meaning to **scarcity**.
solution: Scarcity means a lack or shortage; its opposite, abundance, means a plentiful supply.
working:
Scarcity means a lack or insufficiency; abundance means a plentiful supply. The other options indicate lack or insufficiency.

Independent check: “Scarcity” means a shortage; its opposite is “abundance.”
distractor_notes: B, C and D all suggest a lack or insufficiency rather than its opposite.

brief: Analogy pair such as 'Benevolent : Kind :: ? : ?' where the student picks the pair with the same synonym-intensity or degree relationship; distractors shift the relationship type.
stem: Annoyed : Furious :: Pleased : _____
solution: “Furious” is a stronger degree of annoyance; similarly, “delighted” is a stronger degree of pleasure.
working:
Furious is a stronger degree of annoyance; delighted is a stronger degree of pleasure. Grateful, calm and surprised describe different states, not intensified pleasure.

Independent check: Furious is a stronger degree of annoyance; delighted is a stronger degree of pleasure.
distractor_notes: B is appreciation; C is a calm state; D is a reaction to the unexpected.
critic_notes: [minor] The item is a word analogy (Annoyed : Furious :: Pleased : ___), not sentence completion, so the stem instruction/tag should be corrected to "Choose the word that completes the analogy".

brief: Give an action verb (e.g., 'embellish' or 'mitigate') in a one-line context and ask for the closest meaning from four options; distractors are loosely related but imprecise.
stem: The new measures were introduced to mitigate the effects of the drought. What does **mitigate** mean?
solution: To mitigate something is to make it less severe or harmful; therefore, it means to **lessen**.
working:
To mitigate effects is to make them less severe. Predict means foresee; record means document; prolong means make last longer.

Independent check: “Mitigate” means to make something less severe; therefore, it means “lessen.”
distractor_notes: B means foresee; C means document; D means extend.

stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Urban trees are often valued for their appearance, but their contribution to city life is also practical. A tree’s canopy shades pavements and buildings, reducing the amount of heat absorbed during the day. Leaves also release water vapour, which can cool nearby air. Together, these effects may make tree-lined streets more comfortable during hot weather and reduce the need for air-conditioning in some buildings.

Trees can also help manage rainwater. Their leaves and branches intercept some rainfall, while roots and the surrounding soil allow more water to soak into the ground. This can slow the flow of water into drains during heavy showers. However, trees are not a complete solution to urban flooding: soil conditions, drainage design, and the intensity of rainfall also matter.

The benefits of urban trees depend on thoughtful planning. Species must be suited to local conditions, and young trees need care as they become established. Planting decisions should also consider where shade is most needed and whether roots may interfere with pavements or underground services. A city therefore gains more than decoration by maintaining trees, but it cannot rely on planting alone to solve every environmental problem. Trees are most effective when they form part of a wider approach to designing healthy, resilient neighbourhoods.

What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Urban trees can eliminate the need for effective drainage systems.
Urban trees provide useful benefits, but require planning and support.
Cities should choose tree species mainly for their visual appearance.
Urban trees are beneficial only during periods of hot weather.
solution: The passage explains that urban trees provide shade and help manage rainwater, but their benefits depend on careful planning and support. Thus, they are useful but not a complete solution to environmental problems.
working: The passage describes trees’ benefits for shade and rainwater, then emphasizes that careful planning is needed and trees cannot solve every problem alone.
distractor_notes: B mistakes a partial aid to drainage for a complete replacement. C contradicts the emphasis on practical benefits and local suitability. D overlooks benefits related to rainwater and neighbourhood resilience.

stem: According to the passage, how can trees help manage rainwater?
options: Their leaves and branches intercept rain, while roots help water soak into soil.
Their roots direct rainfall quickly into city drains during heavy showers.
Their canopies prevent rain from reaching pavements and underground services.
Their leaves absorb all rainfall before it can contribute to urban flooding.
solution: Leaves and branches intercept some rainfall, while roots and surrounding soil help water soak into the ground.
working: The passage states that leaves and branches intercept some rainfall and roots and surrounding soil allow more water to soak into the ground.
distractor_notes: B reverses the stated effect of roots and soil. C overstates what canopies do and misrepresents the concern about roots. D changes “some rainfall” into all rainfall.

brief: Short family description; ask how many members are male or how many cousins a named person has.
stem: A family consists of a father, a mother, two married sons and an unmarried daughter. Each son has two children: one has two daughters, and the other has a son and a daughter. How many male members are there?
solution:
The male members are the father, the two sons, and the one grandson.
Thus, the total number of male members is $1+2+1=4$. $(A)$
working:
Male members: father + two sons + one grandson = 4.

Independent check: Male members: father (1) + two sons (2) + one grandson (1) = 4.
distractor_notes: A: omits one son or the father. C: counts a female child as male. D: counts both daughters as male.

brief: Four word pairs where three share a hidden relationship (e.g., product-place or worker-tool); pick the pair that breaks the pattern.
stem: Among the following word pairs, three share a relationship. Identify the pair that does not belong.
solution: Bread, cheese and paper are made at a bakery, dairy and mill, respectively. A loom is a tool used to weave cloth, not a place where it is made.
working:
Bread, cheese and paper are products associated with places where they are made: a bakery, dairy and mill. A loom is equipment used to make cloth, not a place.

Independent check: Bread, cheese, and paper are made at a bakery, dairy, and mill, respectively. A loom is a tool used to weave cloth, not a place where it is made.
distractor_notes: A: Bakery is where bread is made. C: Dairy is where cheese is made. D: A mill is where paper is made.
